•era;;,-twor SW., Was tOie rr, STMIC orignuy as she put Nettle's chain into her hand. "I shall be home as soOn as possiblei"- she said., "and I shall be ready for supper, I'm sure. I've had nothing but that piece of bread and butter since twelve o'clock this morning." • The evening was an espekially trying one, Lord Billy being slighly inebriated as well as morosely uncivil.. On their final exit, 'however, he appeared to wake out of his apathy, and with 4 brutal aria. suddenly put out a splay- toot, and_deliberately• treading on the gauzy 'train of he' • white gown, caused a rent of a _yard wide, and then stazzerad unsteadily away, with his-bullet-head sunk between hunchy shoulders, which shook with ill- suppressed merriment. There were tears of rage and mortification in Violet's eyes, and she bit 'her lips in the effort te control herself as her companions of the dressing- sown offered their insincere sympathy, the while their eyes danced with mischievous enjoyment of ker discomfiture.

The girl was not popular; she was considered proud and exclusive. Moreover, she had ' more than once shewn her contempt for the open court that. was paid to Lord Billy, and that she should stiffer some humiliation at his hands was by no means disagreeable to her lady companions. "Well, darling, you'll have to sew that up, anyway," one of them remarked. "It is a shame! It loots almost as if he did it on purpose, too. It'll ravel all the way down, if you don't. catch it together, dear, at any rate." One by one they quitted the cold, barn-like, evils smelling dressing-room, but Violet still struggled to repair„ the serious injuries in her pretty new gown cauSed by the callous man's impertinence. The light was bad, and her tired eyes smarted. Her fingers, too, weie cold, and shook with weari- ness and chilling mortification, and yet she was aware any complaint against Mr. Lennox would he ignored. It was more. than suspected he had paid for the position be occupied in the company, and his explanation that the occurrence was accidental would undoubtedly be accepted at once. - "It's degrading," she murmured, the tears rising in her eyes. "It is such men as he who lower the tone of the stage. "Thank goodness that's done at last," she cried, rising and making pre- parations for leaving. "Oh. what a comfort it is I came across Mrs. Smith. I'll fix my thoughts on her and on that kitchen fire. I'm nearly famished. I hope they'll give me my supper by that fire. I'm sure I shall not mind Mr. Smith. I prefer Nature's noblemen to the other sort, taking Mr. Lennox as a type of his: class." She was hastily putting on her sailor hat, when the caretaker knocked at. the door to ask if he might put out the lights. "It's nearly half-past. eleven, miss, and I wants to get home," he grumbled. "Don't you live here ?-" she inquired, thrusting her arms into her ulster. "No, this theatre ain't often used, and I don't live on the premises. Look sharp, please, miss." Buttoning up her coat as she went, the girl left the room, and 4roping her way through the passage went out into the street..

The cold had increased, and now, instead of rain, snow was falling heavily. She was still putting up her umbrella when the caretaker came out, and locking the door strode off quickly. In a minute he disappeared round a corner, and Vie;let found herself alone in the long, deserted High-street. Not a gleam of light sbewed in any of the windows. Even the taverns had closed half an hour before. But in the distance two bright lamps indicated the situation of the one respectable Hotel of S .

"What a wretched place," she muttered. "Oh, dear! how thankful I shall be to get to my bed to- night. Well, I've had a Jong day of it. I was up at six this morning, packing." Facing the wind she walked a few steps, and then, with a sharp exclamation of actual dread, she came to an abrupt stop, and staggering on her feet giddily, tottered to the wall and leant up against it, while her cheeks grew suddenly of an ashen whiteness, and her lips began to quiver .con- vulsively.

"Oh, no, no," she murmured, piteously. "it would be too horriLle. How could I have been so completely idiotic'? But I was so rushed and so afraid of being late, Good Heavens! What shall Idoif I can't recognise the street ? But I won't think of that, I won't think of anything s truly awful."

- The clock in the Town Hall was striking twelve, when once more Violet Merlon emerged into the desolate High-street. Her month was haggard, and in her distended eyes was a feverish gleam. She walked stiffly and slowly, and her boots were ali-iody soaked with the icy shish of thawed snow.

"I must go to the hotel," she muttered, thickly ; "there is no help for it. I have-no money, but I can pay in the morning. I couldn't drag myself to the station, and very likely they don't keep open all night: Oh, those terrible, lonely, dark streets, with no ray of light from any window to give one courage." The door of the hotel was being closed as the girl stumbled up the steps, and the waiter regarded her with an air of open suspicion as, hoarse with apprehension, she asked whether she could be accommodated 'with a bedroom and supper. "Well, I don't know," he said, rudely.- "We don't take in promiscuous ladies without luggage at this time of night." _
"I am a member of the company at the theatre," she faltered. _ _
"Ph! Then how is it you didn't Come sooner?"

"1-bav-e7CiU-ne-a. ;el:3; 'foolish thing," the poor girl explained, striving vainly to appear calm. "I secured lodgings this afternoon, but I came away from them without taking the address, and I cannot recognise the street • they are so exactly alike. I only know the landlady is a; Mrs. Smith."
`cOlt, really ! Quite an uncommon name that !" the man replied; with an open• sneer. "And you say you are one of the ladies at the theatre?"

"1 am," the girl answered, faintly. • • With a shrug of the shoulders he went away, and in a moment returned,. flowed by Mrs. Lennox, obviously in an advanced sta7,e of intoxication. "Do you know this ere lydy, my lord ?" the waiter asked.

The young fellow lifted his sodden eyes to the agitated face, and then, with an evil smile, he drawled slowly and indistinctly: "No, waiter, I've not the pleasure of the lady's acquaintance. " • L. The girl shrank away, but she had not the strength to expo3tulate, and in another minute the door was closed upon her, and the lights ex- tinguished. _
Then, standing at tbe bottom of the steps, Violet Merion clung to the railings. "My God !" she moaned. "I shall die. There is no one to help me. •• I cannot feel the ground, my feet are so numbed."

-Faint and exhausted, her brain reeling and her sight dimmed, she staggered .aimlessly . forward a few steps, and then from the back she received a sudden shock ; something seemed to spring upon her, and with a stifled scream she fell ou her face and lost consciousness.

On recovering her senses, Violet Merlon found herself lying on a mattress before the splendid fire in Mrs. Smith's kitchen. Pressed up against her side, quivering with anxiety, his head in her nerveless hand, was Nettle, and bending over. her Mrs. Smith, and also a grave-faced Ulan in a blue uniform.

"Thank God. miss," the woman cried, "you've come to. Smith said as it was only a faint. I isms for sending for a doctor. It. was that dear, blessed dog who found ypu. He was howling over you fit to raise the dead .when Smith come up to you. He'd given us the slip, bless his heart, and Smith was after him ; and well he did, for but for hhn you might have lain there for hours and caught your death. Now, then, here's some hot soup and some brandy, and then straight off to a warm bed you go. Smith, he picked you up and carried you home right enough." Violet was only a little the worse the next day, and she often said afterwards that her wretched experience was something of a blessing in disguise, for Mr. Lennox never dacl to sinew his face again ln the theatre.

There must be a unanimity of feel- ing between the magistrates and the Corporation and he now asked them the simple question, would they complete the bargain entered into between his clients and the Corporation or would they put the town to a, loss of £2,500? Mr. Halton was as high a class of land- lord as it was possible to bring before a court and there was little doubt that he would conduct the new house in the same capable manner in which he had conducted the old house. The very fact that Messrs. Walker would be the owners of the house was in itself a sufficient guarantee that the house would be conducted properly. Mr. Cuthbert Smith said he opposed the application on behalf of several property owners, the members of the congregation of the Gospel Hall which was situated very close to the proposed hotel, and the members of a Wesleyan Young Men's Club. Mr. W. Roberts: Your's is not a teetotal opposition then? Mr. Smith: It is not.

Mr. Roberts: lam very glad to hear it. Mr. Smith: I was going to say with regard to the charge made against me that:mine is a teetotal opposition directed by improper motives of property owners, that it is nothing of the kind. It is an opposition absolutely and solely in the interests of the neighbourhood gener- ally, and in the intere,sts of those who are trying to carry on a work there, which, they said, must be injured if for the benefit of the Corporation or Messrs. Walker house is to be quartered there in the way suggested. Before a licence could be granted, he continued, the premises must be, in the opinion of the licensing author- ity, structurally fitted for the class of licence for which a certificate was sought. Were the premises in ques- tion at the present moment when a man could go in and begin selling liquor, structurally fitted for the purpose. Further, were they, in the words of the Act, "a fit and convenient house for the purpose of being kept and opened as an inn"? He had had the advantage of viewing the premises that morning, and he thought that if the justices would do the same it would be absolutely impossible for them, however necessary they might think the licence was, as honest men to say that the building was structurally fit for the purpose or a fit and convenient place to be used as an inn. A little low-roomed place, with rooms not 9 feet high,the largest room 14 feet by 13, and the smallest 13ft. 9in. by 10ft. 3in.—it was absurd to say that such premises were structurally fit. He thanked Mr. Knowles for the very candid way in which he had brought the question before the Bench. He said" Will you as a Bench carry out what your Council haveagreed to—will you carry out the bargain ?" He (Mr. Smith) never before heard such an argument addressed to judges. Their worships had nothing whatever to do with the Council of the Borough. They were not there, as his friend rather suggested, as the nominees of the Council. div.head: VIOLET MERTON'S DILEMMA
div.p: VIOLET MERTON'S DILEMMA
By MARY H. TENNYSON,
Author of "The Old Church Clock," "Let-me- look-at-the-tongue," "A Sinless Sinner," "A Cruel Dilemma," &c.
it was a raw-cold November afternoon, and the prospect from the station at S- seemed to Violet 11ferion about the most digtnal she had ever looked upon.

The station was a mile out of the town, and as the dusk had already fallen, she could see before her nothing but a straight, insufficiently-lighted road, covered with a cindery black dust. The girl was slight and elegant, and her face was unusually refined and charming, but the quiet- ness of her costume was almost severe; her long, dark-grey ulster and thickly-veiled black-ribboned sailor hat, being relieved by no fleck of colour. In her left hand she carried an inconveniently heavy hand-bag, her umbrella hangilig on her wrist, and in her right was a substiintial dog- chain, which was wound tightly and painfully round her glove, that she might the better control the irrepressible spirits of the vigorous fox-terrier, who, at the sight of the road, plunged and reared wildly in his ineffectual efforts to get free, after the tedium of the long protracted journey, which had lasted from eight o'clock in the morning.

But although her delicate hand was bruised with the rough chain, Violet knew from dearly-bought experience,, that with a search for lodgings before her in a strange town, to let Nettle free for an instant would be the height of madness. Once she had done so, and he had darted off dn.his own pleasures intent, and she had lost him for over an hour, and to lose Nettle would be an unbearable misfortune. For, although Violet Merion travelled in a theatrical troupe in which there were three other ladies as well as the star actress whom they all supported. it could not be said she had any friend among them, and but for the companionship of her affectionate but disobedient terrier she would have been lonely indeed.'

But although as a rule Violet put up, with an almost philosophical calmness of mind, with the numerous discomforts incidental to her position, this particular afternoon she was thoroughly' depressed, and more than a little angry. Two unpleasant incidents had occurred during the tedious journey, ' and at the recollection of them the girl's cheeks flushed hotly, and the short,well- eut upper lip curled with ineffable disdain. The company included among its members the eldest son of an earl—on the bills known as Mr. Lennox—a frivolous and innately unrefined young fellow, consumed with vanity, and utterly incapable from a histrionic point of view. But the noble lord, being the possessor of some thousands a year, his incapacity was no hindrance to his entering the profession. Nor did his meanness of character, and blatant self-conceit, render him unpopular in the society he was thrown amongst; for a man who could stand unlimited drinks and cigars, even although his generous impulses were very few and far between, might be sure that his shortcomings would be regarded very indulgently. Violet :Merlon, however,, had an intense dislike for the young lordling, who, by what she con- sidered quite a cruel decree of Fate, was cast to enact her lover in every piece in the repertoire, and on that journey matters had come to a crisis between them.

Going into the refreshment buffet at one of the stations, she had encountered the obnoxious young aristocrat, at the moment engaged in a violent flirtation with the attendant who served him with the champagne he was gulping down. Seeing Violet, he had conic up to her with insolent familiarity, and, hooking his arm in hers, bad drawn her towards the counter.
Enraged and disgusted the girl shook herself free, and, without a word, hastening from the saloon, had taken refuge among the other ladies in the train.

Thither the irate Mr. Lennox followed her, and thrusting his heavy,- foolish face into the carriage window, declared she had insulted him by cutting him, and that he would find a means of repaying her.

His tone was brutal, and Cie dog, concealed by his mistress's rug, uttered a sharp growl. At this Mr. Lennox's coarse lips broadened into a smile, and with a laugh he slouched away. A minute after the guard appeared. "The dog's ticket, please ?" _ _

Nettle I.ld no tiolieL For months he had been smuggled in and out of the train, and the officials, always indulgent in such cases, had shut their eyes. But in this instawte they were bound to act, and Violet, with trembling lips, and flashing eyes, made no protest, although, havinc, paid fifteen shillings for Nettle's ticket, she had only a solitary topper left in her purse. "That was Lord Billy's way of paying you, dear," the soubrette of the company laughed. "I saw him speak to the guard. My word! I shouldn't like to be in that young man's bad books. My advice is keep friends with him." "I'll never speak to hint again," Violet cried. "He's a cad! A disgrace to his class and his profession." The other ladies drew down their lips ; the girl's tone was distinctly offensive to them. They said no more, however, contenting themselves with com- pletely ignoring her for the remainder of the journey. It happened all the others were married women, and for once a sense of forlornness came over Violet as she saw them leave-the station in little groups, each couple sharing the load of rugs and bags, which was all the luggage they had brought, as they were only to remain in the small town for two nights. The star and her husband had driven off in' a carriage sent by a friend in the neighbourhood, whose guests they were to be, and Violet was quite alone and uncared for, when at last she started down the road towards the town.
Nettle tugged and made desperate darts forward, and she chid him angrily. But presently 'her heart smote her, and then putting down her heavy ham she stopped a minute and patted his smooth head.

"You couldn't help it, Nettle," she murmured; "it wasn't your fitult, old fellow. But he's a hateful wretch! I haven't a farthing of change now; only that five-pound note at the bottom of the bag. Oh, I'm tired and miserable. I dread my work to-night with that horror. Good Heavens! five o'clock! And I must be at theetheatre at half- past six and no lodgings!" For an hour the girl tramped up and down, but nowhere could she find a room. The last theatrical company had left the town without paying, and at the first mention of the theatre doors had been shut in her face in every direction. It had begun to rain, too. She had no band to hold up an umbrella, and her arms shook with the weight of the bag, and the incessant pulling of the unruly dog.
--; ~ At last, ovith a groan of ater wearines-s, she stopped in the middle of a poor street, the counter- part, it seemed to her, of a dozen others she had already searched. a
"I must try the hotel," she muttered. "I've only half an hour now, but perhaps they wouldn't take Nettle."

At this moment a door opened, and. a cheery- faced woman came Out On the step. "You don't know of any respectable lodgings about here. I suppose ? " Violet faltered, trying to keep the moisture out of her anxious eyes. The woman glanced quickly at the sensitive, tired face. The unspoken appeal in the eyes went to her heart at once, and five minutes later the girl sank into a chair before a splendid kitchen fire and burst into tears. _ _

"There, there," the other said, "(het cry, miss, it'll be all right now. Of course you can have my girl's room, and welcome. She's gone up to London for a week's sight-seeing, and Ir look after the dog for you. Come, now, you drink a cup of hot .tea, and you shall have a good slipper when you come home. Mr. Smith, that's may husband, won't be home till eleven ; he works late at the railway. I'll walk with you to the thntre to shew you the v:ly, so that you'll know how to come back. These streets are so much alike, they confuse strangers."
- Violet had but time to swallow the tea and refresh herself by a wash, before it was incutnbeni. on her to start again. But the woman's kindness had cheered her :and when she uarted from, her at.

A young servant at 13autzen, girl in Saxony, has been sentenced to six months' imprisonment "for having spoken disrespectfully of the general character of the officers of the local garrison." FAILURES IN ENGLAND AND WALES.—According to "Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, November 4th, was 209, viz :New Bankruptcy proceedings published in the London Gazette,ll2; deedsof arrangement registered, 97. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were: Bank- ruptcies, 88 ; deeds of arrangement, 83; total, 173; being a net increase in bankruptcies of 260, and a net ncrease in deeds of arrangement in 1904, to date, of 454.

div.head: GEORGE HOTEL LICENCE.
div.p: THE GEORGE HOTEL LICENCE.
CORPORATION BARGAIN NOT COMPLETED. ---- Application for Transfer Refused.

The Warrington Licensing Bench were on Monday asked to complete the bargain made by the Corpora- tion with Messrs. P. Walker and Sons, for the sale of the licence of the George Hotel, and they in unmistak- able fashion declined to do so by refusing to grant an application for the transfer of the licence to another part of the town. The magistrates present to bear the application were Mr. E. J. Guest (in the chair), Aldermen Hutchinson, Francomb, Smethurst, and Bennett, Councillors Wilkinson, Tinnion and. J. Roberts, and Messrs. T. Birchall, H. Thornton, L. W. Reynolds, E. Woods, S. Wright, J. W. Hayward, S. Wright, W. 1 Roberts and A. J. Jolley, and Dr. Fox. The applica- tion for the transfer was made by Mr. T. Halton' the present licencee, who was represented by Mr. J. W. Knowles. • Opposition was offered by two licence holders, represented by Mr. A. Browne, and the trustees and congregation of the Gospel .Hall Mission, the Bewsey Road Wesl6ran Young Men's Club, and a number of property holders in the neighbourhood in which it was proposed the licence should be placed, who were represented by Mr. Cuthbert Smith (in- structed by Mr. T. S. Steel). • A MAGISTRATE OBJECTED TO.

At the outset Mr. A. Browne objected to magistrates sitting on the Bench who hadtaken part in the prelimin- ari negotiations between the Corporation and Messrs.P. Walker and Sons, quoting a case in support of his objection in which an appeal against a decision by the Sunderland Justices was upheld on the ground that magistrates had heard the original application and also taken part in the preliminary negotiations. He did not desire to be invidious and mention names but there were gentlemen on the Bench who had taken part in the pre- liminary negotiations which had led up to the applica- tion that morning. Mr. Knowles admitted the right of Mr. Browne's contention and said the objection applied equally to those gentlemen who had opposed the sale of the linenc3 as well as to those who had supported it. Mr. Guest: That means every member of the Corporation? Mr. Knowles: Only thoge members who took an active part in the matter. • Mr. Browne: Only those members of the Corporation who voted upon the matter are debarred from sitting on the Bench during the hearing of this application. Mr. Cuthbert Smith: I understand that only one

knocking a hole through th 3 dividing wall and running a counter through them ? Mr. Halton: That has been done as a temporary arrangement. Mr. Smith: Wonld not the view of the police be obstructed by the dividing wall? Mr. Hilton: Yes, t'aough they would only be pre- vented from seeing one .spot. Mr. Browne: Da you seriously say that the house is ,fit for the carrying on of a public-house business? Mr. lialtba : Yes.

Mr. Stanley Wilson (deputy Town Clerk) : Only one gentleman is affected and that gentleman is Mr. Coun- cillor Roberts. He is the only magistrate who voted on the matter in the Council chamber. Councillor Roberts then left the Bench. THE CASE FOR THE APPLICANT.

Mr. Knowles then proceeded with his application explaining at the outset that although the Hotel held by Mr. Halton was commonly - known as the ' "George" its correct title was the "George and Dragon." Mr. Halton applied that the licence should be transferred to a site at the corner of Dudley-street and Earle-street, a site well I subjected to police supervision. Mr. Knowles then proceeded to explain the negotiations between the Cor- poration and Messrs. P. Walker and Sons for the sale of the license for £2.550, adding that Messrs. Walker agreed to purchase it for that sum conditionally upon the magistrates ranting the transfer of the licence from its present site to premises to be selected by them Messrs. Walker). Mr. Knowles further explained that Messrs. Walker practically made the application, they haying bought the licence, though Mr. Halton would act in the capacity of their tenant. With regard to the site selected he ventured to think that both from a brewers point of view and from the public point of view a better site could not possibly have been pitched upon. The nearest possible place where drink of any description was sold was 183 yards away in Longford-street. and consisted of a grocer's license. Within a quarter mile radius there were only two licensed houses, one being fully licensed and the other an off licence. The opposition to the application raised by the two gentle- men represented by Mr. Browne was perfectly natural, as they desired to have all the trade.. The property owners who objected did so because Messrs. Walker had not purchased the particular property owned by them. In spite of that opposition he hoped to show that the license was necessary. Since 1893 within a quarter mile i radius 1,083 new houses had been:built, and the popula- tion had increased by 5,712, In the triangle formed by Orford-lane, Longford-street, and Winwick-road alone the population had increased since 1893 by 3.1242 reckoning 525 persons for every house built since that year. While there had been that large increase in the population during the same period there had not been the slightest increase in the drinking facilities of the neighbourhood. With regard to the price offered for the . licence they knew the rates of the borough were high and that any sum of money going into the Corporation exchequer for the benefit of the rates must be advantageous. His client had offered a fabulous price for that licence—it must be!alabilows price as it MIS over £l,OOO higher than the price offered by anyone else—and that offer had been accepted by the Corporation. The Corporation were an elected body who represented the views of the rate- payers and they felt it would be of advantage that the slllll offered by Messrs. Walker should be accepted. Their worships must feel the same and not say" We will refuse £2,550," in face of 'the constant grumbling at the high rates, and also in face of the Corporation's
The Chief Constable : The proposed premises are composed of tmo six rooca)1 cottages anl. a corner shop? Mr. Halton : • Yes.

Mr. Knowles explained that his clients, if the appli- cation was granted, would submit plans for the re-building of the house. In answer to Mr. Knowles, Mr. Halton said he thought the present accommodation MB sulicient. THE EXISTING FACILITIES.

Mr. Garnett, architect, sAid he prepared the plans for the new premises. He was proceeding to give figures as to the number of licensed houses in the district when he was interrupted by the Chief Constable, who placed before the Bench tha figures taken by the police. Within a quarter-mile radius, he said, there were one ale house, one beer house, and seven off-licences, to a popu- lation of 10,500. Within a half-mile radius there were 9 ale houses, 7 beer houses, and 19 off-licences. In answer to the Chief Constable, Mr. Garnett stated that the largest room in the new premises was fourteen feet by thirteen feet. Mr. Smith: How mi.ny new houses have been built since 1900 in this neighbourhood?
Mr. Garnett: I cnnot say. Mr. Smith: Do you know that an off licence wa.s refused for this very house in 1900? Mr. Garnett : Yes. _ _ _

Mr. Garnett in further answer to Mr. Smith, stated that there was no cellar to the proposed house. The beer barrels would be placed in a room' behind the bar. Mr. Smith asked if it was not possible for a person standing sear the centre of the bar to prevent the police seeing the whole length of the bar ? Mr. Garnett re- plied that it was not. Mr. Browne: The district as regards population is practically in the same condition as it was in 1900 when an application for a grocer's licence for these premises was refused? Mr. Garnett: That is so. Mr. Knowles : The application for a grocer's licence was made by the owner of the property. William Appleton, formerly of TO, Dudley-street, now Why

most gracious Alajesty King Edward Vll—not to deal with the matter as between the Corporation,not to carry out bargains they chose to make with licensed victuallers, but to deal as between the general public, sitting to do justice as to whether or not Messrs. Walker were to have the licence in that place. He did not want to use strong language, but it seemed to him that it was an insult to the Bench to ask them to carry out a bargain. He would like the Bench to ask the Chief Constable his opinion as to whethrir the premises were so con- structed as to allow of adequate police supervision. Hr. Knowles said new premises were to be built, but the Bench had nothing to do with that. Had it ever been the custom to allow a big hotel to be built in what was practically a back street ? It was all nonsense to talk about. it being a main thoroughfare. It was not. At the back of the premises was a building for religious worship, called the Gospel Hall. The people there were trying to do a work— Mr. Knowles: With regard to the Gospel Hall, I have instructions that two members of the Committee of Management were in favour of our application. Has my friend a written instruction from the trustees to appear for them, or are the trustees here? If not I am afraid he cannot

Mr. Smith said he was appearing for the members of the congregation and all the trustees except one. The last mentioned was the gentleman who sold the property to Messrs. Walker so they could understand why he did i not object. Continuing Mr. Smith pointed out that there was only a 15ft. passage between the Gospel Hall and the back entrance of the proposed hotel. The con- gregation had passed a resolution strongly protesting against the granting of the transfer. As Christian people, they stated, they considered it would be unjust to erect an hotel next door to a place cif worship where they ventured to think a considerable 'Amount of good work had been done. Further, they were of opinion that the wants of the neighbourhood were more than amply supplied already. A resolution of protest had also been passed by the members of the young men's club in connection with Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church and Silver-street schools—whose premises were very near the proposed hotel—and they stated that they were unanimously of opinion that the granting of a licence would be exceedingly harmful to the best interests of the Association. Continuing, Mr. Smith said it was clear from the evidence that there had been little increase of building in the neighbourhood since the year MO, when the justices unanimously refused to grant an off-licence for the same premises and another house close to. There were within the half-mile radius 35 licences so that he contended the wants of the neigh- bourhood were well supplied. It would be a hardship on the district t 3 have a house opened there whether the inhabitants liked it or not. in the event of the transfer beinir refused there would be no hardship on Messrs. Walkr, because their arrangement with the Corporation did not bind them to pay a farthing unless their worships sanctioned the transfer. Mr. Knowles • PIUW I U Miutt EMIT BUNS By using Eiffel Tower Bun Flour the most in- experienced person can make light Buns and Cakes with certain success. Try a Id. Pkt

' said the Bench ,were to carry out the bargain because if they did not, the rates would lose the amount of Messrs. Walker's offer. The capital account might, but even that did not necessarily follow. Messrs. Walker could find other sites where they could erect their house without any difficulty to anybody, and where it would be required. "But for goodness sake " said Mr. Smith "merely for the sake of saving the Corporation £2,500 and giving Messrs. Walker a licensed house, don't give them a right to put it down in a place where it is not required." What was £2,500 to a rich Corporation, as compared with the harm that might be done? The Bench must bear in mind that the Licensing Act would soon be in operation, and if the application was granted now Messrs. Walker would be In a better position in regard to compensation. Whatever Was said by Mr. Halton as one of their fellow townsmen it was, to say the least of it, an extraordinary thing that notice was given to the authorities that Mr. Halton was going to apply for a transfer of the licence to a barman at the time that the present application was being made. That, he submitted, was not treating the Bench in a candid way. Mr. Browne desired to emphasise the point that Messrs. Walker were trying to make the Bench a Court of Appeal on the 1900 jastices. He would also point out that the magistrates had nothing to do with the Corporation. They were there as individual justices acting in their individual capacity, to say whether the licence was required or not. They were not legally bound to take into con- sideration whether the Corporation had made a good bargain or not. In about seven weeks the new Licens .ing Act would come into operation, and he submitted that Messrs. Walker were coming in a hurry to make that application before they were compelled to fulfil certain conditions imposed by the Act. If a majority of the justices were in favour of the application, he asked them in the interests of his clients, who depended upon the off-licences for their living, to adjourn the application or to refuse it till the new Act came in force. They would thenhave full power to act far better than they had to-day.

div.head: WIT*ESSES CALLED.
div.p: WIT*ESSES CALLED.

John Taylor, senior trustee of the Gospel Hall, said he was present at both services on Sunday when the resolution of protest was passed. The congregation in the evening numbered about 400. fr. Smith had been instructed on behalf of all the trustees except one. The licence, he considered, would materially interfere with the work the Gospel Hall was carrying on. He did not know who drafted the resolution. In answer to Mr. Knowles witness said he knew the George Hotel adjoined Trinity Church. Mr. Knowles: Do you know that the support of the sign-post of the hotel is against the church on one side and th'e hotel on the other, and therehas never been any complaint, by the church-people as to the conduct of the house?

The Rev. R. Wilkinq Rees produced a copy of the resolution passed by the members of the Wesleyan Young Men's Club. The front of the club premises was exactly opposite the main back entrance of the pro- posed hotel. Witness thought the granting of the transfer would be detrimental to the work of the Association. _ _

Mr. Green, one of the trustees of the Gospel Hall, denied the suggestion made by Mr. Knowles during the hearing that he expressed himself in favour of selling the hall to Messrs. Walker if they would build a new one. _
Mr. Knowles : Do you deny that you told Mr. Peacock it would be a good idea to sell the place and build a hall somewhere else, where it would be more convenient?
Witness: I said if Messrs. Walker had a right to put the place there they had a moral right to buy us out and get another site. THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S VIEW.

The Chief Constable informed the Bench that although he considered the premises in their present state unsuit- able for hotel purposes, he. did not object to them on the ground of police supervision. APPLICATION REFUSED.
After a few minutes consultation the magistrates decided to refuse the transfer.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Buckley-Street P.S.A.

There was a large attendance at an open meeting of the above.society which was held on Sunday. Mr. W. Beswick presided, and the speaker, Mr. Wynne-Jones, gave an address on " Purity, sympathy, ambition." Miss Miller was the soloist, and rendered "Sunshine and shadow" very effectively. Miss M. Plinston acted as accompanist. _ _

div.head: 'Baptist Missionary Anniversary.
div.p: 'Baptist Missionary Anniversary.

The annual missionary sermons in connection with the Warrington and District Baptist Union were preached on Sunday by the Rev. G. A. Smith, a missionary at Kbarar, India. In the morning he occupied the pulpit at the Latchford Blptist Church, in the afternoon at the Golborne street Baptist church, and in the evening at Hill CR& Baptist Church. The collections were in aid of the Missionary Society. On Thursday evening a public meeting was held in the Latchford Baptist Church. On account of the inclemency of the weather there was only a small attendance over which Councillor Ellison presided. An interesting address upon the religious beliefs of the Lilchs was delivered by the Rev. G. A. Smith.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

The usual meeting of the above was held on Sunday last, when there was a fair attendance. Mr. NV. H. J. Jenkins presided, and dwelt upon the great need of united effort, from a Catholic spirit of all sections of Christ's church. He cared not what denomination men belonged to, if they were sincerely trying to do good. The great desire to benefit man could not do less than glorify God. The work of the P.S.A., was to benefit the man, the home, the family and the State. Mr. C. Fooks of Manchester was the speaker, and took as his subject, "Cricket." The 3 wickets he named were purity, love and temperance. The centre wicket was Love. As batsmen we should have to be very careful as we had tremendous bowlers against us who wo.ad send the middle wicket down, and destroy our love, and all things lovable about us. Look well said he, to our temperance in all things, or we should be bowled out. Then purity of life, speech and habits,we should do well to watch, and be regular stonewallers. Mr. J. Owen and Mr. Eccles took part in the meeting. Master Pearce rendered an organ solo. Mr. Payton. Mus. Bac. pre- sided at the organ. The secretary reminded the brethren that the late secretary Mr. T. Wallington, had the day nefore lost the partner of his life by death. A vote of sympathy and condolence was passed to him and his daughters in this hour of their great trial. Five new members joined and received the usual welcome.

div.head: ANNUAL TEA MEETING.
div.p: ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

On Monday night, the annual Tea Meeting took place in Wycliffe Hall and Memorial Buildings. The table was laid at 7 p.m. prompt, when 200 sat down to an excellent tea. The following ladies presided at the tables: Mrs. J. Atkinson, Mrs. R. Atkinson, Mrs. B. Farrar. Mrs. H. Farrar, Mrs. Hawthorn, Mrs. Newhall, Mrs. G. Colley, Mrs. Yeadon, Mrs. Molyneaux, Mrs. Williams, Mrs. Simeocks, The Misses A. Travis, Sparks, Wells, Forster, Jordan, Hall, Atkinson and Simcocks. After tea the company adjourned to the Memorial Hall, when Councillor J. Evans presided over a crowded meeting. He spoke of the pleasure it gave him to be present, and: to take any part in a work which made better men and happier homes.He was quite satisfied that the P.S.A. was largely helping to lift up the morals of the town. The Rev. R. H. Sewell of Liverpool was the speaker of the evening, and his first appearance in War- rington and his excellent address made a good impres- sion. He based his addre% upon "Obedience and duty." The Apollo Quartette party was present, and greatly delighted the meeting, and was repeatedly re-called. Miss A. Griffiths StIC g "In Old Madrid," Miss J. Farrar rendered a pianoforte solo and Mr. A. Cotterill song two solos in his usual good style and voice.—Mr. Yonge said he was pleased to inform Mr. Sewell that his P.S.A. in Liverool was the parent of this Society.—Mr. Farrar proposed a comprehensive vote of thanks to the Chairman, speaker, Mr. Payton, the artistes, and also to the ladies for providing the tea, and all who had helped to make that meeting so enjoyable. Mr. Healey seconded the vote. Shortly after 9.30 one of the best meetings ever held in connec- tion with the P.S.A. was brought to a close. The society's roll now stands at 552, and new members are being enrolled every Sunday.

div.head: AMBULANCE COMPETITION. •
div.p: AMBULANCE COMPETITION. •
Crosfield Challenge Shield goes to Nelson.

Eight teams took part in the annual ambulance com- petition for the Crosfleld Challenge Shield, which was held in the Gymnasium on Saturday. There was a fair attendance of spectators and after a close contest the judges. Dr. Thompson, Oldham, Dr. 10. De B. Pam, Barrowford, placed the first three teams as follows: Nelson, 174 points, Warrington, 156 points, Crompton, 132 points. The unplaced teams were Altrincham, Ashton-under-Lyne, Liverpool, Mersey Mission to Seamen and Dalton-in-Purness. At the close of the contest, on the invitation of Captain G. Crosfteld, the teams adjourned to the Patten Arms Hotel where they were entertained ta supper. During the proceedings which followed the supper the health of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons was heartily drunk, a,nd Captain CROSFIELD in responding said his firm would b 3 pleased ta know that the shield which they gave six years ago was stimulating ambulaoe, work lID and down the country. Mr. STUDER said it had given him great pleasure to see that during the last ten or twelve years, the educa- tion of working men of this country had made enormous strides. There was no doubt that one of the most useful branches of that education was ambulance work, and it was a branch that ought to be encouraged in every possible way, and the larger and more important firms at any rate ought to do their best to further the work by giving all assistance in their power. (Applause.) it was with that object that Messrs. Cros- field and Sons, Limited, some five years ago presented the shield. In a sporting country like England there

was nothing that would rouse the interest, the ambition,. and the energy of the working man so much as com- petition, and it was such actions as that of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons that 'did much to further the cause of ambulance work. He hoped the fact of his being one of the officials of Messrs. Crosflold and Sons' firm would not cause them to think that he was biased in this matter; he should just think and say the same, if he were a stranger to the firm. They might perhaps think it strange that the shield had been competed for six times and that the management of the donors had not yet formed a division of the ambulance corps to be able to take part in the competition. There were various reasons for that apparent neglect. Their men had during the last few years started various. pursuits, which occupied a great deal of their time. Of course they played football and cricket, and There was an angling club, and among the more serious kinds of recreation—if he. might call them so—they, cultivated the art of singing and various brass instru- ments: that was, they had a choir and a brass band. Then, since the war in South Africa caused a certain amount of warlike spirit to spread over these islands, they had formed a volunteer corps, and he might say that it had reached a high standard of efficiency. And it was not many years mace a fire-brigade was formed. Such branches of education or recreation took up a great deal of time, particularly during the first few years after their initiation. Now, however, all these institutions were well organised, and had reached such a standard of efficiency that they were able to turn their attention to something else, and the first thing would be the formation of a division of the ambulance corps. (Applause.) They might infer, perhaps, that they had done nothing at all in the way of ambulance work, but such was not the case. Lectures had been given at the works, and the men had been encouraged by example and otherwise, to attend them and make themselves so efficient as to obtain a certificate of the St. John Ambulance Association. As a matter of fact the work was going on before the fornation of either volunteer of fire brigade. He hoped the formation of a division of the ambulance corps would be only a matter of days, or weeks at the most, and that next year they would not only be able to compete with the brigade for the shield, that was being carried away that night by the Nelson Division, but actually be the ones to wrest the trophy from the present holders, thus bring- ifig it back to the place of its birth at least for twelve months. (Applause.) . . .
During ih nterval songs were indulged in until train time, Sergeant HoHord. of the Liverpool Corps, acted as pi anist.

div.head: TRADES COUNCIL AND THE CORPORATION CONTRACTS CLAUSES. Adherance to the Clauses Recently Adopted.
div.p: TRADES COUNCIL AND THE CORPORATION CONTRACTS CLAUSES. Adherance to the Clauses Recently Adopted.

The attitude taken up by the Town Council in regard to the retention of the contract clauses which they recently adopted, gave rise to a len ci discussion at the monthly meeting of the ~,gton Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday. There was a fair attend- ance of delegates at the meeting, which was presided over by Mr. J. Podmore jun. Councillor STorr, secretary of the Trades Council explained that the Town Council had deferred the con- firmation of the contracts clauses adopted by them on his motion, and had appointed a sub—committee to go into the matter and to try to frame contracts clauses which would be acceptable to the whole of the members of the Council, though he doubted whether the sub-committees would be able to agree, seeing they included gentlemen so strongly opposed to each other on the question as were Councillor Maginn and himself. Councillor Stott asked the Trades Council for some instructions as to the minimum which the Trades Council were prepared to accept. He Stott explaised that he had writtere to the candidates at November elections asking them several questions with regard to their views upon the contracts clauses question, and from Councillors Brough, Barton, Wilkinson, Forshaw, Benson, Skellan I, and Clegg he bad received replies which could be regarded by the Trades Council as very favour- able. Councillor Stott recapitulated the arguments previously advanced by him to show the necessity for the retention by the Corporation of the contracts clauses they had adopted, and explained his inability to induce the Corporation to adopt a penalty clause. He desired to put himself right on'one point. At the last meeting of the Council, Councillor Maginn spoke of the employment of girls and he (Councillor Stott)lflippantly said "Let the men keep them." That remark had been taken seriously by the girl workers in the town and he desired to explain that it was not meant seriously. He had no objection to girls working for their living, unless they came into competition with men,, when he contended they should not work for less wages thau were paid to men. •

The- wheelwright's society, through their representa- tives Messrs. Plumb and Eaton, recommended the hold- ing of a public demonstration so as to show the Tov.m Council that they were determined not to give way in their demands.

The majority of the delegates present however thought the holding of a demonstration rather prema- ture and in the end it was decided to leave that ques- tion in the bands of the executive committee. Coun- cillor Stott was instructed that the principles contained in the contracts clauses in dispute were the irreducible minimum which the Trades Council would accept.

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY LABOUR CANDIDATE.
div.p: THE PARLIAMENTARY LABOUR CANDIDATE.

'Hr. BUCKLEY reported that all the labour candidates who were being brought out at the next general election had been placed in constituencies. If any more were brought forward Warrington's claim would be considered. COUNCILLOR WRIGHT AND MR. DODDS.

Mr. BUCKLEY referred to a statement made in the Bewsey Ward bye-election by Mr. James Dodds that "Councillor Wright had satisfied him with regard to non-trading." That statement was rather misleading as it gave people the impression that Councillor Wright had bound himself to support the Non-traders. He had done nothing of the sort. He had not bound himself to support any party in the Council. Some people had gone so far as to say that the Labour Representation Committee was affiliated with the Non-Trading Associa- tion. That also was incorrect. Councillor STorr stated that Oouncillor Wright'S actual words to Mr. Dodds were "I believe it is abso- lutely necessary there should be the highest form of purity in both Local and National Government." That remark,to which anyone and everyone could subscribe had unfortunately been construed by Mr. Dodds to mean that Mr. Wright agreed with the Non-traders.

div.head: SALUTARY PUNISHMENT FOR PERJURY.
div.p: SALUTARY PUNISHMENT FOR PERJURY.
Local Commercial Traveller Sent to

Wood gave evidence that when ne -- business order-book that he was not working on August 29th and It 30th he came to the conclusion that those were the dates on which he was fishing with Vickers. When he discovered his mistake he wrote to the Chief Constable. Prison2r swooned while under cross-examination. Samuel Gough, furniture dealer, Warrington, having given evidence of Wood's previous good character, Mr. W. B. Yates, who defended, urged that Wood had merely made a mistake in dates, and ought to be acquitted. The jury found a verdict of guilty, with a strong recommendation ta mercy on account oi previous good character. The Judge postponed sentence. Woad fainted and had to be carried below. The case against Frank Vickers was then taken. In defending himself against the charge of betting he had given evidence that he had never done any betting on horse racing. He also said he was fishing on August 29 and 30. Evidence has ing been given to disprove both statements, Vickers went into the witness box and said he got the dates of the fishing excursions from Wood, who seemed certain of them. He denied having made any bets on his premises in June, August, or September, and the betting slips that were ound did not represent _transactions on which he had received or parted with any money. The jury found Viakers guilty, but in his case also they made a strong recommendation to mercy. The Judge pastpanpi sentence till Tuesday morning.

div.head: Prison.
div.p: Prison.

The charges of perjury brought against Prank Vickers, a licensed victualler' of Crewe, and Joseph Barrett Wood, a commercial traveller of Warrington and Crewe, were heard at Chester Assizes on Monday. The prisoners were tried separately, and the case against Wood was heard rir 1:3 Mr. R. V. ankes, who conducted the prosecution, said the case was of very considerable public importance, because, frbm the facts, it was perfectly clear that Wood, a man of educa- tion who ought to have Known better went to the Crewe Petty Sessions on the 27th September, and in a most deliberate way committed perjury in order to defend Vickers, landlord of the Engine Inn, Crewe, who was charged with betting on his licensed premises. The days on which the betting was said to have taken place were August 29th and 30th, and Wood gave evidence that on the first day he and Vickers were fishing near Warrington. His report to his firm of his doings that day showed that he had attended Crewe market, and his report for the following day gave fourteen names and addresses under the heading of "Calls." After the i prisoner had given evidence n defence of Vickers he wrote to his employers saying he had made a mistake in the dates. 'hen he found from his

div.head: SENTENCES.
div.p: THE SENTENCES.

Mr. Justice Bray pronounced sentence on Tuesday. He said he was sorry perjury was not an uncommon offence. It was a crime very difficult to bring home, but when it was it must be punished severely. It was a deliberately planned perjury, and the entry in Wood's notebook must have been made deliberately for the purpose of dc zeiving the court. Imre were, however, considerations which weighed inhis favour. It was not done apparently for the purpose of any gain or advan- tage to him. This was not his only punishment, because the prisoner had lost his position and character, which it would be very difficult to recover. He (the Judge) took into consideration the recommendation of the jury to mercy and sentenced Wood to eighte3n months' im- prisonment. Turning to Vickers, the Judge said his was the worse case becauge one could not help coming to the con- clusion that it was at his suggestion that Wood was a party to the perjury. There were not the same con- siderations in his favour that there were in Wood's. It was done to his own advantage and gain or in the hope of gain. Now that it was the law that persons accused could give evidence on their own behalf, it was abso- lutely necessary that perjury, when it was committed, must receive sevtre punishment. There was a recom- mendation to mercy which he would not ignore, but Vickers must go to penal servitude for three years. PETITION FOR REDUCTION OF SENTENCE. The decision of Justice Bray at Cheater Assizes, com- mitting Frank Vickers, Engine Hotel, Crewe, to three years' penal servitude on a charge of perjury,has caused a sensation in Crewe, and a petition to reduce the sin- tence has been drawn up by:Crewe workmen. Vickers was one of the most popular athletes in Cheshire, and had won valuable prizes both on cycle and running tracks. He was the president of the Crewe Haraiers. THE JOY OF A SPOTLESS SKIN. div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The German Wedding.—The marriage of the German Crown Prince is not it seems to take place until the 22nd March next, which will be the one hundred and eight anniversary of the birth of his great grandfather, the Emperor William I. The old Emperor's favourite abode, Babelsberg Castle, near Potsdam, will afterwards be handed over as a summer residence for the Crown Prince and his bride. Meanwhile the thrifty Mocklen- burgers are not overjoyed at the prospect of providing a trousseau for the Duchess Cecile. In Mecklenburg Schwerin it is customary to raise dowries for members of the Grand Ducal family by a special tax. In this case it amounts to sixpence ahead, and is expected to yield £1750 for the bridal outfit. Some of the taxpayers however are protesting that the custom is out of date, and are complaining against compulsion being resort3d to for what ought to be a purely voluntary gift. It would have been much better left to the generosity of the people, as, in such matters,anything like compulsion is odious, especially as the Duke is very wealthy,though Mecklenburg Schwerin is anything but a rich country. Women Bread Snatchers.—Miss Frances Low's view that women of means ought not to work in competition with those in need, cannot be reconciled with socian laws. Apparently Miss Low would exclude womes from such professions as nursing or literature, unlesl it was necessary for them to earn their living, but it is a curious theory tint people must not work if they are wealthy. There are a few well-to-do women who engage in professional nursing for love of the work, whilst there are numbers with literary ambition who write for no pecuniary reward, or are not in need of it. To say that this is wresting the bread from those who have to live by their work, is rather far-fetched, and would be, if acted upon, contrary to all progress of the world. Women as Billiard-Markers.—The newly opened Lyceum Club for women has engaged a lady expert for itsbilliaxi room, and it is suggested that this opens up a new occupation :for women—they should become billiard-markers. There is however nothing new in this supposed innovation, as many of the ladies' clubs have for years employed women billiard-markers. There is perhaps no more reason why girls should not become billiard-markers thanjbarmaids, but the profession of billiard-marking is generally looked upon a»: filled by those who have failed at every other calling, honest or otherwise, and it is therefore just as well that girls should avoid it, except it be in the respectable atmos- phere of the high class ladies' club. The Question of Knee Breeches.—A ladies' journal says that it rests with woman to decide whether men shall or shall not wear knee breeches instead of trousersl It thereforelinvitesiits readers to advance arguments for and against the change, offering prizes to the writer of the most effective discourse from either point of view. The " mere man " may ,therefore stand aside whilst hel has this momentous question settled for him, but whether he will pay any attention to it, is another matter. A return to the old style would certainly avoid the habit which trousers have,fof becoming baggy at the knees, but Queen Elizabeth, long before there were such things as trousers, used to complain that her laws and rulings were, like men's clothes, straight at the first, but wore loose with time. Probably if it really rested with women, trousers would be abolished, if for no other reason than that the great majority of men—and it is only very few who keep a valet—leave their muddy trousers at home to be brushed by the maid, or anybody else who will undertake the job. • Christmas Gifts to send Abroad.—Many of the new afternoon and evening blouses make very useful and inexpensive Christmas presents to send abroad. These may be had in fascinating variety 3.. t those shops which make such garments a speciality and where the selec- tion of dainty silk, lace, net, and crepe de chine blouses is a truly wonderful one. For half-a-guinea one may secure a really very dressy evening blouse, and for half that sum a pretty afternoon one, such as will give a new lease of life to a skirt that might otherwise be said to have seen its best days. The nun's veiling varieties, and also well-fitting and smart looking shirts of this material, may be had for a few shillings, and very pretty they look showing openwork designs, and faint lines of colour about the throat, wrists and front. The choice of finding something suitable is never a very difficult one, and s uch a gift is always appreciated by our girl friends abroad. Floral Trimmings.—Flowers are being largely worn with evening toilettes, and appear in full clusters and trails, at the shoulders, and waist, and about the skirt of almost all ball gowns. They are also employed to give a pretty set off to the coiffure.and of course match when worn in the hair and on the dress. Roses are perhaps first favourites, but marguerites, lilies of the valley, Iceland poppies, geraniums,. pelargoniums, and Parma violets, figure very largely in floral trimmings. All are exquisite imitations of .Nature, especially those which come from Paris, where the artificial flower trade is almost hereditary, one generation learning it from another, and thus attaining the highest perfection of skill. _

Fur Trimmed Headgear.—The entire fur toque is con- spicuous by its absence, but milliners are by no means dispensing with fur, many of their new felts being freely adorned with the most expensive varieties. Con- trary to what one might expect this headgear is not heavy to wear, a state of affairs probably due to the fact that only real, and light-weight furs are selected by the milliners, and that no other trimming, save a twist of tulle about the crown, or a chiffon lining to the brim, is permitted. Imitation fur is not to be thought ot for a moment in connection with millinery. Modish Footgear.—The latest idea in footgear is,that the upper part of it should match the costume with which it is worn, the lower being goloshed by black patent. Leading tailors and dressmakers send on to their customers' bootmaker, a pattern of the fabric, of which the new toilette is to be built, and this he matches in suede, which comprises the upper part of the boot or shoe. The notion is a somewhat costly one, but those women who can afford to patronise it, should not fail to do so.

Milk and Disease.—Few things are so important in the household as a pure and wholesome milk supply,and the verdict in a recent action at law against a dairy Co., will do good in making dealers more careful to insure the purity of the article they supply to the public. The connection between milk and disease has been traced, times out of number, and in this case led to the death of a customer from typhoid fever. In the action which followed, the result as it stands would fix upon all dealers a heavy responsibility to see to the reliability of their milk. Of late years much more attention has been given to this subject, as regards the connection between milk and disease, and also its influence upon the national physique, as being the chief article of food for infants. As a result there has been a great improve- ment in the quality and purity of the general milk supplies, but precautions are not always taken, and for this reason, the verdict in question will be welcomed by the public as making it to the dealer's own interest to ensure absolute purity. Cats must be kept under Proper Control.--Hitherto the domestic cat has been regarded in the eyes of the law as "a wild animal" but a recent decision in one of tlie London Courts quite alters that, and makes owners responsible for any damage or mischief caused by their pets. Formerly pussy had a legal right to go and scratch up one's, neighbour's bulbs to her heart's content, and the unfortunate garden lover had no remedy. Now however he can sue for damages, just the same as if the mischief was caused by a dog "not under proper control." Obviously, this opens up a rather alarming state of things for the lonely widows and spinsters, who devote their lives to the keeping of a dozen or more feline companions. There will not be much more peace for them in this world, especially if the neigh- bours are also entitled to claim compensation for disturbed rest, owing to the "night-bowlers" being at large. MADGE.

If (says a correspondent of the "Times ") it be the case that the contract for wheels and axles for India has gone to Germany the blame rests with the British tyre and axle makers, who lately combined together to raise their prices.
The Examiner, Saturday, November 12, 1904.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TODAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TODAY.
Ribbon has this season taken a more portant part in the modistic world and realm of millinery that. has been granted to

for some time. -Beautiful wide chine or thick. ribbed silk ribbons are used to make up the sashes used on evening frocks of young giris and debutantes, and these are for the most part patterned in a floral design on a light ground. Sometimes a narrower width is. made up into a smart wide bow arranged across the front of the coiffure, if the hair is dressed high, ttid just above the knot at the back when it v: irn low. The effect is charming, es- :daily when a note of contrast is used is colourings of the ribbon to the rest of the toilette. For instance a black gown will be iyuich improved by a sash, and bow in the hair, of cerise or yellow, according to the com- plexion of the wearer, while a white dress looks very chic with the touches of black or coloured velvet at the waist and in the hair.

div.head: PICTURE HAT.
div.p: A PICTURE HAT.

These little trifles can be made up at home by any girl with a little taste and the odd yards or ribbon purchased for a trifle at the recent summer sales can .be employed profitably in the construction thereof. Narrow ribbons are also used run in rows round the dainty evening skirts of net or tulle or formed into rt,tches which are employed in a hundred and one different ways.

Satin ribbons-, or those which are velvet on one side and satin on the other, arc made up into thick ruches round the crown of the wide low-crowned hats which are so very fashionable this season. Feathers, of course, and particularly ostrich feathers, are much in vogue, and my first illustration shows a charming. picture hat of felt trimmed solely by a irery long and handsome ostrich plume. Of course a feather such as this is expensive, but it is quite worth while saving up for as it always makes a simple but good-looking t, miming for a hat and can transform one which is really inexpensive into the appearance of a model worth three or four guineas. With care a good ostrich feather will wear a long time and after being cleaned and curled will. look as good as new. A good felt is also a safe investment for an economical girl, especially one of the silky, long-haired style, as for a trifling charge, it can be re-modelled

A COMFORTABLE COAT. into this season's shape. "' There are Many pretty shapes this year for one to pick and choose and there should, therefore, be no difficulty in selecting a really becoming one. There are the close-fitting marquise hats, which do not need much trimming, and the wide brimmed hat of picturesque design which demands soft • curling feathers to make it a success. There are some of the all feather hats and toques worn and these look particularly pretty in 'white or grey with a gull's head and wings at the front arranged to lie backwards very little higher than the crown itself. •

Fur toques are also much worn and look well with a fur coat of any description. A cosy coat forms the subject of my second sketch, and is of a style which is altogether delightful in the depth of winter. In this instance tac coat itself is of black caracule witn a wide collar and narrow cuffs of ermine and is therefore a costly one. There are some cloths, however, which closely resemble caraeule and can be purchased by the yard and made up with the aid of a good dressmaker at home for a quarter of the cost of the real skin. A good thick quilted lining is required as the woven material is not, of course, so warm as the real fur. There are also charm- ing plushettes of different colours and makes which imitate various furs in a marvellous manner, but, as I said, these all require a good thick lining cf either wadded land quilted satin or an interlining of a warm flannel.

The three-quarter coat is, of course, a delightfully warm wrap, but there are many .who prefer the short coat set into a band at the waist or the Russian blouse, which, after being caught in by a hand, extends in a panier below the waist.

The pretty evening toilette depicted gives a suggestion for the happy combination of two of last year's gowns employed to form an aifbogether up-to-date. and fashionable dress. AR old lace dress and one of satin having both "seen carefully unpicked and cleaned can be ad-ranged in the fashion illustrated, the satin town forming the underdress and tlie lace being cut out to form panels down the skirt, mud a deep flounce at the hem inlet with -pleating of chiffon, which, of course, must be fresh, and which also 'fors the 'vest down the front of the' bodice. No other new material need be purchased as the lace is used to form the bodice and sleeves with their full flounce, which falls to the wrists. A black gown trimmed with lace arranged .in this manner would look most striking and original and would make a useful evening or dinner dress. The lace should preferably not be pure white but of a creamy tint. In the case of a white underdress being used an ecru lace is, of course, much more effective. while even a black lace on a white gown would only express the newest and latest Parisien 'fashion. A bright crimson rose at the decolletage and a velvet bow to match in the hair would look charming as a contrast to the black and whits. Coguaws.
A PRETTY TOILETTE.

div.head: nth HUIAL Vili TU ZMULAND.
div.p: nth HUIAL Vili TU ZMULAND.

'Pk s week King Edward has been celebrat. oig his birthday at Sandringham in his favourite role of country squire, shooting over his famous preserves and visiting his tenantry. Next week he entertains the King and Queen of Portugal at Windsor Castle, where a great party will be gathered to meet them. Upon the occasion of King Carlos' last visit two years ago it will be remembered that his Consort was unable to accompany him owing to ill health, but this time fortunately she is much better and able to undertake the journey. Their Majesties will be met by the royal yacht at Cherbourg and escorted to Portsmouth by the cruiser squadron under Admiral Sir W. H. Fawkes, and the Home Fleet will be assembled at Spithead to salute them upon their arrival next Monday: The Prince of Wales will meet them on the King's behalf at Ports- mouth. They will be accompanied. by 111.. de Soveral, the Portuguese Al:nister King Edward's great personal friend, and one of Ins birthday guests at Sandringham—and. will proceed straight to Windsor .on the Tuesday afternoon by special train. There they will find the royal borough decorated in their honour, and an address of welcome will be presented by the Mayor and Corporation. On the following day .the royal party will shoot • over Windsor Park, and in the evening' a State banquet will be given in ,St. George's Hall. On Thumlay the King and Queen of Portugal. visit London and are to be enter- tained to luncheon at the Guildhall, where an address will be presented from the City of London. In the evening a. command performance will be given at Windsor by Mr. Bqerbohm Tree and his company from His Majesty's, including Mrs. Tree. The piece selected is "A Man's Shadow." On Saturday Mr. Lewis Waller will also give a command .performance with his Imperial Company, and " Monsieur Beaucaire " will be played with Miss Evelyn Millard as "Lady Mary, Carlisle," and Mr. Waller as the hero. The Vacant days will for the most part be occupied in shooting, and it is well known that King Carlos is one of the finest shots in Europe. The visit will terminate on Mon- day, Novembei 21st, when the King apd Queen of Portugal will proceed to Chats- worth to . visit the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire. After that they will pay a visit •to the Duke and Duchess of Portland at Welbeck, and their stay in England will altogether last about three weeks. The King of Portugal is extremely popular in this country, and their Majesties will be sure of a very hearty welcome wherever they go, and not least of all on their drive to the Guildhall.

div.head: QUEEN OF PORTUGAL.
div.p: QUEEN OF PORTUGAL.

again offered honourable terms of surrender. ;General Stoessel has acquainted the Tsar with his inability to hold out much longer, and it is possible that the authorities at St. Petersburg may order the surrender in view pf this fact to save the brave men within its walls. Despite the general disappointment in Japan, the Emperor's birthday was brilliantly :elebrated in Tokio by a grand full deess review by the Mikado in person, which was followed by a luncheon at which the foreign diplomatists were present. The Mikado him- self gave the toast of the foreign sovereigns and rulers, which was replied to by the Belgian Minister, the doyen of the diplo- matic corps. The Mikado is as popular with his people as King Edward is throughout his Empire and is everywhere received with the utmost enthusiasm. He is now in his fifty- third year and has had the strangest career of any ruling monarch. As a youth he was in Oriental fashion almost a prisoner in his own palace,. when the revolution, headed .by the Marquis Ito, started- the great era Of progiess, which he has led with every effort in his power. To the Mikado is largely due the Europeanisation of Japan and its growth as a first class power. Aided by the F;an- press, he has introdficed modern European' methods throughout the whole of his domin- ions, and the efficient state of the Japanese Army and Navy is the result of his life's work. The Mikado, whose name is Alutsu Hit°. will go down to history as the greatest .of all Japanese rulers and the founder of a new era in his country's national life. In .less than four decades he has achieved results incredible if they were not facts.

div.head: DEATH OF A FAMOUS CRICKETER.
div.p: DEATH OF A FAMOUS CRICKETER.

The sudden death of J. T. Brown, the well- known Yorkshire cricketer e will come as a shock to his many admirers, although he has for some time past not been in the best of health. Only a short time ago an operation was performed, aad it was confidently hoped that he was on the road to corn

plete recovery . He was only _ ----..--- thirty-five year! , - of age, and - ----- should have had -- several y ear s- ,--- ........,,, more good cricket in him. Like many -• other famous ...- ~ batsmen, J. T. _..._ Brown started as a bowler, and his cricket car eer proper be- gan as profes- I sional to the Perth club.
where,he always THE LATE J. T. BROWN. used to say, he

A year later, in xBB9, he first played for York- shire, but bad health retarded him; and it was not till 1893 that he took his place amongst the foremost batsmen of the day. Since then he was always in the first flight, and showed averages of 45 in 1896, 43 in 1897, and 44 in 1899, and in all 25 centuries stand credited to his name. The latter include two mammoth innings, 311 against Sussex in 1897, and 300 against Derby in 1898. In the latter match he, with Tunnicliffe, set up the monster record of 554 for a first wicket partnership. Four years ago in the sensational second innings of the Players at Lord's he scored 163, which is a record for the iirofessionals in the great annual contests. But the greatest day of his life was March 6th, 1895, when he scored iio for Stoddart's team in the second innings and, With the help of Albert Ward, won the test match and rubber for England.

div.head: WEST MONMOUTH ELECTION.
div.p: THE WEST MONMOUTH ELECTION.

The elcction for the vacancy in West Mon- mouth, caused by the death of Sir William Harcourt, ended in a victory for Mr. Tom Richards, the Labour candidate, over Sir John Cockburn, the Tariff Reform candidate. The poll was a very heavy one, fifty per cent. heavier
than in 1900, and the Liberals
increased their
majority by
over a thousand.

Co ckbu-rn's
peculiar pp si- t i op. He pro-
fessed advanced Liberal views on
every pbint, ex-

cept Tariff Re- form, and he was in consequence disowned by the Conservatives at headquarters. He also fell foul Of the Liberals upon his great plank of Tariff Reform and may be said to have fought the first election on that point, and that point only. . Mr. Tom Richards, his successful opponent, is a well-knows name in labour circles. Born in 1859, his educational facilities were limited, and at twelve yeats of age he was working in a colliery. In 1888 he became the miner's agent for the Ebbw Valley Collieries, and his name came into prominence two years later fit connection with the sliding scale agree- ment. Since 1895 Mr. Richards has been a member of the Ebbw Valley District Council, and from 1901 chairman and ex officio a magistrate. He is also a County Councillor for Monmouth, a manager of the Ebbw Vale County School, and was a member of the late Llangat tock School Board.

div.head: LORD MAYOR'S SHOW.
div.p: THE LORD MAYOR'S SHOW.

This week, prior to the visit of the King and Queen of Portugal, London has been eight-seeing as on Wednesday the • annual Lord Mayor's Show was held on the occasion of the installation of Mr. Alderman John Pound at the Mansion House. The new Lord Mayor, who is a fine - looking dignified old man of seventy- five, belongs to the old school of City magnate, and his desire was to revive some of the past glories of the famous show, which has of late years been rather over- shadowed by the numer- ous royal pro- cessions. I n addition to the THE NEW CITY 7.IARSHAI bands a n d

varions customary features there were four allegorical bars on an ambitious scale, representing the four greatest empires in the history of the world. First came Egypt with the God' of the Nile, supported by priests under a canopy with two. sphinxes in front. Next followed Greece represented by a chariot with a column :showing the nine Muses in bas-relief, supported by Apollo .with his lyre and representatives of the arts of Greece. Be- hind it was the car of Rome with the "Columna Rostrata," supporting the statue of Victory, a copy of the one in the Naples Museum, with a group of Roman soldiers, including Julius C:esar, round: the base. Last came the car of Great Britain, with Britannia seated on a throne supported by griffin; bearing the British Ants and liohs crouching. On the steps of the throne were allegorical groups representing Navigation and Commerce, and round the base was a group of representative colonies. It made a fine and impressive show and was warmly, welcomed. Last week the vacant post of City Marshal, about which there has recently been so- much discussion, was filled up prior to the show by the selection of Captain Kearns, the riding master of the Army Service Corps. He was selected from several • hundred candidates for, this orna- mental post, which carries with it a salary of 300 a year and allowances. Captain Kearns, who was a "ranker," may be said to have been born in the Army. .He is forty-three years of age, and has seen active service in the Zulu, Ashanti, and South African cam- paigns. He received his commission in 1896 and was promoted in 1902 to the rank Of captain for special service in the. field. He is a strong teetotaller, and was one of the founders of the Army.
