div.head: MEMORIAL TO FALLEN SOLDIERS. Concert to Aid the Workingmen's Fund.
div.p: MEMORIAL TO FALLEN SOLDIERS. Concert to Aid the Workingmen's Fund.

To worthily honour the memories of the gallant men who fell in the South African campaign is a project which must commend itself to Warringtonians for no town in the kingdom did its share more loyally in send- ing forth troops when necessity arose. As the home of the old Fighting Fortietb, it is only fitting that War- rington should possess a monument to the members of that famous regiment who sacrificed life itself in their country's service, and the efforts which are being put forth to "commemorate the dead" are commendable and deserve generous support. No organization has worked more zealously in furtherance of this object than the Workingmen's Committee comprising representatives of most of the places of industry in Warrington, and through its exertions a handsomesum has been added to the memorial fund. As a final effort an enjoyable con- cert was held in the Parr Hall on Saturday even- ing. The services of numerous well-known local artistes were willingly given, with the result that a programme of exceptional attractiveness was arranged. The members of the committee, aided by energetic and capable officials, worked hard to dispose of tickets' and the public response was gratifying. Although the hall was not quite filled, the assembly was large and appreciative. As an open- ing item the overture "Poet and Peasant" by the band of the Bth and 40th Regimental districts, under the conductorship of Mr. C. Wainwright proved popular, and the general approbation found expression in hearty applause. During the evening the band gave further evidence of its efficiency, and each piece was well received. Corporal Byrne had the honour of an encore for a picollo solo, which was given with marked taste and skill. Interest in the vocal items was increased by the fact that two of the artistes attained such signal successes in leading roles in the recent amateur opera. Miss Arline Harrison's sweet voice found good scope in" Angels guard Thee" and "Scenes that are brightest "but she was heard to the best advantage in the latter item. Mr. J. Rabbit soon established him- self in the favour of the audience and for a stirring and soulful rendering of " Let me like a soldier fall he was vigorously recalled. As an encore piece he was allied with Miss Harrison in a pleasing duet. Mr. i Rabbit did himself equal justice n "River of Dart." A,contribution which was distinctly appropriate to the oena-sion was " Land of hope and glory" and Miss Mary Collin's interpretation was 'effectivel and went with a delightful swing. In the second part of the programme she feelingly gave" Sing ime to sleep." Mr. E. Pownall was happy n his selec- tion of songs, the popular compositions "The Old Brigade" and" Heroes and Gentlemen" rousing the enthusiasm of the assembly. One of the most pleasing features of the concert was Miss Kate Beesley's recita- tion of "The Song of the Forgotten Dead "—the powerful appeal on behalf of the memorial fund penned by Alderman Bennett a short time ago. Miss Beesley's2 exceptional talents as an elocutionist and the merit of the poem itself held the audience spell-bound, as it were, and every point was convincingly brought home. A touching allusion to the late Colonel O'Leary, who fell at Pieter's Hill, evoked applause, and no doubt the recitation would re- sult .in an acceptable addition to the fund. Miss B3esley also recited Kiplipg's "Soldier, soldier come from.the war "in an equally meritorious manner. Mention must be made of the services of the Apollo Quartette (Messrs. R. NV. Cook, W. Critchley, P.George and NV. Woodcock) whose voices blended admirably in "My old Kentucky Home "and" Eileen Alannah." Two well-deserved encores were accorded and responded to. There was no lack of humour,this part of the programme being in the capable hands of Mr.! Jack INlacDermott and -Mr. Alfred B. Millard who mightily amused the gathering. Although their styles are quite distinct their humour was equally "catching "but Mr. MacDermott's singing deserves special praise. The accompaniments were tastefully played by Mr.W. H. Payton,Muc Bac. The Mayor, who holds the presidency of the committee was prevented from attending and Mr. Henry Roberts briefly addressed the audience. Some people said, he remarked, that in these days there was no such thing as gratitude for public service: He was not one to believe that slander. Whether it might or might be so in some parts of the country they in Warrington at any rate were determined to keep green the memories of those men'wlao went from their midst a few years ago and cheerfully gave up their lives for their country. (Applause.) It had been determined to raise a fund of £l,OOO or £1,200 for the purpose of erecting, in some prominent position in the town, a public memorial, so that their children and their children's children could be reminded of the deeds of valour of their townspeople. Towards the amount required the Workingmen's Com- mittee had already raised no less than £l5O and,judging by the number present that night, the proceeds of the concert would be substantial. (Applause.)

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.
The Auto-Cycle Club trials for tri-cars, which took place upon November sth, cannot be accounted a brilliant success.

lhe route was from Hatfield to Newmarket and back, the return journey being made via Royston. The total distance of 100 miles was permitted to be taken in two doses of fifty miles each, a stop of fifteen minutes being allowed hallway. were fresh water could, if required, be taken, but no additional petrol. In every case the passenger was to be an observer chosen by the Club, and all stops for any reason whatever were to be reported.

The general idea of the trials was good;but,unfortun- ately, it was but indifferently carried out. Notwith- standing the fact that a large number of officials was present, the course was very badly marshalled,at least three competitors missing their way at Puckeridge on the outward journey and proceeding through Royston,whilst we ourselves were instrumental in saving yet another from going aotray on the home- ward trip at Wades Mill, where the turn is unexpected and a marshall should certainly have been stationed.

The behaviour of the tri-cars themselves was dis- appointing. Considering that all the engines were of fairly high h.p.—the highest was a 6h .p. and the lowest h.p.—it is astonishing that so many failed to surmount the hills out of Hertford. When nearing the summit, the drivers were called upon to start and re-start; but this part of the programme seemed to be 'somewhat saddled by the officials in charge, who did not make it sufficiently clear to the competitors what was expe3ted of them. To see a man rush forward and flurriedly wave a flag in the driver's face does not con- vey very lucidly that he is expected to bring his mount to a standstill and then start afresh, whilst the object of stopping a tri-car almost at the summit of a steep incline is a little mysterious. It is customary to hold break tests downhill.

Mr. C. G. Wridgway, of record-breaking fame over the classical Brighton-and-back course, has experienced a rather extraordinary accident whilst racing in America. The road was extremely rough, and in sweeping round a bend at high speed, the seat of his racer became loose and he was jerked off backwards from his car. With no one on board, the vehicle' dashed on, ran clean through some railings, and was finally brought up by crash- ing into the walls of an out-building. The car—a 24 h.p. Peerless—of course is absolutely wrecked; but Wridgway, fortunately, seems to have sustained little injury beyond a few bruises and a deep cut underneath one eye.

We are pleased to record the appearance of a new four-cylinder light car which has just been placed upon the market by Mr. Hutton and is English-made through- out. It is well designed and up-to-date in every respect whilst it embodies many detail improvements which are sometimes looked for in vain upon expensive cars of far higher h.p. The new Hutton is a 10-12 h.p. The four cylinders are separately cast. All the valves are mechanically operated and are placed side by side in the cylinder heads. The ignition is the ordinary high- tension type, the commutator being placed outside the frame just under the front of the bonnet. Transmission to the road wheels is by live axle and Cardan propeller shaft. The car is silent, free from vibration and speedy on hills. Altogether it is a welcome. addition to the ranks of English-made cars.

V4e believe that the action taken by Mr. Moffat ford last year in respect to the speed of electric trains has recently been repeated at the instance of a certain omnibus company. Times were taken in Camberwell- road, and all the cars passing over a distance were found to be travelling at a speed from 134 to 14 miles per hour, whilst the maximum permissible is 10 miles per. hour.

div.head: LAND VALUES.
div.p: LAND VALUES.
Mr. Shackleton, M.P., on Taxation and
Assessments.

Speaking at the Houldsworth Institute, Reddish, on Tuesday night, on "Labour and Land," Mr. Shackleton, M.P., who was described by the chairman (Councillor Hollis) as one of Lancashire's true Labour leaders, said, in regard to the question of law governing the opera- tion of trades unions, that they were seeking nothing that was unreasonable as between employer and employed. Unfortunately they had traitors in their own ranks. They had men who were willing to sell their votes fora "pint pot." A trade unionist should be held personally responsible for any illegal act he committed, and then they would have strikes better conducted.

6n the land question, he strongly contended for the taxation of land values as the only solution of the difficulties of municipalities desirous of making neces- sary improvements. A landowner in Harrogate asked £1,200 for an acre of land for burial purposes,whilst the assessment stood at ss. Failing land nationalisation a landowner, if unwilling to sell at a reasonable price, should be taxed on the value he placed upon it himself. On a low estimate the Derby family was receiving £l,OOO per day for rents, the land having, in many ases, been bought for the price of a mere song.

div.head: Mr. R. A. Naylor and the Carnarvon Boroughs.
div.p: Mr. R. A. Naylor and the Carnarvon Boroughs.

Mr. Naylor Unionist candidate for Carnarvon. Boroughs, spoke at the Carnarvon Conservative Club on Monday evening. Dealing with the education question, he maintained that the position of what was called the Welsh, national party was untenable. It was absolutely illegal and false, and therefore, could never be effective. (Hear, hear.) It had been said that the so-called Welsh policy had behind it a united Wales, but it was not true. (Hear, hear). If the Carnarvon Boroughs wee taken as an example it would be found that the nation ivai pretty evenly divided. At the last election the majority against the Unionists was only 296, and at the present moment there was a growing feeling among many who -bad at first supported the illugal plan of campaign that things had goee too far. If the other boroughs only worked with the same persistency as Conway and Carnarvon, he had no hesitation in saying that at the next Parliamentary election the Unionist candidate would be returned by a substantial majority. (Cheers.)

div.head: BEAN MIRACLE.
div.p: A BEAN MIRACLE.
Woman Saved From Death.
Friends were Summoned to Her Bedside. Now She can Visit Her Friends.
Ulcerated Stomach, Debility, and Anwmia
Cured.

One of the most astonishing cures of modern times has recently been effected by Charles Forde's Bile Beans for Biliousness. The subject is Mrs. Sarah Anti Smith, of 52, Chesterton Road, Sparkbrook, Birming- ham. This is the story of her suffering and her cure as told to a "Birmingham Telegram "reporter : "My illness, "said she, "came about gradually. In the first place I began to lose flesh so rapidly that I really thought I was in a galloping consumption. I could not eat, and for the life of me I could not tell what was hanging over me. The first doctor I consulted said it was nervous debility, and that I had become thoroughly run down. His treatment, however, did not seem to bring me any relief, so I consulted another medical man. His opinion was that it was chronic indigestion. As you will bear later on, it proved to be something worse than that, but I little knew it at the time. From the second doctor I obtained very little benefit, and I decided to go to the Hospital at Birmingham as an out-patient. "Specialists examined me and treated me, but still I got we. I then went to the General ElospitPl, and was an out-patient at the hospital for six months-- making in all twelve months' hospital treatment. This time the doctors said it was heart disease that I suffered from. rhe agony I endured was something awful. When I tried to walk I simply staggered along, and the floor seemed as though it were slipping under me. I became so depressed that at times I used to earnestly pray to be kept from giving way to committing suicide. _ _ _

" All the time I was taking bottle after bottle of medicine from the hospital, but with very little good result. I was at last compelled to take to my bed. Another doctor was called in, and he ordered a nurse for me, as he said it wax not safe to leavl me alone. I was told T was so armmic that practically all my blood was turning into water, and this I was prepared to believe, becattse I got so thin that my bones protruded. "Before my illness I weighed 13 stone, but I fell away till I only weighed 7 stone. "Thinking it might do me good, my husband had me moved to the country. To effect my removal I had to be carried to the station, for I had become so weak that I could not stand up. I lived on sterilised milk, and at last, even this would not stay on my stomach. The change of air seemed to do me no good, so I was brought home again, and still another doctor was summoned, and a nurse again requisitioned. From this doctor we learned the real facts of my case. _

He asked my husband to go to his surgery, and there told him that my case was hopeless. He said my stomach had been almost completely eaten away by ulcers, and consequently nothing ou earth could save me. My relatives, including my mother, who is now well on in years, were summoned to my bedside one day, as it was thought I was dying, and a minister attended and administered the Holy Communion. I was truly at that time face to face with death. "Then a brother of mine who was present said to my husband;' William, you have tried almost everything for her, but why not try those Bile Beans 'which there is so much talk about. I have just been reading a case of a woman at Walsall who was cured be them.'

"My husband pondered for a while, and the result was that I commenced a course of Bile Beans. "After I had taken the first box I was able to take a little bread and butter and a cup of cocoa. This was certainly a sign of improvement, because just before this if I took even a little drop of milk it would cause such violent pain that I had to be held down in bed. As I continued with the Bile Beans I felt a gradual improvement, and after it little while'l was able to leave my bed and sit up for a few hours every day. "Then I got strong enough to walk downstairs. Ni Of course, was only obtained by persevering with Bile Beans. From the time I began with Bile Beans no other medicine passed my lips, and to the amazement of everybody who knows me, they not only saved me from the grave, but have now restored me to health. I never felt better in my life than I do now. 3ly appetite is good, and no matter what kind of food I eat I feel no ill effects."

Lord LANSDOWNE'S THE OUTLOOK FOR speech has been ARBITRATION. received with general

approval. It is recognised that our case for redress from Russia is not prejudiced in any way by the conditions of the international inquiry, and the Czar lias so far withstood the pressure of the war party at St. Petersburg. According to the correspondent of the "Standard "in that city, the Russian Govern- ment have had recourse to a singular expedient. They have offered "handsome rewards to all per- sons furnishing information about the presence of suspicious vessels in the North Sea, or any other facts that might be 2onnected with the incident on the Dogger Bank." This is a confession of conscious weakness. "Certainly," proceeds the" Standard" correspondent, "if Russia finds it necessary to offer to purchase corroboration in this matter, it shews that there can be no serious evidence to put forward. Having gained time for the Baltic Fleet to get well on its way to the Far East, it is not impossible that the CZAR'S Government will end by admitting the mistake made by Russian naval officers." It would seem that St. Petersburg is beginning to see that it will not do to affirm the existence of the Japanese torpedo-boats without any evidence to shew whence they came and whither they went. Rewards for corrobora- tion may produce the class of testimony which was permitted to influence the verdict of the too famous court-martial at Rennes- But the Inter- national Commission will not:be a tribunal of that type; and witnesses who may be tempted to swear that they saw the Japanese torpedo.boats hiding in "a very deep Norwegian fjord" will be sharply reminded that the Swedish Government has dis- missed that story as a fabrication.

It would be idle to deny that the cause of inter- national arbitration very largely depends upon the judgment of this Commission, and upon the good faith of Russia. Lord LANSDOWNE announced that the American Government hal proposed to him a treaty of arbitration, and that President ROOSEVELT intended to summon another Peace Conference. We are all anxious to make a treaty with the United States. Former negotiations to this end were brought to naught by perversity in the American Senate; but now that Mr. ROOSEVELT commands a majority in both Houses of Congress the obstinacy of a few obstructive politicians is likely to be over- come. Whether the PRESIDENT Will delay tha calling of a Peace Conference until the close of the war in the Far East, or whether he will try the bold plan of using such a Conference as a means to bring that calamitous struggle to an end, it is too soon to say. But Mr. ROOSEVELT has a great opportunity, and he is just the man to seize occa- sion by the hand with masterful zeal. He has received from his countrymen the most striking mandate ever accorded to an American statesman. It could not be put to better account than by an endeavour to subject the combatants in the Far East to the moral suasion of a council of the nations. Such an effort might appeal to the CZAR and to the KAISER, whose impulsive message of congratulation to Mr. ROOSEVELT was manifestly dictated by personal sympathy—the sympathy of a strong man for a kindred spirit. Of all the KAISER'S historical telegrams, this one is certainly the most felicitous, for it has the unique distinc- tion of offending nobody. But it is evident that before a Peace Conference can be called with a real prospect of success for arbitration in the future, the North Sea affair must be settled in accordance I with reason and justice. A very grievous wrong has been done, and only the full redress of that wrong can inspire practical confidence in the settlement of international disputes by purely judicial methods.

In the course of a letter which was read at the weekly debate of the Social Service League last night, Mr. A. H. Crosfield.explains his views with regard to the compulsory military service question. Like ourselves he does not admit that the volun- tary system had had a fair chance,and adds: "I am satisfied that if some moderate remuneration were given to workingmen during the time they serve in camp, and if men saw their way to honourable distinction by loing their duty as volunteers, or in the militia, or in the yeomanry, we would get all the response the nation needs.'

At last there has been a pitched battle between the Traders and the Non-Traders, and the free and enlightened electors of Town Hall ward have given their verdict to the Non-Trader. The res- pective candidates were Mr. A. J. Jolley and Mr. W. Benson, the former being one of the Corpora- tion Inquiry Commissioners who reported against the Non-Traders and the Non-Trading principle, and the latter a professed Non-Trader who was fighting for the third time. Though twice pre- viously unsuccessful, Mr. Benson never, however, fought against such odds as were in the scale against him on Tuesday,and his success is a triumph for the Non-Traders which transcends even the solid verdict of the wards at the elections two years ago. Mr.Jolley was much the better known man of the two; he had the united help—if we may be allowed a little latitude in debcription— of the State, the Church, "the Trade" and the Traders, while his opponent relied entirely upon the support of the Non-Traders. Very little pre- liminary skirmishing was required to narrow the issue down to the trading question, and both sides were active and vigorous in prose- cuting their campaign. Probably, so much mural literature was never circulated in a Warrington municipal election, and the electors, if they had not done so long before were given the fullest opportunity to make up their minds irrevocably on the great question. Those who recorded their votes for Mr. Benson obviously did so, for there was no other consideration either Personal or political which could compel them to vote as they did, and 419 may be taken as repre- senting the net minimum Non-Trading vote in Town Hall ward. With a candidate enjoying the benefit of such miscellaneous and powerful help as Mr. Jolley had the Non-Traders must have re- corded a majority equal to that secured by Mr. Dodds two years ago.

It appears to us,taking all these points into con- sideration, that there can be no disputing the fact that a iarge majority of the people of Warrington are opposed to trading by members of the Council with the Corporation through limited companies. The argument that such trading is legal is no argu- ment worthy ot the name, and its fallaciousness is obviously fully understood by the ratepayers. Of set purpose, they are now returning men to the Council who will not seek to profit by trading with the Corporation under an anomalous law. We earnestly hope, seeing that the Non-Trading principle has once again been clearly affirmed by the public vote, that it will be generally accepted as the basis of municipal representation in War- rington. The advocates of the peculiar view that, so long as a man keeps within the law and sells goods to his Corporation cheaper than anyone else, he nasty make as much as he likes out of his public position, are only ploughing the sands and making increasingly difficult the attainment of a standard of public life which shall be irreproachable in the eyes of all men.

In opening the Emmanuel Sale of Work yesterday, the Rev. John Yonge made a wide departure from the customary tone of speeches at opening ceremonies. After touching upon the causes of cleavage between the members of the Reformed Church and the State Church,he alluded to the frequently vexed question of liturgy. It will surprise many people to learn from his speech that Mr. Yonge has some leanings towards a liturgical service and rather regrets the distaste of Congregationalists for It. This expression of opinion from the rev, gentleman is particularly interesting seeing that he has just celebrated his 28th anniversary at Wycliffe Church. He is obvi- ously not giving expression to views hastily formed, and we should be interested to learn what form of liturgy Mr. Yonge would like to see included in the Congregational service.

There has been no difficulty with the Mayoralty of Warrington this year. Alderman Bolton had signified his willingness to take office again, and there was nothing more to do except to elect him according to the form and ceremony of such occasions. The election took place at the special Council meeting held at noon on Wednesday, and was characterised by complete unanimity. In expressing his thanks for the honour conferred upon him, his Worship volunteered the hope that they would have amicable meetings lasting "about twenty minutes" instead of four or five hours, and immediately proceeded to talk more than anyone else during the discussion of the business—which was just like him. One of Mr. Bolton's faults, only a minor one 'tis true, is that he will argue:with his councillors instead of main- taining a judicial reticence and reserve. This tends to prolong discussion, and we hope his Worship will bear the fact in mind during the Council meetings which are to come. No one is more earnest or sincere in good endeavour than he and we are sure our friendly criticism will not be resented.

Four aldermen were also re-eleeted, namely, Messrs. T. H. Sutton, James Fairclough, W. Pierpoint, and A. B.nnett. They have all a long roll of service behind them, and though the neces- sity for the Aldermanic cffice is often questioned, we should be sorry to see the grey-beards of the Council relegated "to the ranks." By length of tenure and the confidence .of their fellows they have earned the right to a little added dignity,and the only objection we have to them as aldermen is when too many of them are on one committee. It is not right that the deliberations and doings of any authority should be controlled by the men who have ceased to come before the ratepayers for their triennial licence, and we are glad to see that this contention was to some extent recognised and subscribed to in the constitution of the Watch Committee. Aldermen, like spice, should be dis- tributed sparingly. A sprinkling here and there is all that is required. Congratulations to Alder- man Sutton, the " father "of the Council! May his 31st year as a member of the Corporation be a satisfaction to himself and a source of pleasure to his colleagues! A certain amount of amusement they are assured. Alderman Sutton is the wag as well as the "father "of the Council.

Warrington has loomed large in the public eye , for three years at least. It has been described as the most corrupt town, except one, in England, and has become famous on that account. The "most corrupt" town was said to be Blackpool,and yet notwithstanding this splendid "ad." Blackpool spends hundreds of pounds a year in further advertisement and self-glorification. Why should not Warrington do likewise? Councillor Pemberton has put the question plainly and it is to be gravely considered by the General Purposes Com- mittee. Warrington may not be a health resort —like Blackpool—and unlike that town it will not need to draw attention to its death-rate as an inducement to visitors, which is fortunate! Warrington, however, has unrivalled commercial advantages, and we see no reason why these should not be" pushed" in the proper quarters just as much as are the holiday attractions of Blackpool, Southport, and the Isle of Man. Though the idea has its funny aspects it is one worthy of more than a passing thought. Manufacturers are often seek- ing sites, and it would pay Warrington to introduce itself to their notice.

Notwithstanding specious arguments, the attempt to induce the Warrington licensing justices to transfer the licence of the George !Hotel to the Orford end of the town failed com- pletely. Fortunately the majotity of the Bench have a higher conception of the magisterial functions than to imagine that they:imply—as was strongly represented—a unanimity: of feeling with the Corporation and a willingness to seal any bargains which that authority chooses to make with the brewers. They apparently realised that it was their duty to consider whether the opening of a new house was necessary for the requirements ' of the neighbourhood and to give their verdict accordingly. After reviewing the evidence we fail to see how the Court could possibly have come to any other decision than to refuse the. application. So recently as in 1900 their worships declined to grant an outdoor licence for the same premises and there is nothing indicative of an appreciable change in the conditions since that occasion. Thirty-five licences within the half-mile radius should surely ba ample to cater for the needs of

the community. Had the application been satis- factory in this respect, the Bench would hardly have been justified in licensing an ill-adapted building merely on the understanding that plans of alterations would be brought forward. As was pointed out they were bound to satisfy themselves that the premises were suitable for hotel purposes. The Corporation's " bargaining " with Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd., has received a disagreeable check, fpr the firm agreed to purchase the licence conditionally on its being transferred. It would; we believe, have been in the best interests of the town had the Corporation in the first instance taken the opportunity of reducing the number of public houses by allowing the licence to lapse.

Like the visits of the angels, the visits of the manager of the Cheshire Lines Committee to Great Sankey station are few and far between. The advent of that worthy gentleman, which is at length promised, will be something notable in the history of the village, especially if it leads to the much-desired improvement in the booking arrange- ments. The danger attendant upon crossing the line is accentuated by the sharp curve at each approach to the station which hides the trains from view, but we are afraid that so long as the present inconvenient booking system obtains, passengers will run the risk rather than follow the circuitous route from one platform to the other by means of the highway brkige. It is incumbent upon the committee to provide better and safer facilities and we hope their action will not be much longer delayed.

It does not follow because Continental countries have failed with their labour colony schemes that nothing of the kind will answer in our own coun- try. But the report just published by the Board of Trade should make us cautious. The great fault of our Poor Law system has been the want oficourage for some broad line of classification. The coarse and lazy are mixed with those who are simply weaklings who have been unable to Keep up with the fight. The reports from Europe shew that we must not establish labour colonies in the same loose and undiscerning way, if we are to make them succeed. The danger is that chronic out-of-works will use the farms only for a change of air and scenery. They will be treated generously as learners; having learnt they will refuse to apply themselves regularly to farm work; and, recruited in health and strength they will drift back to town, loitering until they are tired of that and inclined for the country again. There must be some sort of a contract with these people,possibly enforced by magisterial order. But there should be discretion in our severity. The saddest thing about many of the out-of-works is not that they have lost employment but that they have lost the desire to be employed They have drifted down and down until their spirit has gone. This is part of the problem which has to be faced. It can be solved only by dis- crimination. Local committees and officials of bodies under popular control have a peculiar difficulty because of the constant criticism. They must be given some responsibility, and trusted.

Coming Events. The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Nursing Association will be held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Tuesday, November 22nd. The Warrington Ragged School and Mission, which has for some time been closed for repairs, will be re-opened to-morrow, when special services will be held-. Mr. R. A. Naylor will be the speaker in the afternoon and evening. The music will form a specia 1 feature as the singing of an augmented choir will be accompanied by Miss Turner's Ladies' Orchestra. . ASA for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERA WATERS.—Advt. Personal. The Rev. G. W. Dickinson, one of the assistau clergy at the Parish Church, has accepted the senior curacy of St. Oswald's Church, Chester, and will leave Warrington in January. Mr. Dickinson has spent six years in Warrington doing an active and usefu work in the town, and his departure will be much regretted. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., has been appointed one of the judges to officiate at next year's Shire Horse and Hackney Horse Societies' show.

" Mr.-John Frederick Cheetha,m of Eastwood,Staly- bridge, has joined the Board of the Manchester and. Liverpool District Banking Company Limited. Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., will address a mass meeting of Liberals in Parr Hall on the 25th inst. Mayor's Sunday. _
The Mayor and Corporation will attend Divine service at the Parish Church, to-morrow (Sundayl morning. The procession will leave the Town Hal at 10 o'clock.

div.p: Proposed New Mission.

A concert was held in the Ellesmere-street Wes- leyan school on Thursday evening in aid of the building fund for the erection of a new Wesleyan Mission in Ellesmere-street. There was a large attendance and an excellent programme was sub- mitted, to which contributions were made by Miss W Pigot, Mr. Clay, Miss Carrie Hastings, and Mr. P. L. Richardson, and a chorus composed of the Misses Robinson, E. Taylor J. Ball, M. Ball, N. Carnson, Gandy, L. Pigot, and Emily Taylor. Mrs. Carusoa acted as accompanist. GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES- ROW on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Edward Fitzgerald. This was the subject of a lecture delivered by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees, at a meeting of the Warring- ton Society, held at the Old Academy last night, and at which there was a fair attendance. Mr. Rees dealt with his subject in an interesting manner speaking Of Fitzgerald's life and works. A poet, painter, musician, writer and scholar Fitzgerald was, said Mr. Rees, all eccentric genius who took more pains to avoid fame than others took to seek it, and had he not shunned notoriety so sedulously he would have achieved a foremost place among the eminent men of his day. Mr. Rees was heartily thanked at the close of Ili3 address,

div.p: Serious Accident. Mrs. Louisa Kelly, 55 years of age, of 15, Victoria- street, was admitted to the Infirmary on Tuesday night, suffering from a fracture of both legs, caused by fall- ing downstairs at her own house. False Alarm of Fire. The Warrington Fire Brigade were called out on sunday evening by a young man who proceeded to the fire station and reported that a fire had broken out in King-street. The brigade at once proceeded to the spots indicated] where they " found that it was only a chimney which was on dire. They promptly returned upon making this discovery. • Fire in Bewsey-street. At about nine o'clock on Sunday morning a fire broke out in the premises occupied by Mr. J. G.. Fletcher, provision dealer, 55 Bewsey-street. In- formation was at once conveyed to the fire station, and the brigade, in charge of Superintendent Frank Turner at once proceeded with the hose reel, ladders and fire escape. It was found that the kitchen was on fire, but after half-an-hour's work, the flames were got under. The kitchen was entirely gutted and much damage, caused by heat and smoke, was done to the upper rooms. The premises are insured, and the damage is estimated at about £2OO.

Cairo-street Debating! Society. A meeting of the above society was held on Tuesday evening, the Rev. C. Harvey Cook occupying the chair. There was a large attendance of both ladies and.gentlemen. The subject discussed was women's suffrage, and, in the course of the debate, views of singular originality were expressed. Mr. David Plinston opened the discussion by moving "That the parliamentary franchise ought to be extended to women." He spoke ably in favour of the motion,and was supported by a number of the:speakers. He was opposed by Mr. T. E. Knowles, whose views also evoked the sympathy of a number of those who entered the discussion. After the debate had ended, 19 votes were recorded in favour of the motion and 12 against it, some of the ladies taking part in the voting.

Resignation of Major Wilkinson. A fine army career (says the Manchester "Courier ") was closed on Saturday by the resigna- tion of Captain and Brevet-Major G. A. Wilkinson, who was recently sent from a Militia adjutancy at Warrington to a Line company in Ireland with a view to posting to India. Major Wilkinson was the prisoner at a court-martial at Warrington during the summer, which attracted a good deal of attention, and which resulted in his being cashiered. He is only 29 years of age, and distinguished himself at the siege of Ladysmith, was mentioned in despatches by Lord Roberts and Lord Kitchener,and was promoted major at the early age of 26,after only three months service as a captain.

Shop Assistants' Gathering. The local members of the National Union of Shop Assistants held a successful smoker at the Blue Bell Hotel, the other evening. There was a capital attend- ance, and Mr. Whittaker presided. An excellent pro- gramme was submitted, the following contributing items :—Messrs. Hayne (Earlestown), Jones, Caffrey, Bennett, Edwards, Gorst, Walfinder, Fish and Clarke. Mr. C. Turner made reference to the present-day conditions of life of the general shop assistant, and urged the need for greater unity. He proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the various artistes --pf the evening, to Mr. Whittaker for presiding, and the host. Mr. E. Bracegirdle seconded, and the vote was heartily accorded. Mr. Oldham, tue secretary, was also thanked for his admirable arrangements.

The Salvation Army Commanding Officers. Adjutant and Mrs. Everness have received orders to proceed to the command of the Ballymacaryat Corps in Ireland after having been twelve months in charge of the Warrington Corps of the Salvation Army, and will leave Warrington on Thursday evening. During the short time they have been at Warrington the work of the Army has been in a very flourishing condition. One of the most notable undertakings engineered by Adjutant Everness, was the Excelsior bazaar, which enabled him to purchase a new set of silver-plated instruments for the band at a cost of over £2OO ;of this £lBO has been paid. Adjutant and Mrs. Everness have made a host of friends, who very much regret that they are to be transferred to another district. At the hall in Academy-street on Sunday evening, a farewell sermon was preached by the Adjutant, who took for his subject two passages : "Hitherto hath the Lord helped up "and "The Lord be with you." Adjutant and Mrs. Searles, of Nelson, have been appointed to succeed in the command of the Warrington Corps.
H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS. I 63. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt.

Warringtonians in the United States. "A regrettable incident occurred on Monday (says the Liverpool Courier') .during a visit of Mr. C. E. Bunch and Mr. T. Atherton, members of the British Iron and Steel Institute, to the Pittsburg Steel Com- pany's works at Monessen, Pennsylvania. The two visitors were escorted by an official.. of the Carnegie Steel Company, and on their applying for admittance to the works they were curtly told they could not enter. The incident is much regretted, and is put down to the fact that owing to the rivalry between the Pittsburg Steel Company and the Carnegie Company the former concern desired to snub the official of the latter, who was acting as 'guide for the Englishmen. The members of the British Institute have inspected all the leading plants in Western Pennsylvania, and intend leaving immediately for St. Louis and other Western cities."' Mr. Bunch and Mr. Atherton, who are well-known in Warrington, are representatives of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles. Memorial Service.

A large congregation assembled in Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday evening when a service was held in memory of the late Sergeant William Bodle. It was conducted by Mr. W. Hickman in the absence through illness, of the Rev. G. H. Carnpon There was a good attendance of soldiers from the barracks. Mr. Hickman preached upon "Moral greatness and its reward," and in the course of his remarks referred to the late Mr. Bodle as a man who lived a godly life, and was a friend to all who needed help. During his connection with the army Sergeant Bodle did a good work among his fellow comrades and in later years he had been a faithful and devoted servant of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Company, and was held in high esteem by all who knew him. His last words were" I am going home. All is well! Meet me in Heaven." Special hymns were sung, and the organist, Mr. F. Hickman, played "0 rest in the Lord during the service and at the close "The soldiers' march."
GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES now on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Licensing Transfers. _

The ma—gistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Monday granted the following transfers of licences : Filecutters' Arms, Fennel-street, from James Jackson to George Eastwood; flop Pole, Horsemarket-street, from Henry Hodgson Foulds to John Looker; off- licence, 46, Wakefield-street, from Joseph Caldwell, deceased, to Hannah Caldwell, widow; Marquis of Granby, Church-street, from Mary Whittle, deceased, to Frank James Whittle; Packet House, Bridge-street, from Elizabeth Monks to Arthur Edward Denham ; King and Queen Inn, Padgate-lane, from Frederick Clare to William Rogers; General Wolfe, Church- street, from William Rogers to Samuel Johnson Beaman; Unicorn, Winxvick-road, from Thomas Jones to Samuel Appleton; Baths Hotel, Sankey-street, from John Davies to Jane Gittens ; off-licence, 107, Manchester-road, from Joseph Colbourne, deceased, to Mary- Jane Colbourne, widow; and off-licence, 109, Sankey-street, from William Bede Houghton to Alfred Joseph Burke. The Thomas Morris Charity. - -

_ - In accordance with the terms laid down by the late Mr. Thomas Morris, for this charity there were distributed at the office of Vfr. Arthur Browne, Sankey- street, Warrington, on Wednesday last, 76 pairs of blankets and 33 red flannel petticoats, to the old women of Warrington. selected by the a Trustees of such committee. The trustees found that the number of applicants was increasing yearly, and this year the number was close upon 300, all of whom were most deserving, being highly recommended by some minister of religion or a magistrate, or some leading tradesman, and they had great difficulty in making the selections, and regretted that they could not give every applicant a portion of the charity. The blankets were supplied by Messrs. Pattison and Perkins, of Sankey-street, and Mr. Councillor Clegg, of Butter- market-street, and the flannel petticoats by Mrs. Joseph Harrison of the Charity Investigation Society, one charity thus helping another. The trustees are the Rev. Canon Willis, -M.A., the Rev. Father Wilson. Rector of St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street, Warrington, the Rev. John Yonge and Mr. Arthur Browne.
the Alleged Libel.

We are informed that cuunsel's opinion as to the alleged libel on officials contained in the report of the Non-Trading Commissioners has been received, but it will not be • made public until it has beep sub- mitted to the Council.

Mr. W. Long's Birthday Party. About 120 workpeople and guests assembled on Saturday evening in the Large Room, Grappenhall, the occasion being the 70th birthday of Mr. W. Long. After tea a concert took place. Mr. A. Grounds gave several songs and sketches. Messrs. Dale, Poulton and Lomas also contributed items. Speeches were made and the health of Mr. Long was heartily drunk. Inspector Hackett's Departure. Yesterday, Inspector Hackett, of the N.S.P.C.C., who for nearly six years has had charge of the work of the Warrington district, left this town to take up his new duties in Sheffield. He has been succeeded by Inspector Edgar Cox, and in future the local office of the society will be at 49,"Bewsey-street.

For the first time this season I had an opportunity of witnessing the performance of the Warrin,gton second string, and of judging by what standard of excellency or slice of luck they had succeeded in head- ing the Combination table. To be candid, I was not much impressed by the cleverness of the Juniors collectively. Though they defeated Rochdale Hornets " A " by 16 points to 5 points they were nothing like so much superior as the score would suggest. For- ward, there was little to choose between the sides, but at half back Warrington had a big v.:vantage through the cleverness of Davies and Duckworth. On the whole, the midfield work of the three-quarters was ragged, though they made up for this by their dash when near the line. Neither Berry nor Jordan rftakes a really good centre, but they should "come on" with practice.

Sad Drowning Case. On Tuesday a young man named Frederick Bucannon (19), of Lower 'Walton, was working on a barge in the river when he missed his footing and fell into the water. All attempts at rescue failed and the body has not yet been recovered. Frederick is the third member of the Bucanon family who has been drowped in the localiiy.

The Perjury Case.—Local Petition. We learn that a petition is being organised in War- rington, on behalf of Joseph Barrett Wood, a resident of the town, who was on the 7th instant sentenced at Chester assizes to a term of eighteen months' liar d labour for perjury. Mr. F. R. Roberts, solicitor is acting in the matter for Mr. Roughley, the fathea-in- law of Wood.
I should think on Saturday's form, that there is more than one defeat in store for Warrington " A" before the championship question is settled.

Warrington Photographic Society. There was a good muster of the members of the above Society at the Old Academy on Tuesday even- ing when an interesting address was given by Mr. W. D. Welford, F.R.C.S., who gave a practical demonstration of le art of photography dealing particularly with the carbon process. The lecture was illustrated by means of splendid photographic specimens, and at the close Mr. Welford was heartily thanked.—Mr. Purse presided.

Two men stood out head and shoulders above the rest, and these were J. Davies and Brooks. The Penygraig man is remarkably clever at getting away from the pack and making an °inning for the c entres while his handling of the ball in all positions takes one back to the palmy days of " Smack " Bate. In Davies the first team have a tip-top reserve who may yet supplant one of the seniors. Brooks showed splo ndid dash on the wing, where he appears more at home than at centre, and he deserved the two tries he got. His pace seems to have improved—in fact both wings were considerably fasten than the centres The latter need to smarten up.

Fatal Fall. Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at Warrington on Thursday, on the body of Arthur Jones, aged forty, of 2, Philip-street, who died on Saturday. The evid- once showed that on October 22nd the deceased retired to bed about 11.30 leaving his wife in the kitchen. Shortly afterwards she heard a thud on the bedroom floor, and.on going upstairs found her hus- band bleeding from a slight wound on the forehead. He told her that he had slipped and fallen on a piece of broken vase. No notice was taken at the time of the injury, but on the following Thursday erysipelas, which ultimately ended in death, set in. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned.

GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES DOW 011 UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. St. Mary's Dance. The annual dance in connection with St. l'Sary's (R.C.) Schools, Buttermarket-street, was held in Parr Hall, on Monday evening, and was an almost unquali- fied success. There were about 150 present, and dancing was indulged in from 8 till two to music supplied by Mr. R. Whitfield's band. The duties of M.C. were ably discharged by Messrs. G. Vernon, J. Eckersley, W. Dilworth, and H. Houghton. The committee, with Father Mercer as chairman and Mr. S. J. Price as secretary, are deserving of congratula- tion for the excellence of their arrangements.

In the premier league thee were some interesting games. Bradford justified the confidence I placed in them by defeating Leeds, though they had nothing to boast of beside the points at the close of the game. They are now only one point behind Oldham. The latter had an easy journey against a very weak Halifax team, but I foresee rocks ahead of the Oldh.amers. Luck has been with them so far. Runcorn participated in a remarkable game at Hull, where though they scored ten points, they were a dozen in arrear at the end. Hull had a day out against the Linnets, but the latter were short of Houghton, Richardson, and Price. At the other end of the table. Batley were trampled deeper in the mire by Widnes, while Leigh and Wakefield both recorded a welcome victory over Wigan and Swinton respectively.
H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONIC.-63, SANKEY STREET, Warrington.—Advt..

The Musical Society's Concert. We would remind our readers that the first sub. seription concert of the season in connection with the Musical Society will be held in the Parr Hall on Wed- nesday evening. The programme will open with Chopin's "Funeral March" Nyhich will be played by the orchestra as a tribute of respect to the late Dr. Henry Hiles who was the Conductor of the Society from 1865 to 1890 and died on the 20th of last month. The principal work to be presented is A. Goring Thomas's cantata "The Swan and the Skylark" and the soloists will be: Miss Lydia Nervil, soprano; Miss Mabel Henshall, contralto; Mr. James Davis, tenor; Mr. James Coleman, bass. The second part of the programme will be of a miscellaneous character. As usual the chorus and orchestra of over 200 per- formers will be in attendance under the conductorship of Mr. Frank H. Crossley.

Accident to the Motor Mail. The motor mail coach running between Liverpool and Manchester met with an accident at Warrington on Sunday morning. It was nearing the post office when it skidded, and before it could be pulled up, collided with the trolley standard at the corner of Winmarleigh-street. The iron cup surrounding the trolley pole was smashed and the ornamental knob at the top of the pole was dislodged and flung across the roadway and through the plate glass window in the shop of Mr. McNair, picture framer, destroying two pictures and doing damage to the extent of about £l2. The engine of the coach and the steering gear were damaged, though the driver and guard luckily escaped injury. A coach and three horses were quickly obtained from Messrs. Maginn's, Sankey-street, and little delay occurred. The coach was repaired during the course of Sunday afternoon, and was afterwards driven back to Liverpool. Bird Show.
The South-West Lancashire League table up-to-date is as follows :

To-day Lancashire play York•=hire at Oldham, and the Red Rose representatives will have to win if they are to stand any chance for the N.U, County Championship. Fish and Preston will represent Warrington and Lancashire in the home 15. Board- man was originally selected, but his injured hand will not permit of his playing.

The ninth annual show of British and foreign cage birds and pigeons, promoted by the Warrington and District Cage Bird Society, was opened in the Con- servative Club Assembly Room yesterday afeernoon, i and was n the evening especially well attended. In all the classes an improvement was to be noticed in the number of entries and the quality, of the winning birds could hardly have been improved upon. Pigeons and canaries were again greatly in evidence and formed strong classes in which the competition was unusually keen, the judges Mr. J. Pamphilon, Poynton, and Mr. A. Wellings, Prescot, experiencing no small difficulty in making their awards. On account of the lateness of the hour at which the prize list was issued we are unable to publish the names of the winners this week.

There has been a late change in the County team, S. James being unable to play. Hockenhall thus obtains a chance of distinction, and he deserves the opportunity. J. Davies will partner Di Davies behind the Warrington scrummage.

The County match results in Warrington having to take a weakened team to Hull, where the Kingston Rovers are doubtless expecting an easy victory. They may be disappointed, however. Warrington will be able to put a strong side in the field as the follow- ing selection shows :—Hallam, full back ; Short, Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris, threequarters ; Hockenhall and Davies,half-backs ; Thomas, Shugars, Belton, Cook, Naylor, Jolley, Morrison, and Harmer, forwards.

I think Brooks merited the choice for left-wing in Fish's place. He was incomparably ahead of Short on Saturday last, and the latter did not come up to requirements at Oldham. Merit should be better recognised ! •

The "A " team will indulge in a " friendly " with Salford St. Bartholomews, and will be represented as follows :—Knight; Brooks, Berry, Barnes and Jordan; J. Davies and Duckworth; Foster, Coleman, Lunt, Edmondson, Roberts.

Hockey. [BY R.G.P.] The Stockton Heath first eleven followed up their fine victory over West Derby, by easily defeating the Latchford team on their own ground. The score in fa- vour of the visitors was 3-0, but with a little luck this might easily have been doubled. The game was scrappy and at no time of high class,the play being full of vigour, which although spoiling the game from a hookey point of view was not accompanied by any really foul tactics. Considering the local rit alry this speaks well for both elevens.

From the bully off the Stockton Heath forwards got going, and within fifteen minutes S. Baxter scored two goals, while later on R. Pierpoint and S. Baxter had hard lines with lightning shots that only missed by inches. The second half was more even than the first, but R. Pierpoint scored a third before the final whistle. To show how one-sided the play was we might mention that the Stockton Heath goal keeper only had one shot during the whole match.
For the home team R. Hallows at back played a fine game, and only through his efforts was the score kept Within normal bounds.
The second elevens played a draw on the Stockton Heath ground, the score being one all. For Stockton Heath Skelton scored after running more than half the length of the field.

div.head: EMMANUEL SALE OF WORK.
div.p: EMMANUEL SALE OF WORK.
[Continued from. Page 6.]
Thursdays sale brought the total proceeds up to £B3. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. REV. JOHN YONGE AND LITURGICAL SERVICES.

There was again a large attendance at the opening ceremony yesterday, over which the Rev. F. Vaughan presided. The Rev. JOHN YO'.‘:GE in declaring the sale open remarked that all interested in the progress of evan- gelical truth had occasion to feel the greatest sympathy with their friends of Emmanuel Church. It appeared to him that the step they took many years ago in form- ing themselves into a district body, outside the pale of the Established Church as it was at present was the very best possible way in which they could have asserted their adherance to the protestant faith of their forefathers. He did not altogether agree with some of the methods which had been adopted of assert- ingprotestant principles against the ritualistic tend- encies of the Established Church. He was not generally an aggressive individual and certainly did not agree with the noisy protests which appeared to him to stir up more bad blood than anything else. (Hear, hear). Moreover it ap peered to him that the line which had been adopted by those persons, would not in the slighteit advance the cause which they as Protestants had at heart. (Hear, hear.) He felt sure the doctrines preached by Mr. Vaughan would be in accordance with the evangelical faith of their forefathers. It was a great pity in his opinion that any church should be so narrow and arbitrary as to exclude their sympathy from other churches which though differing in creeds were united under the one Head—the Lord Jesus Christ. It appeared to him that just to the extent that those churches shut themselves up they shut themselves out of the Church of Christ, the teaching of which was to regard each other with brotherly love, and he was pleased that they would allow a Dissenter like himself to enter their pulpit. To a certain extent he took a pleasure in a liturgical service, and often wished the Congrega- tionalists could have some element of liturgy in their own services. Attempts had been made occasionally to introduce a little liturgy, but being an old-fashioned people some rather shivered at the innovation. How- ever, he would not be one to stand in the way if he saw any disposition to have a sort of liturgical service combined with a liberty which would not interfere with the privilege which should belong to every church, of making an alteration in the order of the service. (Applause). He had much pleasure in declaring the sale open. (Applause). The Rev. John Yonge was heartily thanked for his services on the motion of Mr. ALLEN, seconded by Mr. HErto.N.

div.head: COMPULSORY SERVICE.
div.p: COMPULSORY SERVICE.
DEBATE LAST NIGHT-LETTER FROM MR. A. H. GROSFIELD.

The subject under debate at last night's meeting of the Social Service League was "Should every man have a period of military or naval training ? ' The Rev. H. Dunnico presided and read a, letter from Mr. A. H. Crosfield in the course of which he stated :

"t believe you are having a debate to-night in con- nection with the National Service League. 1 think that league has done very valuable service in the coun- try by bringing to the fore the great question of National and Imperial Defence, and making us all I' consider the lines on which it can best be attained. We I all agree with the great object, but while fully appreciating the zeal and energy which my brother Captain Crosfield, has devoted to the matter in order to awaken public opinion, there is one point—and an important point too—on which, so far as I can at present form a judgment, I differ from himand with regard to which I think the National Service scheme might with advantage be modified. My brother may be right and I may be wrong, and perhaps some dayl shall see the error of my ways, but at present having a very strong opinion on this point—which we have discussed at considerable length—my brother has very frankly asked me to explain my views so that he can reply to my objections. If we are unable on voluntary, lines to obtain adequate means of defence, then we should all be justified in sup- porting a system of compulsory service which is really a mild form of conscription. But a voluntary scheme has never yet had a fair chance. The volunteers have had more kicks than half-pence from those in authority and I say it is putting the cart before the horse to ask us to go in for compulsory service before a voluntary scheme has been fairly tried. Parliament may have to interfere to see that employers do not prevent their workmen having a fair opportunity of serving, and a general appeal through all classes should certainly be made to National honour to respond to the call of duty and then you will get those men serving who are best cut out for military work, and others rendering equally good service to their coun- try in different ways. With our enormous navy and regular army for service abroad we do not require a nation in arms at home as well. To develop militarism to that extent—beyond anything that rational measures for safety really require—would. lam sure you will I agree with me, be a bad thing for the ne.tion. It would' be bad fromithe point of view of foreign policy, owing to the temptation to military adventure abroad, the policy from which we have suffered so disastrously the last eight or ten years, and even owing to the influence this would have in the long run on home politics. I I am sure a thoughtful public spirited man like yourself will see easily enough the ramifications of such influences and the effects in many directions of compulsory ser- vice. Its advocates are a little apt, I think, to concen- trate their attention on the advantages without con- I sidering the immediate, and the less obvious though not less real disadvantages, and they lay special emphasis on the compulsory plan as a necessity for national self-preservation. Well of course if it were so the case would be entirely different, but I am satisfied that if some moderate remuneration were given to workingmen during the time they serve in camp (far from anything in the nature of a bribe), and if men saw their way to honourable distinction by doing their duty as volunteers, or in the militia, or in the yeomanry (according to their means and social position) we would get all the response the nation needs. Igo further and say that if we chose to over-do the thing we get more than what is needed. And again I put it to you and your friends, are we to go in for compulsion as a good thing in itself? People who do lip service to English character should remember that the comparative liberty we possess, which has been so dearly bought, has had an enormous influence on the formation of that character, which some of us at least prefer to the character of any other nation on the face of the globe. It is true we compel people to pay taxes, serve on juries and so forth, but as a matter of principle however healthy we may consider discipline for youths and girls who are not of age' we do not believe compulsion is per se desirable for full grown men and women. Liberty and the freedom which has begotten responsibility and stability amongst this great democracy far beyond what exists in any other country has proved the best policy, and is the best policy for the whole English speaking portion of the Empire. I am no expert in military matters myself, butl have taken the opinions of those who are, some of them, eminent military men in high positions. More than one I must admit has recommended forced service but most of the authorities say at once that voluntary service gives you more dash and courage in the field, so that man for man auxiliary forces raised this way would be the more efficient fighing forces. Perhaps I maybe allowed to quote one man who has done more than anyone else for the volunteers in our own town, and whose splendid record will never be forgotten, I won't say by his intimate personal friends,for that goes without saying—but by many hundreds of men in War- rington who have benefitted by the influence and discip- line of a true Englishman and a fine soldier of the King. Major:Roome often used to impress on me the fact Ihave just alluded to, and although he now holds that, a vol- untary solution can not be really adequate, I wish, in pressing this question forward in Warrineton,Liverpool and elsewhere he had seen his way to stick to the old lines on which we have discussed the matter. Well, it may have to be threshed out yet further,- we shall not be the.worse friends on that account. I trust Major Roome will not think it out of place if, now you are about to debate a question so much to the fore, and in whichhe takes such a deep interest, 1 take the oppor- tunity of expressing on my own behalf and on behalf of many others our sense of indebtedness and gratitude to himself, and the permanent and cordial regard that is felt for him in Warrington.—Yours Truly, A. H. CROSFIELD.

Captain G. R. Crosfield opened the debate in the affirmative and advocated the proposals-of the National Service League. Air. Dale seconded, and the discussion was taken part in by Messrs. H. P. Hughes, J. Morton, E. England, H. E. Hawthorne, and E. W. Jones. The debate was adjourned until next Friday evening

div.head: "THE TRUE MESSAGE OF THE CHRISTIAN PULPIT."
div.p: "THE TRUE MESSAGE OF THE CHRISTIAN PULPIT."

This was the subject of the Rev. John Yonge's sermon at Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening, the text being taken from Ist John vii. "This is the Record that God hath given to us eternal life: and this life is in His Son." They were frequently being assured, said the preacher, that the supreme want of these later days was a new Gospel, more adapted to modern thought and necessities, and they frequently saw various attempts at the discovery of their new 'gospel. There was no wisdom in speaking disparagingly of such attempts, if they were honest, and if they were not contradictory of the truth of Jesus Christ. It did not follow, however, that because a thing was new, it was therefore true and ought to be accepted at the cost of the denial or sacrifice of that which was old and which had also been proved true by long generations of agreeing and confirming testimony. Thetaessage of the Christian pulpit in these modern days might quite well and fitly be set in modern terms, and with modern applications. It might well be regulated also by the definite and positive results of the higher criticism or the social needs of this twentieth century. But the position, it seemed to him, for all of them to assume was that man's spiritual condition, necessity, and destiny were tht same now as when Jesus preached and taught and when the Church of the Redeemer was first established by the witnesses of the Resurrection. If that be so, then the old gospel was adapted to the necessities of this new age and the message of the Christian pulpit must be ever surely founded lupoi? the Old Gospel. The preacher proceeded to make la brief allusion to his twenty-eighth anniversary as minister at Wycliffe, and to the first sermons which he preached in that capacity in November, 1876. How- ever feebly and imperfectly at the best he had fulfilled the function of a messenger, he did know this—that it had been when most conscious of the Gospel as God's 'message to men that he had most justified his presence 'in that pulpit. The minister of the Gospel was supremely a messenger and if he failed toconvey God's message and to help men to be conscious of it, he failed utterly in his work. The Christian Gospel made in all its doctrine far the broadest and completest development of human welfare. Its principles were those of justice, peace, and good-will amongst men. Wherever the teachiqg of Christ found the greatest acceptance and obedience, there would be found the largest illustration of human happiness of every kind. But the direct and distin- guishing message of the pulpit dealt primarily and ,supremely with the moral, the spiritual and the eternal. It dealt with men as heirs of immortality, as 'children of God,. and it sought to make them realize it.

div.head: PROTECTION. " I KNOWS WHAT I'M A-TARKIN' ABOOT." ,
div.p: PROTECTION. " I KNOWS WHAT I'M A-TARKIN' ABOOT." ,

"The long straight road, drawn like a white line across the green fields, lay before me. The grey stone walls dissected the country on either side like a map. The bine sky was overhead, and the hedges showed no sign of autumn, save for the dust that clung to them, the legacy of a long dry summer. The mettle of the hard road was characteristic of the strong, northern land where flint abounds. So too was the figure of the road-mender who bent over his work, but straightened out his broad shoulders when I stopped for a moment to greet him. _ _ _ . _

In spite of his white hair, his face was unwrinkled, with a colour as pink as a child's, and his eyes were blue as forget-me-note. The firm chin and mouth were clean-shaven, tufts of white hair growing only under the square jaw. He stopped work and leaned on his spade, glad of the diversion from the monotony of toil. He told me he was just back from harvesting, and his thin, leather-coloured hands spoke of days under the August sun. Our talk wandered from the crop to the price of food, and then I uttered a word which roused as by magic the spirit of the man. " Pertection ? " he said,a world of scorn in his voice, , " Pertection ? Let no one tark ter me about Per- tection. I've lived under it. I knows what I'm a-tarkin' aboot." He shaded his face with his brown hand and looked curiously at me, almost as though to invite contradiction; but•l, being eager to learn,seated myself on the white heap of gtone by the wayside and asked him to give me his experience which should be of more value than mere views on this much-debated question. "I'll tipll yer what Pertection means. It means that when I was a yongster we 'ad black barley bread; never see'd a bit o' white bread, 'cept on a Soonday, and then nan on us 'ad a sloice bigger nar ma two fingurs. Ma mither used ta tak' the white loaf and coot what we aided a ruond, size o' the palm of ma 'and, and that into fower agin, and each one of us children 'ad a bite o' white bread, and a sloice o' barley bread as well; on'y time I iver sees white bread. Pertection?" he said again, with a withering contempt; "starvation, that's w'at it were."

"What did we eat? Well, we never eat enuf. Children never 'ad a belly full, alias 'aegry, that's a fact," he said, bringing down his big hand emphatically on his spade. "They'd eat anything, ony they could get it. I tell yer," he said, bending over me and speaking low," the food as we gives to the ducks and the pigs' ud 'ave bin a good dinner for 'em then. 'Ungry, allus 'angry, that's wat we was, and so was most all the children. Price of a loaf of bread? Elevenpence, that's wat it war ; tea, fourpence a ounce. Mony's the toime I've bin sent by ma.mither for twolounces.o' tea, that's eightpence—and sugar was eightpence a pound. Wages, eleven shillin's, the best, and stop wark wet doiys. 'cep' arvest toime, and thin twelve shillin's and victuals. Rent, three pound ten; an' coals, pound a ton. The farmers used ter carry the coals for us as Warked for 'em, in the empty corn wagging, as they, coom back; but I tell yer this, there warsn't noo cum- fort inside or out for a por maanner a ouman. Children 'adn't ony boots, they was eight shillin's ter piy for a , boy's boots. We used ter go ter school toes all oout and torn ter bits. Clothes was dear; we was on'y warm in bed ; and wark, wark from bein' a lad to an ould man, and alias 'angry at that." I asked him about their way of living, what furniture they could buy, and he said, smiling pityingly at my question, " Furniture ? 'Ardly none. There warsn't noo cumfort fer the people. I say there was noo cumfort, 'cept in bed, and the 'omespun blankets was waarm. Noo cumfort inside of yer ner out," he repeated slowly, looking at me full in the face with his clear blue eyes. Again I questioned him as to whether wages would rise as profits increased. "Rise !" he said. "Why should they? They was low enuf then, we 'ad an per- tection you could get; they'll not rise. It'd be the sime ould story—rents 'ad go up, that's an as will rise. The landlord an' the parson, they'd 'ave a better time; but the farmer'll say to 'is men, 'Rents is goon oup, cout down the wages'; the warkin' man'll get noune of it, noune. They'll be joust where they was, on'y a soight wurse off fur food; they'll go back to where they was, an' ave ter put oup wi' wat we 'ad—waater porridge far breakfast, black bread and cheese dinner time, 'an black bread soopper time, wi' a bit o' bacon for those as is loocky and 'av' a pig. A bit o' meat Soonday, that's the on'y day we iver see'd it. Barley I bread, barley bread—l tell yer oi'd like ter give that 'ere Joerhamberlain a taste o' the barley bread, and, fer the matter o' that, an the folks as tarks aboout the good ole toimes, as they know nothin' aboot." "Let the warkin' maan understan' Pertection, an' e'll know it spells ruin fer 'im; an' oi say this, there's not a maan i' the world' as ought iver ter tark o' taxin' fooed. God knows it's 'ard enuf ter wark now, with five men to ev'ry maaster as wants a 'and, but starve them oout, an' England's dun fer. I've lived through it an' I knows " ; and the old man looked like a prophet as his eyes gleamed and his mouth shut firm and strong. "It's a fraud, and if the warkin' maan is taken in over it let 'im ast them as conld tell 'im. The trewth is, there's too mony to live orf the land—there's the landlord, and the farmer, and the warkin' maan, and the land doan't stand it, and there's too much land oout o' cultivation. Look yonder," he said, pointing to the acres of copse where game is preserved, which stretched across the horizon. "There's miles o' land there, not a thing planted, an as foine land as iver a crow flew over. Let 'em look an' see if there bean% some'ut wrong there." I bade the old man good day, and went on my way down the road. Must every generation buy its own experience? I wondered. Does all the suffering by which knowledge is gained ko for nothing.? I looked back, and I saw the tall figure had bent to his work again. ISABEL SOMERSET. [From the " Westminster Gazette."]

div.head: COMPENSATION FOR THE LOSS OF AN EYE. Warrington Order Reduced. Atthe Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Jud,ge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., Mr. Chapman. solicitor, Nianchester, applied on behalf of Messrs. Joseph Crostlald and Sons, Limited, Warrington to have a weekly payment of 12s. 61 made to Patrtck Tannion, Orford-street, under the Workmen's Compensation Act terminated or reduced.—Mr. W. J. Forshaw represented the respondent. – –
div.p: COMPENSATION FOR THE LOSS OF AN EYE. Warrington Order Reduced. Atthe Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Jud,ge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., Mr. Chap- man. solicitor, Nianchester, applied on behalf of Messrs. Joseph Crostlald and Sons, Limited, Warrington to have a weekly payment of 12s. 61 made to Patrtck Tannion, Orford-street, under the Workmen's Compensation Act terminated or reduced.—Mr. W. J. Forshaw represented the respondent. - -

--- Mr. Chapman said the case was a very celebrated one, and had been quoted in possibly every County Court in England during the past four years. It had been before the Court of Appeal, and had previously been dealt withby his Honour's predecessors. The accident took place on January 28th, 1899. Tannion was a labourer in Messrs. Crosfield's employ, and was steaming caustic pipes when some caustic fluid was blown into his right eye. In consequenoo the ball of •the eye had to be removed. An order of 12s. 6d. per week was made, and subsequently the firm applied for a reduction. Judge James held that it was an attempt to carry some technical objection which was not filed, and refused to (disturb the award of Judge Foulkes. The matter was taken to the Court of Appeal on June 30th, 1900. His Honour said the case was known to him from beginning to end. The effect of the decision was that they could not re-open or touch any point decided in the original award. What Mr. Chapman had to show was that there had been some alteration in Tannion's circumstances and in his wage-earning clpa,city or, something that entitled the firm to a diminution or cessation of the order.

Mr. Chapman said he was instructed that defendant's average wages were £1 9s. 101 d, per week. In fixing the amount of the order regard must be had to the average amount earned before and after the accident. Although the respondent had lost his right eye he was employed as a labourer. A labourer did not require an excessive amount of eye-sight. His Honour: What a pity Providence gave him two eyes to begin with! Mr. Chapman said since the accident he had been earning over £1 a week in some cases, but always the sum of about 18s. a week. He had worked at a great many places duting the last four years, but he appeared to have worked when he liked, no doubt feeling himself in a comfortable position with no inducement to put all his energies into the work. He had taken jobs and left them just when he liked for no accountable reason. He was able to earn practically the same amount that he earned before the accident. The order of 12s. 6d. per week was a very large one—representing a wage earning capacity of 255, per week—and under it the firm had paid Tannion £l9O. As respondent was,' now able to earn at least 18s. per:week, applicants asked for a substantial reduction. _ _

Evidence was called to show that since the accident the respondent had received wages varying from 18s. to 225. 6d. per week. It was stated that he had left several places when there was no necessity to do so. Mr. Forshaw submitted that Mr. Chapman had not proved that respondent's wage earning • capacity was greater to-day than it was when the award was made. Dr. Langdale said respondent's right eye had gone, and on examining the left eye witness found it was slightly inflamed, and the vision was not as good as in a normal eye. Patrick Taunton, the respondent, gave evidence as to his earnings since the award. It was only when he was in the employ of Mr. George;Wallington for a fortnight that he earned over 18s. per week. He was able to give reasons for leaving work. His Honour (to Mr. Forshaw) : How do you make out that the applicants are not entitled to some reduc- tion?

Mr. Forshaw : He was able at the time the award was made to earn higher wages than at present. His Honour said he was convinced on the evidence that some reduction must be made. Respondent did not ascribe his ceasing work on any occasion to inability in consequence of defective vision. If he could give judgment sympathetically he would give it in respon- dent's favour without question. Under the circum- stances he must reduce the order to 9s. per week. _
--His Honour allowed ;the respondent three guineas costs.•
