div.head: SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
div.p: SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
BY JOHN TAYLOR Author of "Search Lights on Lana, Labour
and Social Problems."
THE RUSSIAN NAVY,

"Too oft the sight of means to do ill deeds makes ill deeds dOIIe."—SRAKESPEARE. When Peter the Great was the Czar of Russia he took it into his head that his people ought to be a maritime nation, and that they ought to build cruisers and battle- ships of their own. So he came to this country, and spent some time among our ship-wrights, learning the art and craft of ship building, and then he went back to Russia to teach his countrymen what bits of informa- tion he had picked up, and to urge them to build a fleet of their own. Now lam not blaming Peter the Great for picking up new notions and setting up high ideals for his country, but I do blame him for trying to make an inland nation like Russia into a seafaring and maritime people, and initiating wild cat schemes that could never be carried out successfully, 'and that were bound to involve Russia in endless quarrels, and bloody wars, and frightful expense. I.—NATURE NEVER MEANT RUSSIA TO BE A.

div.head: GREAT MARITDIE NATION.
div.p: GREAT MARITDIE NATION.

You can usually tell what a merciful Providence intends to do with any of His creatures when you see what provision He has made for them, and what oppor- tunities He has provided. When von see the web foot of a duck you know the owner of that foot was intended to swim, and when you find a creature endowed with wings you expect it to beable to fly. And when you see nations like England and Japan entirely surrounded by the sea, and plentifully supplied with safe harbours and natural shelters for ships, you expect their people to be good sailors, And have com- mand of the sea.

But Russia has no such natural advantages. I admit that she has thousands of miles of coast-line, hnd several large rivlrs and seaports on her northern boundaries,bnt they are of no earthly use to her for nine months in each year, because their waters are frozen to a depth of several feet. Vladivostok, on the Pacific coast was the only decent harbour Russia had in the Far East till she bullied and bluffed the Japs out of Port Arthur, and it is ice-bound and inaccessible every winter. So it comes to pass that the Russian Navy has to be broken no into three distinct and isolated fleets. One of these is always situated in the Baltic sea,and another in the Black Sea, while the third is in the Pacific, and supposed to look after Russian interests in the Far East.

Her Baltic Fleet suffers every winter the inconveni- ences and limitations of ice-bound ports, and must lay its ships up till the ice melts in the spring. If you add to these disadvantages the risks of a voyage through the Sound, and the Cattegat, before the fleet can reach the outside world, you will agree with me that Russia gets a maximum of worry, and expense, and trouble, and a minimum of benefit out of her fleets in those waters.

Her Black Sea Fleet has open ports alai accessible harbours all the year round, but her warships there are treaty bound. They are not allowed to leave the Black Sea and go through the Bosphorus without the consent of the Sultan of Turkey, and if he lets them out he will not let them in again. So you see Russia is'maintainine three fleets that are frost bound or treaty bound, and unable to combine for the defence of their country. Theyare costing millions of pounds every year to man and equip them, and in my judgment they are a sourse of weakness and tempta- tion to the Czar and his advisers, and if the Japs would hammer every Russian ship into scrap iron it would be a real kindness to the Russian people.
IL-THE RUSSIAN NAVY IS LARGELY RES- PONSIBLE FOR 'rum NATION'S AGGRESSIVE
FOREIGN POLICY.

It is on these three fleets that the Czarand his advisers rely for carrying out their wild schemes of an Empire beyond the sea. One of the Japanese cartoons represents Russia as a giant octopus, with its body resting on a huge map os northern Asia. This octopus is spreading out it, tentacles westward, and eating up Poland and Finland. and trying to grab Sweden and Norway into the bar- gain. Eastward it is annexinc, Manchuria, and Siberia, and Corea, and is reaching out Port Arthur and Japan. Now this game of grab is comparatively easy so long as Russia only absorbs weaker and smaller nations, and confines her energies to the lands where her armies can easily march and fight. It is when she challenges nations that are more than a match for her, and whose terri- tories lie across the sea, that she makes her mistake. When Japan awoke from the sleep af ages, and began to educate her children, and teach them new industries, and assert her right to be heard in the councils of the nations, she arpused the envy and jealousy of the Russian Government. The Czar and his advisers commenced an era of ship building, but they made two fatal mistakes. They imagined that Russia could build as good battle- ships and cruisers as anybody else, and it did not matter about speed or mobility, provided they were as big and strong as floating batteries. *So they turned out some huge, unwieldy, home-made lumber, that could neither fight or fly, and that made fine targets for the Japanese torpedo boats and destroyers. And yet it was on the strength of these obsolete, antiquated,home-made battleships and cruisers that the Russians relied when they bluffed Japan and seized Port Arthur, and provoked a war that has destroyed their Pacific Fleet and rolled back their army in Manchuria, and is costing them a million pounds a week. The nimble-witted, clear-headed Japanese made no such mistake about their ships of war, and guns, and armaments. They bought these things from the best makers in the world, and they taught their own people to make some as good as the best. Their statesmen knew by bitter experience the chicanery, and lying, and fraud, and deception of Russian diplomacy, and that sooner or later they would have to tight for their very existence as a nation against one of the strongest, and most aggressive, and unscrupulous nations in the world.

But let me ask you if this great war between Japan. and Russia would ever have happened if there had been no aggressive Russian fleet in the Pacific? When Russia multiplied her cruisers and battle ships round the coasts of Japan, and began to fortify Port Arthur, she flung down a gauntlet that Japan was bound to pick up No nation can permit an enemy to set up fortifications, and bring ships of war close to her front door, and it is idle for Russia to plead that she has no hostile inten- tions towards Japan by these acts of intimidation and aggression. Some people tell us that" to be prepared for war is the best guarantee of peace." Ido not believe it. In this case, at. any rate, it was Russia's preparation for war 4,hat provoked the war. Let us see how these principles would work out in family life. Christmas is coming round once more; and if some fond father wants a merry Christmas he has only to buy a real revolver and bullets for his oldest boy, and a bowie knife and sheath for his second boy, and a few shillingsworth of fireworks and some matches for the youngest, and shut them all up in a room together and ask no questions on Christmas Eve. If that house does not get burnt down and if some of those rough lads do not get killed, it is not that fond parent's fault, for he has given them the most likely tools he could think of for the purpose. "Too of the sight of means to do ill deeds, makes ill deeds done." _ _ _

Now all this happened to the Russian people. They wanted cruisers. and battleships, and torpedo boats of their own, and they have got them, but they would have been infinitely better off without them. If they had never possessed such engines of mischief they would never have been tempted to use them, and thei would have behaved respectfully and honestly to other nations and there would have been no war between Russia and Japan. If any min thinks I am slandering the Russian. navy he should read the report of Admiral Tehuchin, the commander of the Black Sea fleet, on his recent naval manceurves. He complains bitterly of the rotten,ruined obsolete, lame ducks of ships under his command, and of the ignorant, incompetent, demoralised officers who have charge of them. He says : Incompetence prevails throughout the fleet, and the most appalling muddles occurred because the officers had no interest in their profession.and no love for their work- If the Black Sea fleet has the misfortune to meet the enemy it will be completely wiped out." If the attack on our fishing boats off the 'Dogger Bank by the Baltic Fleet had not been such a tragedy it would have been a comedy. That fleet has been under orders to sail for Port Arthur for months, but leaky boilers, and cranky engines, and incompetent crews, and coaling difficulties, and festivities have delayed its departure. There is a story told of two of our Cabinet Ministers in the reign of George 111.. who drank three or four bottles of wine each over dinner. When they reached the House of Commons one of them said. "I have had too much wine, and I cannot see the Speaker." His friend replied, "Cant you see the Speaker? Why I can see two of them." The Acers and crews of those warships that fired on our fishing boats must have been in that condition. They had been drinking " schnapps " and " vodki "till they could not see a hole in a ladder, and yet they believed they could see Japanese gunboats fifteen thou- sand miles away. It is to be hoped they will get sober before they fall into the hands of any Japanese warships, for they will not get time enough then to blaze away into anything. The sooner that fleet is sent back to the Baltic, and broken up into scrap iron, the better for the pace of the world and for the honour of the Russian people.

div.p: THE BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.

It is seldom that any discovery of science is such as will benefit all classes of people. Some of the greatest discoveries of the age, while they have proved directly beneficial to thousands, have also, at least for a time, injured other thousands. Even some of the best medi- cinal preparations, however much they may do to remove one class of disease, or suit some constitutions, at the same time either deepen the hold of another disease, or leave it entirely untouched, or if theybenefit one class of patients, they may injure another. Now the great need of the age is some scientifically arranged preparation which will cope effectually with the pre- valent diseases of this country, which will be certain to do good when fairly tried, which will be equally adopted to. the needs of the merchant and the Workman, the professional man, and he who wins his bread by the sweat of his brow, the student, the clerk, the factory hand, the miner, and the roadside labourer. It should be, too, such a pre paration as contains no injurious ingredients, and which may be taken with impunity by the weakly child, or the delicate lady, as well as by the stronger constituted man. Such a discovery would deserve to be called The Perfection of Medicinal Preparations, and would indeed be an Invaluable Boon to Suffering Humanity. Now this much needed boon has been found, has been tried, has been proved, and wherever proved, it has been found satisfactory. We refer to Gwilym' Evans' Quinine Bitters, The Vegetable Tonic, which when once tried, has been always recommended, and has proved successful when all other medicine has failed to give relief, and we may say further, that it has proved per- manently benefidial, when other preparations at best gave only temporary relief. div.head: WORD TO TOWN COUNCILLORS. Sermon by the Rev H. Dunnico.
div.p: A WORD TO TOWN COUNCILLORS. Sermon by the Rev H. Dunnico.
SHOULD THE NON-TRADING AGITATION NOW CEASE?

The Parr Hall was packed on Sunday evening when the Rev. H. Dunnico continued his series of services to the people. The subject of his address was " A word to Town Councillors and those who elect them," and his remarks he based on the words "Wisdom is before him that hath understanding, but the eyes of the fool are in the ends of the earth," or as it was, he said, given in another part of the Scriptures," The eyes of a wise man are in his head but the eyes of the fool are in the ends of the earth." Next Sunday, he said, the Mayors and members of the Corporations would be wending their way to Church to ask the blessing of God upon their deliber- ations and he therefore thought it would not be out of place to address a few words to their Town councillors and also to those who elected them. He intended to speak plainly, and, he hoped, as a Christian minister should speak, not from the point of view of any party, political or otherwise, but from the standpoint of a Christian citizen. The wisdom referred to in his text was not that of a man learned in scientific pursuits but the knowledge and understanding of the Bible, wisdom which determined his character and his ultimate destina- tion. "The eyes of the wise man are in his head," that was to say that the wise man troubled himself with his immediate surroundings and did not concern himself as did the fool named in the text with things which did not concern him. There were many men he knew who came under the classification of the fool—men who could not get their breakfasts unless they took up their morning paper to see how Russia and Japan were going on,and whose first action in the evening was to ascertain the result of battles or negotiations in the Far East, but who throughout the day gave hardly a moment's thought to the great moral battle which was constantly being waged in the streets of our town. Men took more interest in degenerates in South Africa than they did in degenerates in this country. Let them assist by all means in the salvation of the world, in any work which would make the world a better and brighter place, but for Heaven's sake let them "go into the world and preach the gospel, but let them begin at Jerusalem." He had received a number of letters criticising—or attempting to criticise him for taking such a subject as he had taken that night for his sermon. He was told that it was not a minister's duty to discuss perplexing political problems or scientific subjects which he did not under- stand but to preach the Gospel. He granted that, but the Gospel was wider than many people imagined. Not long ago a man said he (Mr. Dunnico) preached for 57 minutes on Socialism and three minutes on the Gospel. In the first place that was an absolute lie. In the second place that gentleman was one of the men who said ministers lived up in the clouds and thought of nothing but crowns and angels, and did not belong to the earth. He contended that it was the duty of every Christian minister to take up every question which affected the welfare of their country or their town, and if the side he took upon any question was opposed by any party that was not his fault but the fault of the party. He maintained that it was the duty of every minister to take up the great social questions from the standpoint of Christian citizenship and get at the root of them. There was daring the present day,too much hymn singing, too many prayers, there was too much cant in the world. We wanted prayers but they, were worthless unless manifested in a life spent in trying to make the world more like the world which God intended it should be. That was his firm belief and because that was his belief he spoke upon what some people had said were secular subjects. The Acts of Parliament which granted boroughs the power of self government were the finest acts ever passed by the English nation. By those Acts municipal councils were given the power to do magnifi- cent work, work which would make this world brighter and better than it was. The powers vested in municipal councils were so enormous that they were beyond even the slightest conception of the great bulk of the people They had more power vested in them for doing good and affecting the welfare of the country than had the representatives of the people in Parliament. They had the power to improve the town by exterminating the slums, of preventing crime by means of stricter police 'supervision. They could deal with the great question of the unemployed,could see that the town had a healthy sanitation, and do a thousand and one things which would make the towns of -;ngland far better than they had been. We often asked for certain laws little dreaming that the laws were already in existence together with other laws which if they were put into operation would make this land of ours a veritable paradise. We wanted to recognise that fact. We required to learn that in our hands were certain powers which if used rightly would make men better and cleaner and more like the men of God intended they should be. The Council Chamber was a chamber where to a great extent were decided human destinies. In his opinion in every, town there were two kinds of ministers—the minister of the soul and the minister of the body. He was one who ministered unto the soul, while in their Council Chamber they had the men who ministered unto the body, and the latter should be equally as anxious about the salva- tion of men as the man who stood up in the pulpit and preached. The Kingdom of God would have to come through their great governing bodies as well as through the pulpit, and they wanted the Town Councillors of Warrington to recognize the fact that they had a great opportunity of making the town better and that if they neglected that opportunity they did so at their peril. There was something sacred about the vocation of a town councillor, and their town
IMMNIE11•11

councillors should be made to feel conscious of their high vocation. It was a disgrace to the people of the country if they returned men who were incapable of realizing their high office, and a disgrace and a crime if those who were returned failed to recognize and main- tain the dignity of their positions and carried on the business of the town in a slovenly manner or allowed their debates to be characterized by unseemly behaviour. Men were not sent into Council Chambers to be a part of some political machine but to make the town cleaner arid brighter and to do their very utmost to 'bring in the Kingdom of God upon earth. If there were men on their Town Council who were there for political purposes he main- tained they had no right there, and that the greatest benefit they could confer upon the town would be to retire and make room for better men. They wanted men on their councils who were there purely and solely to further the interests of the town, men who recog- nized the sacredness of their c:lling, and who sought to the best of their ability to carry out their obligations. The Town Council of Warrington could, if they desired, sweepaway the slums in our midst. If they felt so dis- posed they could next week wipe out of existence those dirty sordid places in the town wherein it was almost impossible for anyone to lead a clean and moral life, and substitute places which would be at the least, clean and well ventilated. He knew there were difficulties in the way, especi- ally with regard to the profitableness of such an undertaking but he maintained that they were traitors to the high trust placed in them if they did not see that every man had a house in which he could bring up a family in decency and cleanliness. There was another question. There were in Warring- ton hundreds of men who wanted work but who could not get work. He was quite willing to admit that the problem of the unemployed was a very complicated one arid one which would baffle the wisest of men. No problem was, however, ever solved without experiments being made in the first instance, and it was their Town Council as a body which had to make the experiment with regard to tke unemployed. It was a problem which might never be solved apart from some system of co-operation but however it was solvoil the Town Council was the body which would have! to solve it.. They had the power to pave streets and rather than a man should be allowed to starve or seek relief from the poor law he maintained it was the duty of the Town Council to see that those men who were willing to work were given work to do. Men who would not work he would have whipped in the town square. In tackling the question of the unemployed the Town Council would have to face an expenditure of from £lO,OOO to £20,000, but he firmly believed that if the work was undertaken it could be made to pay. But admitting the whole of the money was lost would it be ' the first £20,000 the Corporation had squandered? He rather thought it would not. He contended most strongly that it was the duty of the Town Council to see that the poorer citizens of the town did not starve. It was a disgrace to a Christian nation that men, strong,able-bodied men with wivesand families to keep, should have to tramp the country in search of employ- ment. It should not be necessary. There was sufficient money in the country to keep them all in comfort and Town Councils must tackle the problem and solve it. Town Councils had under their control the licensing laws and the suppression of crime. Some people said that magistrates granted the licenses and that therefore the Town Councils had no say in the matter. That was so and yet it was not so. The Town Council appointed the police who supervised and inspected the public houses, and it was witnin the power of the police to have all public houses closed which were not conducted properly. That matter was one which closely affected the moral and spiritual well being of their town and their Watch Committee should therefore be composed of men who had no axes to grind—men who were not publicans or brewers and who were not interested in the "trade "in any way. It was essential for the well governing of their town that the Watch Committee should be composed of men who were absolutely above suspicion. So far as Warrington was: eoncerned he must make one protest against the con- stitution of the Watch Committee as he noticed that on that committee there were only three councillors, the rest being aldermen. That he said most emphatically was not right as the aldermen were not responsible to the ratepayers He would like to know how long it was since some of their alderman had appealed to the ratepayers? The aldermen were not the direct repre- sentatives of the ratepayers and the Watch Committee should be composed solely of men who were directly responsible to the ratepayers for their acts, and who had to appeal to the ratepayers at the end of every three years. There was the great question of municipal purity which they had to consider. He did not take sides in that m tter. The non-trading party or the trading party were nothing to him and as parties he cared little for either. He did not know any of the principal men on either side, and both the leader of the non-trading and of the trading parties had spoken about him in terms not altogether lovable. He mentioned that to show that he was speaking from neither a selfish nor a party point of view. He looked at the matter solely from the standpoint of Christian citizenship'. If he could only obtain the friendship of any man by sacrificing his conviction he would rather have that man's enmity than his friendship. If their town councillors were to properly carry out their duties and retain the confidence of the people they must be absolutely and unconditionally above sus- picion, whereas he recognized that to-day the great curse of our public life was self interest. He had no sympathy whatever with the spleen and jealousy which had been manifested to a certain degree by both sides, during the agitation for municipal purity in Warring- ton. A certain amount of spleen was inevitable in such a controversy, but he maintained that if gentlemen wanted to serve the Town Council and the community, and wanted to retain the confidence of the people they must not shrink from making any sacrifice to show that they did not desire to serve on their corporate body for the purpose of advancing self-interest. The question of municipal purity would never be solved by an agitation such as they had witnessed in Warring- ton, because in that agitation both sides had stooped to things to which they ought not to have stooped. They found in Warrington men on both sides who were sacri- ficing principle fora the sake of furthering a policy Only a short time ago the leader of one party supported a publican in Howley Ward although he had condemned others for doing such things in another ward. In the recent fight in Bewsey Ward they found men holding offices in a Chestian Church and profession;temperance principles supporting a publican against a Christian philanithropist. They must not sink their principles aimply because of their policy. It was time the agitation ended. They had had it long enough and it was not doing the town any good and would not do any good sa long as it lasted. If things had been done which ought not to have been done they could not be undone and therefore they ought to let the agitation finish. " Don't go and condemn a man publicly and privately" continued Mr. Minnie() " un- less you have sure and good grounds for condemning him. Remember a man will make mistakes. Even though prompted by the best of motives, the best of men are liable to err. I say Jet the agitation drop. It is killing our town. It is dividing good men and stopping moral progress. It is dividing the power of religion against the Dower of sin. We cannot afford to lose good men. We want to see them united in one c immon crusade against all that is im- pure and bad. I say let it drop and let us see that we put no men into the Council for the purpose of further- ing their own private interests, or the interests of a political party. We want men there who are pure and honest and who will not stoopito political trickery to get there,men with a high sense of their great responsibility and who are there solely in the public interest. In the long run we as a community have no right to criticise our public men. We put them there and because we put them there we are responsible in the last degree for everything they do. We put them there and at the proper time can if neeessary see that they are removed." Continning,Mr. Minnie() said we must put men into the Council not because they belonged to this or that party, but because of their sterling characters and sincerity of purpose. Mr. Dunnico went on to speak on the subject of bribery at elections. Only the previous week, he said, he had seen a man sell his vote for a pot of beer. That man and those who were like him deserved to Ibe sent to gaol and deprived of his right to vote for all time, and the man who • bought his vote deserved kicking out of all respectable society. So long as that continued they would never get men on their Council because they were thinking men or, as it should be, because they were prepared to join in the common crusade against all that was bad. It was time they stopped choosing cash instead of character to represent them on their Council and in Parliament. It was time they stopped putting cash before character, birth before brains. They wanted men who recognized their responsibilities. Carlyle had said that political parties would some day cease to exist,and that there would be two parties" believers"
iIIIIMIIMIENI

and " unbelievers "and he believed that woull come to pass. The political parties divided the force of good- ness but the time would come when men would sink all political differencss and would unite upon one common ground—the bringing of the Kingdom of God upon earth. It might seem &wild dream, but the nation was composed of individuals, and it was for the individuals to seek by honesty andsincerity, to do all they could to usher in the Kingdom of Righteousness.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
A BAD CA.E OP CRUELTY.

At the Newton Police Court, on Thursday, Mary M'Carthy and Thomas M'Carthy, of Burtonwood, were charged with having neglected their two children, aged twelve and seven years respectively. The evidence was to the effect that the father, a collier, was a worthless drunken fellow, and spent his earnings at the public- house. The woman had done her best for the children, but was unable to buy .either food, coal, clothing, or soap to wash the children. One child was covered.with vermin. The case against the woman was withdrawn,but the Bench, in sending the man- to gaol for three months said it was the most sickening case they had ever had before them.

div.head: THREE MONTHS FOR ASSAULTING THE POLICE.
div.p: THREE MONTHS FOR ASSAULTING THE POLICE.

At the Newton-le-Willows Police Court on Thursday Patrick Hannon, a collier, of Burtonwood, was sent to gaol for three months for assaulting two policemen, and fined 20s. and costs, and ss. and costs, respectively, for refusing to quit the Elm Tree Inn, Thartonwood, and with having been drunk and disorderly. Police-constable Dugdale admitted striking prisoner in defence of Police- constable Rainford.
EARLESTOWN CHILD'S PECULIAR DEATH. COMPLAINT AGAINST WARRINGTON WORKHOUSE.

An inquest was held at the Earlestown Town Hall on Thursday touching the death of Ada Marsh, aged three, daughter of James Marsh, a colliery fireman who had deserted his wife, the latter now residing at Hazel- grove, Earlestown. The Coroner said Mrs. Marsh had been left in poor circumstances with a large family,and was some time ago arrested on a charge of deserting her children, but was discharged on promising to go to the workhouse with the children. Two months ago she took her discharge from the workhouse, and deceased was taken charge of by a Mrs. Taylor, of Birch-street, Earlestown, whilst the woman went to Haydock as a housekeeper. Ultimately the child was taken back to its mother, and it died on Saturday from chronic meningitis, accelerated by semi-starvation and uncleanli- ness, as revealed by post mortem examination. In reply to the coroner, Mrs. Marsh said she left the workhouse because the food did not suit her. The Coroner (Mr. Brighouse) said his experience was that if the workhouse was called by another name it would be a nice place. He happened to be the chairman of the Ormskirk Board of Guardians, and he would not mind living in their own workhouse. He lead never heard before of such an accusation against the Warring- ton Workhouse, and he knew something of it. The Coroner said the child appeared to have been knocked about from pillar to post. Mrs. Marsh admitted to the coroner that her• husband had been sent to gaol in relation to the death of a child some time ago. The jury said they would like further evidence of deceased's sister, and the inquiry was adjourned until Wednesday.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
&TIP CANAL DANGER.

At Runcorn, on lonclay. five boy:, named John Parry, Percy Williamson, Fred Kirkham, Leonard White, and , Leonard Heys were charged with throwing stones into the Ship Canal.—Police-sergeant Williams proved the case.—Detective-sergeant Hankinson, of the Ship Canal police, deposed to the great nuisance and danger of the practice. Recently the captain and pilot of the steam- ship Mystic narrowly escaped being struck with a piece of sheet lead. So many bricks had been thrown into ' the canal at Old Quay that a dredger would be legnired ,to get them out. Parry denied the charge, and was dis- missed. The other defendants were each ordered to pay the costs—as.

) ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN. I Thomas Ball, stonemason, of Egerton-street,Runcorn, lon Sunday attempted to commit suicide try cutting his throat with a razor. Dr. Brunton stitched the wound, • and the unfortunate man was removed to the workhouse , hospital. It appears that a few weeks ago he had a narrow escape from falling off a high scaffold at St. John's new church, and the shook had upset his nerves, : and he had been under the treatment of Dc. Robinson, who advised that he should be carefully watched.

div.head: BRUTAL CABDRIVER.
div.p: A BRUTAL CABDRIVER.

At Runcorn on Monday, William Baines, cabdriver to Messrs. Yarwood, was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a horse. Mr. H. N. Linaker, solicitor, was the principal witness, and said he was approaching the railway station on the Ist inst., when he saw the defendant strike a grey horse with a whip twenty or thirty times. He spoke to the defendant, who seemed to resent this, and, stepping back, took a running punch at the horse's stomach. Police-constable Brayford deposed to finding five marks on the horse. The defendant was fined ss. and costs (10s. 611, or fourteen days. Superintendent Ennion, on behalf of the police, thanke,d Mr. Linaker for his action.

div.head: Goad Tempiary.—Opening of a New Room.
div.p: Goad Tempiary.—Opening of a New Room.

Wednesday last week was-a " red letter" day in the annals of the Temperance Mission lodge of the 1.0.G.T. After meeting in Ebenezer Church for two and a half years, the lodge was removed to new quarters in a room to be known as the Mersey-street Mission Room. This room presented a very pleasing ,appearance when a" social was held. About sixty members and friends attended and Bro. Bate P.C.T., presided. The programin was opaaei by Bro. Merlin leading in prayer. A very go od concertina solo was given by Bro. Litigate, and Sister Ada Li ttle wood followed with a pleasing rendering of " Msrry Dick." Some excellent selections were given by Bro. Smith of Earlestown, and were heartily applauded. Sister Emily Littlewood was heard to advantage in "Scenes that are brightest." Bro. Merlin then gave a brief address, explaining the aims and objects of the Good Templar Order. After outlining the objects he urged all those presentwho were members to be true to their pledge. They had undertaken a great work in open- ing that room as a Sunday mission room. They had got together a ban I of thorough-going Christians and it was felt that there was a great need for Christian work in that neighbourhood. He asked for the co-operation of all who were present to make the mission a success. If anyone did not go to any place of worship they would be welcome there and they (the workers) would be pleased to see anyone at both the mission (which would be opened on Sunday the 13th inst), and tho lodge. (Applause.) Those present then took part in a few interesting games which old and young alike heartily enjoyed. An autoharp solo was nicely rendered by Bro. Ludgate. A few more selections on the gramophone including a very fine one, of part of the funeral service of the late President M'Kinley, and a solo by Sister Houghton entitled "Whisper and I shall hear," concluded the programme. During the evening light refreshments were served. A vote of thanks was heartily passed to the artistes and to the lady members of the lodge on the proposition of Bro. J. Sheath, D.G.C.T., seconded by :Bro. J. Brandwood. A very enjoyable evening was brought to a close about ten o'clock by the singing of the Doxology.

div.head: NON-TRADERS TRIUMPH.
div.p: NON-TRADERS TRIUMPH.
EXCITING CONTEST IN TOWN HALL WARD.
William Benson Non-Trader) 419 Alfred J. Jolley ,C) -- Majority 4l

After one of the most exciting municipal contests on record, the Non-Traders achieved a striking victory as the result of the by-election in Town Hall Ward on Tuesday. The importance of this trial of strength was fully realized, and all Warrington was keenly interested in the verdiet of the burgesses. The trad- ing question around which so much heated discus- sion has waged was the one great issue before the ward, and in view of the pub- lication of the long-awaited inquiry reports there was natarally much speculation as to whether the electors would declare their adherence to the principles which they supported in so unmistakable a manner when they returned Mr. James Dodds to the Council two years ago. It was the resignation of Mr. Dodds which created the casual vacancy, and two candidates were soon in the field. The Non-Traders, anxious to retain the representation of the leading, ward, selected Mr. William Benson, a well-known tradesman who has been a warm supporter of the move ment from its inception. The Conservativesafound a candidate in Mr. Alfred J. Jolley who was defeated on the trading question in Fairfield Ward when the Non-Traders scored their remarkable series of triumphs. As a well-known resident in the Ward he was considered a strong nominee. In his address Mr. Jolley denounced the agitation as a "campaign of calumny which had sullied the reputation of the town," and as sine of the Commissioners originally appointed by the Council to conduct the inquiry declared himself "satisfied that the agitation which has so seriously injured the town was unjustifiable." On the other hand Mr. Benson announced that he had been in entire sympathy with "the movement for the purification of the administration of the municipal life of the borough." The election was entered upon with extraordinary enthusiasm, and the band of workers on each side was numerous. Against Mr. Benson there was a formid- able array of forces, the Conservative candidate hav- ing the assistance of townsmen of both political colours who united in opposition to the agitation. To meet such heavy odds, the Non-Traders rallied energetically round Mr. Benson and it speaks much for the completeness of their electioneering work that victory was attained The Ward was thoroughly canvassed by both parties, and the interest which the burgesses took in the campaign is shown by the heavy poll. Of mural literature there was a remarkable variety, practically all dealing with the • trading question. Mr. Henry Roberts joined in the fray, and addressed the electors in the following terms : ' Mr. James Dodds challenges Mr. A. J. Jolley to prove that he (Mr. Dodds) has ever made an 'incorrect state- ment' in connection-with the Non-trading agitation. I accept Mr. Dodds's challenge. Quoting from the Commissioners' report, Mr. Dodds says Page 13 contains a list of 15 large contracts recently let by the Council, amounting in all to £171,476. In every one of these cases the Warrington Slate Company as sub-con- tractors supplied materials in large quantities.' Mr. Dodds further describes this as the enormous indirect tradinc, of Mr. Roberts through the Warrington Slate 'Company ?' Henry'ln the report, pages 249 295, the actual amount of this enormous indirect trading' is given, and it is £12,728 on contracts for £171,476 or not eight per cent. of the total amount of the contracts. These figures were known to Mr. Dodds when he made the foregoing incorrect statement.' Is such conduct honest or fair? In the same report, page 197, it is shown that the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company have done ,C 34,666 worth of indirect trading with the Corporation, or nearly three times as much of the enormous amount of the indirect trading of the Warrington Slate Company in the same period. Mr. Dodds is the Secretary of Pearson and Knowles,his salary is paid'out of the profits on the business of the firm, and he was disqualified during the whole time that he was a member of the Corporation, because according to the opinion of the 'most eminent counsel in England,' he was an official of a Limited Company trading with the Council of which he was a member.' These facts prove that Mr. Dodds is a self-condemned trader with the Corporation! He is included by the inquiry Com- missioners in their report as ' a trailer! ! ! I now challenge Mr. Dodds to reconcile his conduct in the following case with his professions as the leader of the Non-traders :—The Pearson and Knowles Company recently secured a contract for several thousands of pounds from the Corporation of Liverpool for tram car sheds. The Chairman of the Pearson and Knowles Com- pany was a member of Liverpool Corporation Tramways Committee at the time, and also chairman of the Finance Committee. Will MR. DODDS GIVE A. STRAIGHT ANSWER . . . _ .

to the following questions? (a), Why is this sort of trading moral in Liverpool and immoral inWarrington? (b) Why is this sort of trading moral when it is done by the Pearson and Knowles Company and immoral when Monks, Hall and Company or the Slate Company do it? (c) Has Mr. Dodds one code of morals for himself and his own business and another for his neighbours? Mr. Norbury Williams said that Warrington was the most corrupt town in England except one. Mr. Dodds was present when this was said and never opened his mouth to rebuke him. He must, therefore, share the responsibility for the damage which this often repeated statement has done to our town. Not a tittle of evidence to justify such a slander has been given; but, on the contrary, there is abundant evidence which provas that all the trading between limited companies and the Corporation has been honourable and honest and of the greatest pecuniary advantage to the town. The question for you to decide is this: Are you willing that your own townsmen, on honest and honourable terms, shall be allowed to compete in the open market for the business of your own town or do you prefer to drive your trade away, and keep successful and honourable business men out of the Council, and to hand over the control of your municipal concerns, having a capital of over one-and-a-half millions sterling to the management of a class of men of no commercial experience or know- ledge and utterly unequal to the task.? As part of the address was issued in the form of a poster, Mr. Dodds published the following reply on the hoardings on-Tuesday morning : Mr. Henry Roborts asks for some straight answers. Here they are :—First I consider immoral trading equally wrong in Liverpool as in Warrington, and if I were a ratepayer in Liverpool I should denounce it there; second, I say trading is as immoral if done by Pearson awl Knowles if they have shareholders in a Council, as if done by the Slate Company, or Monks Hall and Company; and, therefore, third, I have not one code of morals for myself and my own business,and another for my neighbours.' Although I do not for a moment defend any improper trading by Pearson and Knowles or any other company, it is only just that I should mention that its chairman doea not own a single share in Pearson and Knowles in his own right, but simply as an executor, whereas Mr. Henry. Roberts and his family hold five-eights of the whole share capital of the Slate Company. I • ASK MR. HENRY 'ROBERTS FOR A STRAIGHT ANSWER. to a straight question. I left the Council a few days ago n ot having made a penny profit or received a penny for expenses. What did Mr. Henry Roberts make when he was in the Council ?"

div.head: ARGUMENTS ON BOTH SIDES.
div.p: ARGUMENTS ON BOTH SIDES.

On behalf of Mr. Jolley it was urged that " the non- trading agitation is driving trade out of the town, for articles which are made by Warrington xvorkpeople. Amarican goods are being used to-day in our own rate- supported public buildings, paid for out of our rates, when the same articles, equal in quality.s,re made in our own town by our own working men. Do you want your own townsmen to walk about idle, while their wives and children starve? Do you desire that Warrington trade should go to America to be paid for out of your hard earnings, instead of to your own townspeople, to whom it legally and morally belongs ? Don't be hum- bugged any longer." The Non-Traders distributed quite a sheaf of litera-

ture which called forth a retort from Mr. Jolley to what he termed "disgraceful dodges." Subjects which were dealt with were the Borough Bill of 1899 which involved a lavish expenditure,and the suppression of the auditors' report by the Council in 1900. Attention was called by the Non-Traders to Mr. Jolley's advocacy of the spending of overl£7,soo for the Workhouse extension. "This"it was stated "is in order to force people into the house, and•brand them as paupers, instead of giving temporary outdoor relief to honest, willing but unfortunate workpeeple, who owing to these exceptional times of depression in trade and scarcity of employment are compelled to seek a little temporary assistance." In a circular headed "What Non-Traders have done" it was claimed that "They have broken up the compact and made free men of the electors. They have done away with the agree- ment by which a man once an alderman was to be always an alderman and made free men of councillors, They have broken up the exclusiveness of committees and forced masterful chairmen to "let members, and through them the public, know something of what is going on 'behind the scenes.' fhey have made the opening of tenders except in a regular manner impos- sible by fear of exposure. • They have made it difficult for anyone in the Council to suppress the auditors re- ports, the chief safeguard the ratepayers have to show that their money has been honestly spent. They have cleared the Council of traders and most of those inter- ested in the traders. The inquiry has done good and will be a lasting benefit to the town."____

div.head: THE-POLLING AND RESULT.
div.p: THE-POLLING AND RESULT.

_ Polling throughout the day was brisk, 800 electors out of 934 entitled to the franchise recording their votes. The booth was at the Infant school, Kendrick- street, the officials in charge being :—Presiding officers. Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins and Alfred Starkey; poll clerks, Messrs. W.T. Crank and H. Essenhigh. At eight o'clock the boxes were conveyed to the Tom; Hall and the counting was proceeded with in the committee room in the presence of Alderman Smethurst. (returning officer), Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Wilson), the candidates and others. The counting occupied less than half an hour,and to the gratification of the Non-Trading workers it was found that Mr. Benson had, as recorded at the head of this report, triumphed by a majority of 41. There were only two spoilt papers. Councillor BENSON, in proposing a vote of thanks to Alderman Smethurst for his services as returning officer, said he need hardly speak about the officials, who had always been very agreeable. He wished also to say the same about the opposing candidate. There had been no ill-feeling whatever between them. Mr. JOLLEY seconded, and said that so far as their personal relations were concerned they had been of the most friendly character. The election could not have been conducted in a better manner. He seconded the proposition that their thanks be given to the Returning Officer and to all who had officially taken part in the election.
The m3tion was carried, ant Atdrmrn SmertiugsT riefly returned thanks. SPEECHES FRONI TEIE TOWN HALL STEPS.

A large crowd assembled outside the Town Hall to hear the declaration of the result, and loud cheers were raised when Mr. Benson's success was known. Councillor BENSON thanked the electors most cordi- ally for returning him, and said he should endeavour to give satisfaction. He was much obliged, not only on his own behalf, but on behalf of the Non-traders whom he represented. The contest on his part was a duty more than anything else. He desired to thank all the workers for their services. There had been no ill-feeling on the part of the opposite side. He returned all his .hearty thanks. (Applause). Mr. PEMBERTON, who was received with applause, said he must thank them most heartily for the return of Mr. Benson. (Cheers and some cries of "Rats.") It had not altogether been a ques- tion of Mr. Benson against Mr. Jolley, but whether the town should allow itself to go back to trading as against Non-trading. (Hear, hear.) They had been under the impression that trading was dead, but it seemed that because they had not won many elections and had not worked at them last November, tne opposition had thought they would go back to trading. The unfortunate thing about the matter was this : that thousands and thousands of pounds had been spent which otherwise would not have been. It was not altogether the amount of money that had been got in the way of trade profits, but the enormous amount of money that had been spent to get those profits. There had been hundreds of thousands of pounds spent that were unnecessary. He would grant that some of the expenditure was necessary, but there were hundreds df thousands totally unnecessary and which had been spent to get a few handrei nounis of profit on materials that had been supplied. The question all depended on the ratepayers of the town. They had it in their power to say what should be done in that Town Hall and what should not be done. If the rates went up the rents were bound to go up. Look at the rents in Man- chester and Liverpool. For a roar-roomed house in Liver- pool they had to pay ss. 6d. a week because the rates were high. Because they did not pay the rates direct they might think they were not paying any, but they paid in the rent, and as sure as they were present if their rates want up in that town their rents were bound to follow. Manufacturers would be kept from coming to the town and the town would be kept from progress- ing. As trade was so badand rates so high, all expendi- tureshould be stopped unless it was absolutely necessary for 'the time being, until the ratable value had been allowed to recover itself and they could bring more manufacturers into the borough. Then they might spend more money. No money ought to be spent except what was absolutely necessary, and with the help of the public the Non-Traders would help to carry that out. He was much obliged to the electors for supporting the cause. (Applause.) The crowd then dispersed.

div.head: LONG PASTORATE. Rev. John Yonge's Twenty-eighth Anniversary,
div.p: A LONG PASTORATE. Rev. John Yonge's Twenty-eighth Anniversary,

The attainment by the Rev. Sohn Yonge of his twenty-eighth anniversary as pastor of Wycliffe Con- gregational Church was fittingly recognized at the close of the service on Sunday evening. The incident was all the more pleasing as it was quite unexpected on Mr. Yonge's part, and it bore eloquent testimony to the esteem in which he is held by the members of his congregation. Mr. EDWARD WALLINGTON, addressing the large assembly, said a number of members of the, congrega- tion thought they ought to take advantage of the opportunity of congratulating Mr. Yonge on his twenty-eighth anniversary as minister at Wycliffe, and he had been asked to give expression to those wishes. Very few churches indeed were able to celebrate such an anniversary as they at Wycliffe could that day, and in having had Mr. Yonge as their minister for so many years they had been most highly favoured. Turning to iNir. Yonge, Mr. Wallington said: In the name of the members of the church and congregation worshipping at Wycliffe and at Cockhedge, I beg to offer you and Mrs. Yonge our heartiest congratulations on this the 'twenty-eighth year of your ministry at Wycliffe, to assure you that you retain undiminished our honour and esteem, while our love and affection have become more and more intensified as the years have passed by. We earnestly pray that you may yet be spared to us for many years, cheered and encouraged by the love and affection of your people, and that you may ever be calmly conscious of the approval of the Master whom you have so long and faithfully served. I Mr. J. PODMORE added a few words, and the congre- gation expressed their approval of the congratulatory sentiments by standing. The Rev. JOHN YONGE briefly expressed the gratifica- tion which it afforded him to receive such an expression of esteem and affection after twenty-eight years of ministry at Wycliffe. He felt hampered by the sudden- ness of the expression and scarcely knew how to respond to it; except to assure the congregation that all their expressions of confidence and regard were cordially I• reciprocated by Mrs. Yonge and himself. Although I when a man reciprocated, his (Mr. Yonge's) age he sometimes had misgivings as to whether he could with propriety much longer retain such a position, it was a consider- able source of satisfaction to be assured that the desire of the people was that he should continue to act as their minister so long as health might enable him.
EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN Y OUNG MEN'S _BIBLE CLASS.

In Connection with the above class, a lecture was given in the Wesleyan Chapel, Earlestown o n Thursday evening, by the Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford of Leeds ,on "The Priest on his trial." Mr. Thomas Ormand, J.P. presided and there was a large audience.—The lecture was of an interesting .character dealing in the man with the spread of Romantan in the Anglican church. The teachings and precepts of the Roman Church were dealt with, and the lecturer advised his hearers to hold fast in the faith of Jesus Christ. Votes of thanks to the lecturer and chairman were heartily accorded.

div.head: EMMANUEL SALE OF WORK.
div.p: EMMANUEL SALE OF WORK.

The opening ceremony in connection with the annual sale of work in aid of the funds of Emmanuel Church attracted a large gathering to the schoolroom (over Arpley Station) on Wednesday. The Rev. F. VAUGHAN presided and at the outset re- marked that for many years the sale of work had been regularly held, for the simple reason that at the present time it was a vital necessity for the well-being of Emmanuel Church. To-day they remained staunch and true to the principles which animated their forefathers who saw fit to start a branch of Christian work known as the Emmanuel Reformed Episcopal Church. To-day , they stood in the heritage of their forefathers whose memories they honoured by remaining true to their principles. They stood as Christian people and as suchtfelt they had a claim 'upon the sympathies of other Christian bodies who joined with them in the one common head—their Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ They were gathered together as Protestants— persons who by their very existence pro- tested against the innovations of Romanism, ritualism and priestcraft, which had crept into established churches of the land, and which made the worship of the staunch children of the church practic- ally impossible. They stood there as Evangelical Church people believing in the fundamental principle of brotherly love and friendship and believing that in the conduct of their services they had retained all that was dignified, all that was true and evangelical. They believed they had expunged from the Book of Common Prayer all those phrases which lent themselves to the Romanising influences of the priesthood, and they had endeavoured to bind together the enthusiasm of Methodism and the dignity of a liturgical service. Tt was in that way they were desirous of helping forward the work of God's church and to him it was a great privilege to find himself surrounded by such an earnest band of workers. It was with the object of helping for- ward their work, by helping the expenses of the church, that the sale of -work was being held as without the assistance they got from the sale of work it would be impossible to carry on the work of the church. They were face to face with a great difficulty. For seven- teen years they had held their Sunday school in that room which the railway company now required for purposes of their own. The consequence was that they had to look for another place in which to bold their school, and he, personally was of the opinion that the time had arrived when they should build schools of their own in which their children could be nourished in the faith of their fathers in which their views would not be warped by the seditious influences of Jesuitical priestcraft. (Applause.) Mr. JOAN TAYLOR said they had every reason to feel proud of the unity which existed amongst the people of Emmanuel Church, and of the work done by the members of the Church. At their head they ha,d a man who could be described as the right man in the right place—(hear, hear,)—and to Mr. Vaughan he would say that it was in parochial work that the value lay. He was especially pleased to see that their minister followed the practice of visiting the members of his congregation especially the poorer members, and he would strongly urge the great good by, and the progress which resulted from constant visitation. He wished the Church every prosperity and hoped the sale, which he had pleasure in declaring open, would be a success. (Applause.) Mr. TAYLOR was heartily thanked for his services on , the motion of Mr. T. ALLEN, seconded by Mr. WILLrAm I ATHERTON, and the sales for the day commenced. _ _

The Rev.F.VAuGHAN announced that he kad received £l2 13s. 6d. in donations. (Applause.) The stalls which contained a large variety of articles useful as well as ornamental were in the charge of the following Fidies :—Minister's stall, Mrs. Vaughan, con- gregation stall, Mrs. Norman; Sunday School stall, Mrs Gandy; flower stall, Miss Heald. Miss Hodge, Miss Carriage; children's stall, Miss Booth; and refreshment stall, Miss Lees, Mrs. A. Landon. General assistance was given by the officers and friends of the Church. In the evening concerts, which were well attended, were given by Miss Turner's Mandoline band, and Mr. Ditchfleld who gave a number of selections on the gramophone. The sales for Wednesday realized £5O Os. THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

There was a crowded attendance at the opening ceremony on Thursday. The Rev. F. Vaughan again presided and explained the object of the sale. There were certain current theories with regard to apostolic succession and certainly the belief in the direct succes- sion of the life, work,. and methods of the apostles was the foundation of their church. They believed persons were in the apostolic succession when they were animated by the apostolic spirit and who were ever ready to help forward any good work. If they believed that, it seemed to him they had the privilege that afternoon of having in their midst one who was in the apostolic line of God's children, in the person of Miss Bessie Dutton. (Applause.) Miss BESSIE DUTTON thanked Mr. Vaughan for his kindness though she feared he had placed her upon a higher platform than she had a right to occupy. She was sorry they had to give up those rooms which had suited their requirements as a Sunday school for so many years, though good might arise from their adver- sity, as people hearing of their difficulty might be con- strained to help to a greater extent than they had intended and they might receive practical help from directions from which it might not otherwise have been forthcom- ing. Sales of work did a great good in bringing people together, and in inducing one congregation to regard another conregation with a little more love than was sometimes the case. They had had a great deal of trouble over the recent educational enactment but if they had to protest against the real in- justices of that Act let them do it in as brotherly and charitable a manner as was possible. No educational enactment could be permanent in this country which did not see that justice was done to every religious denomination, so we hada perfect right to hope that there would shortly be something better than there was at the present time, but while they worked with that object in view let them do it with as much love as possible. (Applause). She had great pleasure in declaring the sale open, and hoped it would be in every way a success. (Applause). ' On the motion of Mr. Allen seconded by Mr. Gandy (Earlestown) Miss Dutton was thanked for her serviees and the sales for the day commenced.

div.head: Funeral of the Late Mr. Jno. Hedgeock.
div.p: Funeral of the Late Mr. Jno. Hedgeock.

The funeral of the late Mr. Jno. Hedgcock, whose death was recorded last week, took place at the Hill Cliff. burial ground on Saturday afternoon in the presence of a large number of relatives and friends The chief mourners were :—Messrs. There were a large gnumber of wreaths sent including the following :—The family, Mesdames Barlow and Wild (sisters), Mr. AV. Barlow and family, the nephews and nieces, Mr. and Mrs. W. J. a little along the cushion, the use ot this sige would inevitably cause the .red to kiss the _while which, of course, would mean no cannon beibc, made. If, however, the cue-ball be struck with plenty of running side the red ball will come off the cushion very squarely, and in this way a kiss may be avoided. Of course, however well the stroke may be played the kiss is only just avoided. When the stroke is played with run- ning side the cannon may often be got even though a- kiss take place between the object balls, provided the kiss be not very pronounced, for should the kiss only slightly move the second object ball the cue-ball will catch it up. The running side causes the cue-ball to run on after striking the cushion, even though the stroke be played quite gently, whereas )check side would stop the cue-ball immediately it struck the cushion. Running side also increases the cue- ball's angle of deflection off the cushion, and this assists in making the stroke (should a slight kiss take place between the object balls.) • This run-through cannon is not an easy stroke to get, as owing to the cue-ball being SO CIOSO te the red, a very good touch is required to make the cue-ball run on after contact with the object ball. Moreover, although a fine example of the rffect that side on a cue-ball has on an object ball dead on a cushion, the stroke is not of very much use, as firstly, such a position very seldom occurs; and secondly, a successful cannon gener- ally leaves bad position. If players will try this stroke they will find that when they get the cannon a cover -will often be left for the next stroke, and even when this does not occur the position will be none too grand. div.head: ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS.
div.p: ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS.

" Enquirer " (Bristol).—When the striker's ball is touching another ball, the red goes on the spot and the object white on the centre spot, and the player plays from the D. When a ball is exactly on the baulk line the ball is not playable, but if it is the least bit over the line it-may be hit anywhere. "Potting the White" (Rochdale).—Certainly it is the game to pot the white when it suits you to do so, but why only pot it when you want just two for game? J. Murphy (Drogheda).—You are wrong about the Irish champion's record. He has never made a 500 break under the present rules. Five years ago he made a break of 279 against John Roberts and this has remained his record break until about a fortnight ago, when playing a match in Glasgow he made a break of 288. I believe Duncan is the first professional this year to beat his record. The break was made with crystalate balls, and last year no less than five professionals beat their records when playing with these balls, notably Stevenson when be made 703._ _

E. McLaren (Edinburgh.)—lt is true that Aiken beat Roberts by very nearly the points he received, but you must not forget that a felv weeks ago Aiken beat Stevenson quite as easily. C. E. Jones (Wakefield).—You will find the averages of the leading players given every week in "The World of Billiards.';

" Run-through ;(Bridlington).—lt so happens that my next ten or twelve articles will treat entirely on run-throughs, so that you will find this branch of the game dealt witl very thoroughly. H. P. Tozer (Plymouth).—lf you can give your opponent 40 in a hundred and instead of giving him points you want to owe a number, you should owe 65 or 70 (the proportion works out at 662-3). H. W. W. (Wolverhampton).—The measurements you require are as follows :—Baulk line 12 inches from the cushion, D line 10 inches, spot 5 inches from nose of cushion. The cushion should be a little higher than half the diameter of the balls. With 11 inch balls seven- eighths of an inch would be a good height. Next week some notes will be given on the game now in progress between Roberts and Reece. RISO LEVI.

On the start Rylands' pressed, and Clare made a fine run arid scored an easy try. Up to half time play was slightly in favour of the " Wirepullers." On play being resumed, the home team were conspicuous by the fine tackling of Foster and Peen:, whilst a more promising full back than Backhouse it would be hard to find. LEIGH v. WIGAN.

Played at Leigh, before 8,000 spectators. In the first half Wigan, with the wind behind them, had the best of play, but could not score, though they tried sever4l long shots at goal, which failed. After changing ends Burgess dropped a goal for Leigh, who pressed hard Neville almost scored after a fine run. Result—Leigh, 2 points: Wigan, nil. HU:s;SLET v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

Played at Hunslet, before 5,000 people. In the first half Hunslet put on a couple of goals, Walter Gold- thorpe placing one of them and his brother Albert the other. In the second half Hunslet continued to have the best of play, and Albert Goldthorpe kicked a third goal. Result—Hunslet, 3 goals; Broughton Rangers, nil.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON " A " ROCHDALE HORNETS "A."

There was another capital attendance on Saturday at the Warrington enclosure, when the " A " team added another win to their long sequence of victories. Roch- dale had the assistance of a strong breeze during the initial half, and the opening phases of the match were warmly contested at mid-field. By the aid of superior combination,Warrington got within measurable distance of the Rochdale line, and Davies and Duckworth fre- quently opened out the game' but the tackling was safe and the danger was averted. Booth cleared and Knight, in responding, raced round several backs, but in essay- ing to make further progress, lost possession of the ball, and Fielding, securing, raced over the Warrington line from his own half. A goal followed. This turn of events put the home men on their mettle and Berry and Davies were the leaders in a movement which gave the visitors trouble. The attack was main- tained and Brooks scored cleverly,Knight failing to im- prove. Another round of passing ended in Brooks be- ing pulled up on the line. Warrington attacked again, and a fine dribble by Harmer was deserving of reward, the player taking the ball over the line, but had the hard luck to have the ball kicked from under him. Half-time : Rochdale Hornets, five points ; Warring- ton three points. Resuming the home men forced the pace, and the game rarely escaped the visitors' quarters. A capital round of passing ended in Brooks scoring a try which Knight improved upon. As the game pro- ceeded the efforts of the Rochdale men to check the locals became more feeble,andafter Knight had dropped , a goal, further tries were scored by Jordan and Forster. I Final: Warrington " A," two goals four tries (16 points) ; Rochdale Hornets 'A," one goal one try (five points).

Even play followed till Robertson's were penalised, and Kennedy tried for goal but failed. The home forwards now rushed the ball up the field, and from a scrimmage Fell, Robertson's half back received and tricked all opposi- tion and scored a splendid try. The same player then added the goal. Even play followed till half time the score being Robertson's, 5 points; Widnes Rangers, nil. The visitors resumed and play for a while settled/ in the home 25 until Watkins relieved by a splendid kick in touch: Following a scrimmage Kennedy received and passed to the centre who dashed over the line. Resuming the home team rushed the ball into the visitors'quarters, and Fell receiving the ball from the pack, kicked over the line, one of their centres tackled, and Winstanley touched do wn,•but the point was disallowed. From the scrummage Burgess re- ceived and passed to Green who was knocked over the corner flag. Result—Robertson's, 5 points ;`, Widnes Rangers, 5 points.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

ATTEMPTED TILL ROBBERY.—At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, James Foster,a.tramp, was charged with attempting to steal the sum of £ll 6s. the pro- perty of Mrs. Elizabeth West, grocer, 31, Walton-road Stockton Heath.—Mrs. West said she was in the kitchen on October 25th when she saw a shadow on the wall. On going into the shop she saw the prisoner inside the counter with his hand in the cash drawer. She asked him what he was doing, and he replied that he was looking for her. She held him and called her daughter. The latter looked if prisoner had taken any money, but as none was missing she let him go, and informed the police.—P.C. Williams, said that when arrested prisoner said it was the first he had heard of it—it must have been someone else.—Prisoner said he went to the shop to ask for something to eat. He denied having his hand on the drawer.—Forster, who bore a bad character was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour. FINED Fon. TRESPASSING.—CharIes Birchall, 73, Walton-road, Stockton Heath, was summoned at Dares- bury St ssions on Tuesday, for trespassing on land belonging to Mr. Jonathan Barrow, Grappenhall, on October 16th, in pursuit of game. Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Browne, solicitor, appeared to prose- cute, and said defendant was caught at the time by a constable, whom he asked to look over the offence as he was very sorry. Constable Williams was standing near the field when he saw the defendant urge his dog to go in the field for the purpose of getting game. The constable told him that he had no right to send his dog in the field.—Constable Williams bore out Mr. Browne's statement.—Defendant said be was unaware that the dog was hr the field. When the animal came out he thrashed it.—Birchall was fined 20s. and costs, together with the advocate's fee. A DANGEROUS PRACTICE.—Robert Tipping, Lumb Brook Cottage, Stockton Heath, was charged at the Daresbury Sessions, with firing off a gun on the public highway at Latchford Without on October 15th.—The evidence showed that defendant was standing on the footpath and discharged a gun. There were several cyclists passing at the time.—Defendant said he was not aware that it was wrong to fire on the highroad, when the gun was turned in the opposite direction. He was firing over the canal.—He wits fined ss.

div.head: Another Constable Required. —The Recent Robbery.
div.p: Another Constable Required. —The Recent Robbery.

The Great Sankey Parish Council met on Monday evening under the presidency of Mr, George Thompson. There were also present :—Messrs. W. Furness, J. Taylor,, F. Jefferson, H. Fairclough and Joseph Smith (clerk).

div.head: LIGHTING OF CEMETERY ROAD.
div.p: THE LIGHTING OF CEMETERY ROAD.
The Chairman reported that this road was now satis- factorily lighted, and the cost of laying the main had been only 10s. to each of the townships (Sankey and Penketh.)

div.head: DANGERS OF SANKEY STATION.
div.p: THE DANGERS OF SANKEY STATION.

The Clerk informed the Council that he had com- municated with Mr. James Pinion, the recently appointed manager of the Cheshire Lines Committee, stating that the Parish Council felt it was very desir- able that facilities should be provided for passengers booking for Warrington and beyond by means of an office on the north platform or alternatively a foot bridge or a subway. The existing arrangsment necessitated crossing the line by means of the road bridge;which was a considerable distance from the book- ing office, or by going over the rails. Apart from the fatality which occurred about two years ago, attention had been called to the ever-present danger consequent upon passengers running the risk through want of time and a more convenient arrangement. The members of the Council felt that a great responsibility rested upon them individually until they had made every effort to induce the committee to provide means whereby the public might avoid the present risk and inconvenience. Mr. Pinion had replied that it was his intention to visit the station at the first opportunity, after which he would write Mr. Smith further. No additional com- munication had been received, although the letter was dated September Bth.

div.head: DELIVERY OF LETTERS.
div.p: THE DELIVERY OF LETTERS.

The Clerk said that as instructed by the Council he had written to the Postmaster calling attention' to the fact that letters &c. addressed to Great Sankey were being sent on to Peiketh instead of being delivered direct from Warrington, thus causing considerable in- convenience and annoyance. He (Mr. Smith) could personally testify to that fact, as be received over 2,000 letters per anntim.—The letter was duly acknow- leqed, but since then he had received several communi- cations which had been sent on to Penketh and re- delivered.

div.head: POLICING OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: THE POLICING OF THE DISTRICT.

The Chairman alluded to the recent case of shop- breaking at Sankey, and said a great • many people in Cuerdley, Penketb, and Sankey considered the district was inadequately policed. The population of the three townships numbered nearly 3,000, and the combined acreage was about 4,005 acres. To serve that large district there were only three police officers—a sergeant and two constables. A great deal of the sergeant's time was occu- pied in clerical and supervising work, and such heavy duties devolved upon the officers that it was thought Sankey ought to have another constable. Police superintendents had been approached, hut with no satis- factory result, and he (Mr. Thompson) had been informed that the best course to adopt was to consult the Chief Constable of the county. Mr. Furness asked if the Chairman had any idea as to the policing of other districts of the same area. The Clerk remarked that there were two constables at Burtonwood, and a third was employed by the Collins Green Colliery Company. There was only one sergeant for Burtonwood, Cuerdley, Penketh and Sankey. On the motion of Mr. Fairclough seconded by Mr. Furness the clerk was instructed to write to the Chief Constable asking for an additional constable to be stationedat Sankey.

A WATER QUESTION.-MR. FURNESS'S PROTEST. The Council proceeded to Consider the question of the proposed water supply to Mr. Harry Fairclough's farm, Long-lane, which had been referred to them by the District Council. Mr. F. W. Kerfoot, inspector to the District Council, wrote stating that Mr. Deas' the Corporation water engineer, estimated the cost of laying the main at £l.BO and the Corporation would undertake to provida and lay the necessary service pipe, taps Sco., for £3 2s. Their terms for the water would. be 8 per cent on the outlay for seven years. Mr. Fair- clough had stated that the anent flr the property (Mr. Selby) would be responsible one half of the expense, and he himself was prepared to contribute an addi- tional £2O.

M. Furness said he did not think it was the Council's duty to provide water in the interests of one individual and throw the responsibility on the rates. If there was an immediate prospect of building operations being commenced it might be a different matter, but as it was the expenditure would be considerable and he objected to the rates of the parish being pledged to save the pockets of the landlords. It was the duty of the land- lord, he contended, to supply Mr. Eairclough with water. If the Council acceded to the present applica- tion they did not know where the matter was going to end. His objection was not in the least a personal one. Mr. Fairclough said his landlord was prepared to pay half of the expense, and he thought that was a very good offer.

Mr. Furness: I think he ought to pay the whole lot. Mr. Fairclough: I don't. It has been done for one and I say it should be done for another. Mr. Furness: That is my point. It should not have been done at all. The principle is radically wrong. If it was in the interests of a number of parishioners it would be a different thing altogether. We should be lacking in our duty if we allowed ourselves to be led away by a precedent of this kind. If you decide by a majolity that Mr. Fairclough in to have the water and we are to take the responsibility, I think before you do that you ought to consult the'parishioners. I am in- cliped to think that if the matter is left as it is and pressure is brought to bear on the landlords they will see the advisability of putting water in. Mr. Fairclough said Mr. Selby, the agent, told him he would not go any further in the matter. Mr. Furness: It is a question for Mr. Selby and the Warrington water department. Mr. Fairclough said he had not any water for domestic purpOses. The Chairman said that in the case of Mr. Taylor the Council considered that almost the whole of the cost would be met by the rates he would pay. The other property in the neighbourhood must ultimately pay more than the balance of expenditure, and the Council would not be liable for any money there for very long. Mr. Furness said he did not see much objection to the extension where there was a prospect of an adequate I return, but in this case there was pot. He moved a resolution that while the Council were of opinion that Mr. Fairclough ought to have and his landlord ought to provide an adequate supply, they could not see their way to enter into any responsibility in the matter. There was no seconder.
The Clerk said he estimated that the supply would entail an annual charge upon the township for seven years of .£4 145... .1 . .

After further discussion it was decided that Messrs. Furness and Jefferson should wilt upon the Town Clerk, inform him that the Council considered the charge excessive, and try to obtain a reduction. The clerk was instructed to write to Mr. Michoel Hughes, who owns property in the Long-lane neighbourhood, asking him to contribute towards the expenditure. Mr. Furness withdrew his resolution.

div.head: An Interesting Anniversary.
div.p: An Interesting Anniversary.

To the thousands who peruse our columns the advertisements of Angier's Emulsion that have appeared regularly in this journal will be "old, familiar friends." And to not a few of our readers the remedy itself will be an "old, familiar friend." We feel, therefore, that we shall be giving a certain item of News to-day that will be of wide interest when we state that on the 12th November twelve years ago to-day the first bottle of Angier's Emulsion was sold in the United Kingdom. It is now sold by practically every chemist in England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, and is in request alike in the large towns and the small villages. In short, wherever there is a chemist Angiers' Emulsion can be obtained. A success of this magnitude, after only twelve years, is truly phenomenal, and it can only have been achieved through genuine merit. • o amount of advertising can win permanent success for an inferior article. Angier's Emulsion has proved its value. It deserves its success, and its " birthday" is the more worthy of recognition in that the remedy—unlike so many new medicines—is not a mere new combination of old familiar drugs. It is a genuinely new remedy—one never before used in modern pharmacy. In fact, had it not been for the proprietors of Angier's Emulsion, and their discovery of new methods of purifying petroleum, this valuable remedy would have' been lost to us, per- haps for generations. Altogether, therefore, we heartily congratulate the Angier Chemical Company on the most notable anniversary they celebrate to-day, and we hope that their deserved success may long continne.
