div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not later than Thursday. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases sent their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

div.head: Town Hall Ward Election. Mr. Dodds and Mr. Henry Roberts.
div.p: Town Hall Ward Election. Mr. Dodds and Mr. Henry Roberts.

Sir,—lna circular issued on the eve of the Town Hall Ward election Mr. Henry Roberts accepted a challenge of mine to Mr. A. J. Jolley to give a single instance of an incorrect statement I had ever made during the Non- trading agitation. Mr. Roberts does not find his alleged instance in anything I had said during the agitation, but in a subsequent clause in the letter con- taining the challenge. Disingenuously, indeed *unscrupulously I fear, Mr. Roberts puts a statement into my mouth which I never made. I never described the fact of the Warrington Slate Company having supplied materials in large quantities under each of 15 large contracts, recently let by the Warrington Council amounting to £171,476, as the" enormous indirect trad- ing of Mr. Henry Roberts through the Warrington Slate Company." A comparison of my letter with the circular will at once prove this. Mr. Roberts proceeds :—" In the Report pages 294 and 295, the actual amount of "this enormous indirect trading" is given, and it is £12,728 on contracts for £171,476, or not 8 per cent. of the total amount of the contracts." I turn to pages 294 and 295 of the Report and I find that £12,828 is the amount supplied by the Slate Company (211,983 direct and £845 through Mr. J. B. Johnson) in respect only of the six contracts of C. W. Davenport, amounting together to £76,202—n0t £171,496 as "inadvertently" stated by Mr. Henry Roberti ! Moreover, this £12,828 does not include any- thing for goods supplied by the Slate Company in res- pect of the contracts included in the £76,202, through Davenport's sub-contractors other than J. B. Johnson! How much this may have been the Commissioners found it impossible to state owing to the refusal of Mr. Henry Roberts to attend before them and give evidence, Then as regards the balance of the " contracts recently let by the Council," that is nine contracts representing £88,583, and in respect of which "in every case the Slate Company, as sub-contractors, supplied materials in large quantities,"—owing again to Mr. H. Roberts' refusal to give evidence—it was found impossible to state the value so supplied by the Slate Company. From the report(277)we find that onaccomit of one of such jobs (the"Winwick Reservoir Contract" amount £18503), Mr. Dean stated that" he believed the Slate Company supplied the material." On the same page of the report we find that Mr. Haddock stated that most of the stuff for the Gas Works Extension (another of such contracts) came from the Slate Com- pany. Clearly I was absolutely justified instating that for'a company with about £17,000 paid up capital, the indirect trading of the Slate Company represented "an enormous amount" and lam prepared to venture to estimate from carefully obtained outside expert assistance and evidence which I have been able to secure that the trading direct and indirect of the Slate Company_with the Warrington Corporation during the seven years of the inquiry has been several times the sum of the ascertained £16,660 of direct trading. I have asked Mr.,Roberts to state what he made out of the Corporation while he was in the Council. I now further challenge him to open his books to independent accountants to be agreed upon by the Council and the Non-Trading Association, and to thereby disprove my above estimate of the amount of indirkt trading his Company has done, in other words to prove that my statement that an "enormous amount of indirect trad- ing has been done by him through his Company during the seven inquiry years, is incorrect." Mr. Roberts knows from the report that the only orders received by Pearson and Knowles during the part of the seven years I was in the Council amounted to about nineteen shillings (report 157); he knows, also that I was not a shareholder in Pearson and Knowles while in the Council, and he knows further (report 288) that I was entirely outside any connection with any trading as defined by the resolutions governing the Inquiry, and that therefore my name was wrongly inclOed by Messrs. Birchall, Greening and Jolley, in their starred list of traders. He also knows that, every penny of the seven years' trading of Pearson and Knowles £34,660 (a relatively insignificant item out of that company's total sales, lea; indeed than one-third of one per cent, of the same) represented fair and honourable business secured while they had no interested representative in the Council. It is peculiarly gratifying to meto have gone through an ardous struggle without having made one statement that has been successfully challenged; it is also a satis- faction to known from Tuesday's election, that the in- dependent and disinterested ratepayers of Warrington are still at the back of the Non-traders,—Yours &c.. JAMES DODDS. November 10th, 1904.

div.head: Mr. Dodds and the Rev. N. Dunnico.
div.p: Mr. Dodds and the Rev. N. Dunnico.

Sir,—l have read the report of the sermon of the Rev. H. Dnnnico in Parr Hall on Sunday last. With much that he said I am in agreement, but there are two personal references upon which I propose to remark. Ist. The preacher is reported to have said, in regard to the Non-trading movement that "there had been too much spleen and bitterness and jealousy manifested on both sides," that "he had come into conflict with the leaders of both parties," also that "rather than retain a man's friendship as the sacrifice of conviction or the price of silence he would prefer that man's enmity." I do not know how far this refers to me. I will only say that I never saw Mr. Dunnico until last week, and only then by the purest accident, and that I nave never sought his acquaintance—on the other hand he has himself twice appealed directly to me by letter for financial help in his work. On the first occasion I sent him a guinea, but on the receipt of his second application, I declined to contri- bute until he had publicly withdrawn an assertion he had just previously and publicly made to the effect that the Non-Trading movement was the "outcome of spleen and jealously." He replied explaining that he did not include me in his condemnation, that in fact he had excluded men, as I was not at the time he spoke a mem- ber of the Non-Trading Association. 2nd. Further on in his address Mr. Dunnico says "only a short time ago the leader of one party sup- ported a publican in Howley Ward, although he had condemned others for doing such things in another." This reference is clearly to myself, and I now desire to say that it is quite true I supported a publican in Howley Ward, and further that as the leader of the purity agita- tion I had no alternative even had I wished it. 'Every little boy in Warrington knows" that I broke with the majority of the leaders of the Non-Trading movement in connection with Mr. Fred Stott's candidature a year ago, and that that majority contended that although Mr. Stott was sound on the Non-Trading issue, they could not support him owing to his being a socialist. I combated this view, and i held (as also n a speech at Parr Hall) that as non- traders we had no concern whatever with a candidate's politics, religion or occupation, so long as he was res- pectable and was an honest supporter of our platform. These I believed Mr. Stott to be, and I did all in my power to help him as against the official Non-Trading candidates, who was by the way _a publican. When the casual vacancy in the Howley Ward occurred, we had the same Conservative Candidate whom we had fought and defeated some months previously. Against him Mr. Thomas Chantler,a publican,came out as a thorough non-trader, and I was not only bound to support him, but having known him for over 20 years as an employe of my fins, and as a thoroughly reliable and intelligent man I was glad to do so. I have known many publicans during my 26 years in Warrington, and amongst them some good and estimable men. If a publican or a brewer will help me by a donation or by services in a good cause I will accept his aid ; if he undertakes a good work I will support him. On the other hand I will neither help him nor seek, nor welcome his aid in a questionable or bad cause, and hence my strictures upon the action of Mr. Councillor Luke Ellison in regard to the Non- trading cause, which has aimed only, as I know, at the purification of our local administration by the Aoppage of immoral trading and the breaking up of a political compact which has fostered and sheltered it. Mr. Ellison has not only defended and supported trading and the compact, but while a leading teetotaller (which lam not) a leader of the Recha,bites and of the Good Templars (whose main object I believe is the overthrow of the liquor traffic)—and while a steward of the Wesleyan Church and an official of the Liberal party (neither of which I am) he has gone olit of his way to support a Tory brewer, who- was pledged to oppose the purity movement. I have written this letter solely in vindication of my consistency throughout, and not in any controversial spirit; had I desired to be hypercritical I might have asked Mr. Dunnico how it comes that he makes such insulting references to the poor publicans, while so far as I know he has allowed two elections of a former publican and a present wealthy brewer to the dignity of the Mayoralty of the town to pass unchallenged! I approved of Mr. Bolton's selection and believe that he is the best available man for' the office, but for the life of me I cannot see why in regard to a publican (as I am not S, teetotaller) I may not look over the hedge, whilst in regard toe, brewer the Rev. H. Dunnico (a strong teetotaller) may steal the horse. In respect to the suggestion made by Mr. Dunnico, so far as lam personally concerned lam quite prepared as I have always been to "let bygones be bygones" pro- vided the Company traders, although perhaps not legally required to do so, will undertake to henceforth act in the full spirit of Mr. H. Robert's Non-Trading manifesto of November 28th, 1900, and in the spirit of the Municipal Corporations Act 1882, which disqualifies any man from being a member of a Council who has. "directly or indirectly, by himself or byhis partner, any share or interest in any contracts, or employment with, by, or on behalf of the Council."—Yours, &c. JAMES DODDS. November 10th. 1901.

div.head: Warrington Workhouse Building Scheme.
div.p: Warrington Workhouse Building Scheme.
Sir,—Herewith I enclose correspondence, and I am quite willing for the ratepayers to put their own value on the statements made by its supporters.—Yours, &c. W. HICKMAN.

div.head: [copy.]
div.p: [copy.]

11, Lyme-street, Warrington, November 7,1904. Dear Mi. Billinge,—Will you kindly inform me on what authority you stated last Wednesday :—" The old hospital block of buildings had been condemned by the Local Government Board ten years ago, and we were only partially using them by the courtesy of the Local Government Inspector." I should like to have the dates of the letters for this statement, as Ido not intend to let it go unchallenged. Awaiting your favour, —I am, yours respeetfully. Wm. HICKMAN. [COPY.] _

The Willows, Haydock: November 8, 1904. My dear sir,—Your memo duly to hand,for which please accept my thanks. All being well, Ido hope to be over at the House Committee on Friday next,and then we can talk over the same as we go round. Hoping all is well and prosperous with you and yours.—Believe me, yours faithfully, J. BILLINGE. _NV. Hickman, Esq. In haste.

[copy]. 13, Arpley-street, Warrington, November 9th, 1904. Dear Mr. Billinge.—Yours dated the Bth inst to hand, which evades the questions at issue. If Ido not get answers to the questions in my letter by next post I shall send this correspondenee to the Press, as I am determined to do all one man can to stop this un- necessary building scheme.—Believe me, yours faith- fully, W. HICKMAN.
Sir,—Below you will find copy of letter forwarded to the Board of Guardians.
T. J. HOPKINS.
J. C. Sutton, Esq., Clerk to the Board of Guardians.

Dear Sir,—l am instructed to forward you a copy of resolution unanimously passed at a meeting of the above association on Monday evening last, and shall be glad if you will kindly bring same before the next meeting of Guardians. "That this associ- ation representing a rateable value of upwards of £120,000 emphatically protests against any further expenditure for new buildings in connection with the Warrington Workhouse. Considering the present depressed state of trade and the prospective increase in the rates, they are of opinion that it is an inopportune time for any such expenditure and trust that the Board of Guardians will reconsider their decision to erect new buildings at a cost of £7,000." They also consider that all building schemes for the present ought to be suspended, unless absolutely necessary. Yours truly,

div.head: T. J. 116PKINS, Secretary.
div.p: T. J. 116PKINS, Secretary.
Should Dancing Be Encouraged in Christian Churches P

Sir,—lt has often struck me as being very much out of keeping with the teaching of Christ to see placards posted outside and often on the doors of churches announcing that "The Annual Parish Dance will be held in—Hall onlMonday next. Tickets to be obtained from the Rector or any of the Churchwardens." It is in my opinion very well expressed in the old saying that this is a way of "Getting money from the devil to pay Christ." Personally as a Churchman I think that it is a crying disgrace to a Christian Church that its young people should be taught this deplorable habit within the sacred church.

Dancing becomes a fascination to our young people (I speak from a personal knoWledge) and they are led away, unknowingly at first, into a very hull of sin," ignominious, immoral and un-Christ-like. I won't particularize the many well-known sins aris- ing from dancing, but I do. appeal to our Church of England ministers in Warrington to have the courage to denounce this growing sin and to abolish it from their midst, although they might be financially worse off.
"What shall it profit a man if he gain the whole world and lose his own soul ? "—Yours truly, CHURCHMAN.

div.head: Health of Warrington —Our . Markets.
div.p: The Health of Warrington —Our . Markets.
Sir,—l am pleased to find that at least two persons take an interest in this matter and I thank your two correspondents for their letters in last week's "Examiner."

One of these correspondents, Mr.E. W. Evans, invites me to join the Social Service League and by so doing take a step forward towards the realization of my hopes. Without entering into any explanation here I may say at once that I do not see my way clear to join the League, at present I mean. Your second correspondent "A Ratepayer" draws attention to the emptying of the fish bins and endorses my suggestion that the full bins should be taken away and thoroughly cleansed before being returned. He also mentions, as I have done, the slipshod arrangement of stalls. This is, I think a serious matter to the stall- holders. It must here be pointed out on their behalf that it would not be fair say,to have two or three sweet and biscuit stalls in tht bottom or general market and to remove the sweet and biscuit stalls in the fish market to the meat market. In the fish market these stalls have a very fair stand and are able to compete in position with the stalls in the fruit market. But remove the stalls in the fish market into the meat market, and what would be the result? In all probability an increase of business to those stalls in the fruit market. To be of anypractical use then, any classification scheme must arrange for stalls of a like character to be classed together—of course the word classification itself in connection with this matter means just this classing together. In this matter let us try to be fair to all parties—including the ratepayer. But I should like to say that in my opinion import- ant as these things are affecting the fish market they are not more important than those in connection with the fruit market. The question of fruit, decayed and rotten being allowed to lie about in all directions so that any poor urchins can have their fill on such 'indigestible stuff, is one of gravest consequence. Just picture, for instance, one of those children growing up to manhood, or womanhood, as the case may be, &lan turn bringing children themselves into the world sicklyand deformed in mind and these in turn doing likewise. Who can tell where the evil effects begin, who can tell where and how they may end, if end they can? Heredity is a wonderful thing but we must not forget that it is also an awful thing and it is our bounden duty to see that the conditions of life are such, that if heredity is to enter as a determining factor of the quality of future genera- tions, as will endow the parents of the present with pure and healthy mental and physical powers so that thereby it might almost be made impossible for other than pure and healthy mental and physical powers to be trans- mitted from parent to offspring. Further we have I believe a Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children and yet this Society allows under its very nose a cruelty to children of the most flagrant and dangerous character. It is surely high time that the really grave importance of this matter under discussion was gener- ally realized by the public. Be it far from my intention to raise a mountain out of a molehill. Only from a sincere and convinced belief and opinion that this eating of rotten fruit by poor children (and other evils in any way similar to this) is an evil of some enormity, in proportion to its extent, do I persist in bringing the matter forward.

Now that the subject has come under the notice of one of the members of the Social Service League and that member being interested in the subject, I hope he will bring it forward at one of their meetings and impress upon his fellow members the extreme gravity of the evil and the urgent necessity for taking some immediate and forward step in the matter. Your corres- pondent Mr. E. W. Evans knows now through this corres- pondence as much as I do about the matter and he knows what is wanted. Let his league then discuss the best remedy and the quickest means of putting such a remedy into full operation. _ _

I might: however offer another suggestion which would if put into effect help considerably in maintain- ing a proper condition of affairs, and it is this, that there should be instituted in the markets an effective police supervision. As it is children are almost free to roam where they will with no check whatever upon their movements. There is another improvement also which would be made under good energetic police government. It may not be known generally that bett- ing and card playing are carried on under the shelter of the market bordering on Queen-street, and also I am inclined to think, as regards betting, among the men in the fish market. Twice, the week before this, I saw a number of young men card playing. Obviously this kind of thing ought not to be allowed and strict measures are necessary to aholish it. Thus by bettering the policesupervision two birds will be killed with one stone and the greatest good will have been done by preventing children consuming any stray fruit accidentally left about after the alterations and improvements affecting the storage of rotten fruit advocated in this correspondence have been put into fair working order. fear, Sir, my letter is longer than it ought to be but in view of the importance :of the subjects written of I trust you will publish my letter whole and I may say in extenuation of my offence that in all probability it will not be repeated. "The tear down childhood's cheek that flows, Ts like the dewdrop on the rose; When next the summer breeze comes by, And waves the bush, the flower is dry." Sir W. Scott. Let " the tear down childhood's cheek that flows," nfluence you in this matter."—Yours,
L. W. E.
In the French Chamber on Thursday, amid the cheers of all the groups of the majority, Mr. Combes, the Premier, introduced a bill for the separation of Church and State.
SCGAR IS D. PER LB. DEARER.—Advt.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 12, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 12, 1904.
DEPUTY MAYOR AND CHAPLAIN.
The MAXOR then formally appointed Alderman Fairclough to act as his deputy, and. the Rev. Canon Willis as his chaplain. THE ALLEGED LIBEL ON OFFICIALS.

The MAYOR then asked the Council to confirm the minutes of the meeting held on October 25th. Councillor PEMBERTON said that before the minutes were passed he would like to know whether they included the resolution passed at the Council meeting after the public had been excluded.
4The No,that was not a Council meeting. I took you into my confidence to ask your opinion. Councillor PEMBERTON : A resolution was carried but I am quite content if it is not included in the minutes.

The MAYOR: It is not in the minutes. I only took you into my confidence. I was in a diffi.cult position and I asked the Council what they could do to help me out, and. I took their recommendation. There is nothing on the minutes neither one way nor the other. Councillor PEMBERTON: r am to be excused for asking the question because there are resolutions passed here under standing order 9 which are not on the printed _minutes.
- The ATA.YOR : There is nothing to be passed except what is printed. Councillor LORD: Was there a resolution passed which binds this Council?

- . The MA.YOR. i : There s nothing on the minutes. All you are asked to pass is this (producing the printed minutes.) If there 4 anything you object to in it, let us have it. If not, let us go on with the business Councillor LORD: I give way but lam not satisfied. The MAYOR: I am not surprised at that. (Laughter.) The minutes were then confirmed. DATES OF MEETINGS. The Council then fixed quarterly meeting; for the first Tuesday in February,lVlay and August, and monthly meetings for the first Tuesday in each month, except February, May and August. It was also decided to hold an additional meeting on the last Tuesday in October.

THE PRINTING OF MINUTES. COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND THE STANDING ORDER. COUNCILLOR TINNION AND "GROSS MISREPRESENTATION." The MAYOR moved the adoption of the Standing orders for the regulation of the proceedings of the Council and committees.

Councillor PEMBERTON objected to standing order No. 9, which provides that "the rown Clerk shall issue with the Council summons a print of all important minutes passed by the committees to be taken into con- sideration by the Council; the chairman of each com- mittee to decide which minutes are so to be printed." He moved that it be altered to the effect that all minutes which involved the sp3nding of money should be printed._ _ _

The NIA.YOR : That is so now. Hidn't. you better leave it to the General Purposes Committee? Councillor PEMBERTON : I raised the same objection last year. I have to ask you the question simply because upder the standing order the Council can pass expenditure which is not mentioned in the minutes.
the MAYort : You might have raised the —discussion last Friday. _

Councilfor PEMBERTON : I have a complaint to make I never received a notice of the caucus meeting. It is not the first occasion, I am sorry to say, on which I have not had notice. 1 have complained two or three times previously about it.

The DEPUTY tOWN CLERK said he could prove that the notice was served at Mr. Pemberton's house, or that it was sent from the office with other notices. It was quite a common thing for members'to receive notice and not to find it until two or three days afterwards. Councillor PEMBERTON: I received the Council summons and the minutes of the last meeting of the Education Committee, butno circular calling the caucus meeting.

The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: If you got the Council summons you must have got the notice of meeting. Councillor PEMBERTON: I did not get it, with all respect to you. I don't mean to say it was done on purpose, but it is v ery unfortunate. Councillor LORD seconded Councillor Pemberton's proposition. He knew for a fact that minutes had been passed by the Council which \ would have been thrown out had not the members been in ignorance that they were passing them. He could see no objection what- ever to the alteration. He referred more particularly to the raising of salaries. Alderman SUTTON moved an amendment that the question be adjourned until the next meeting of the General Purposes Committee. It was a very unusual thing to consider questions which would involve a great amount of discussion at the annual Council meeting, and it was better to have them settled in committee.
Councillor CELAIK : Whose duty is it to see that the Standing Orders are carried out. Is it the Town Clerk's?

The MAYOR : It is the Council's duty. The Town Clerk and other officials act under your instructions. Alderman FRANCOMB : Was it not understood that a sub-committee was appointed to revise these standing orders ?

The MAvott : Not this particular one. They are only revising the orders relating to contracts. Councillor EvA_Ns suggested that the matter should be referred to the sub-committee appointed to consider the fair wage clauses. It should not be left to the chair- man of any committee to say which minutes should be printed. If a minute was important enough to be recorded in the minute book it was important enough to be submitted to the Council. The MAYOR said that in the case of some contracts firms would not tender if their prices were made public. t Councillor TINNION protested against the insinuation that in a hole and corner way—a sort of back-door busi- ness—with the intention of deceiving the ratepayers, business was transacted in committee and withheld from the public, and not placed on the printed minutes with that particular object. Councillor EVANS : I rise to a point of order. have not insinuated anything of the kind. Councillor TLNNION : Councillor Evans is not the only member of the Council._ - - -

Councillor PEMBERTON : I rise to a point of order. Councillor LORD : I also object. The MAYOR: If the cap fits you all it must be a very good one. (Laughter.) Councillor TINNION said it was because of the insinua- tions and the gross misrepresentation of facts that he had got up to speak. He was a member of many com- mittees and chairman of some, and he did his duty. He was not afraid of anything he had done being known to every ratepayer. Councillor PEMBERTON: Have it printed on the agenda paper, then. Councillor TINNEON instanced how iu regard to the Gymnasium Committee only routine and unimportant items were omitted from the printed minutes. The Council were no doubt aware that all salaries above a certain amount—£loo a year he believed—could only be raised on a certain day. Councillor LORD: We are quite aware of that. Councillor TINNION : You are quite aware of a great deal. It's a pity you don't let the public know a great deal more that you are aware of, instead of only telling them half truths. I like the thing to be fair and honest from both sides. Councillor PEMBERTON: You should tell them.

Councillor Ttxxiox : I challenge Councillor Pemberton or any other man to prove that I have ever done anything at all unfair. lam quite content that my public career should be investigated by any member or any committee. I have come through this business and through every business where there have been any accusations scathless. I challenge any man to prove that I have clone anything that is in the least deroga- tory to my position as a councillor. Continuing he said he had not the least objection to an amendment of the standing order if anyone would prove that there had been injustice done, or that the order had sheltered anything which the ratepayers ought to know. He did not want, as chairman of any committees, to take the res- ponsibility of saying which minutes should be printed. He agreed with the suggestion that the standing order should be considered by the sub-committee. Let them have the orders put on such a basis that there would be no possibility of anyone saying that anything unfair or irregular could be done in compliance with them. The MAYOR said some minutes were of a routine character, and were not worth spending printer's ink upon. The insinuation that chairmen of committees had some particular interest in cloaking something that would not stand the light was altogether a mistake. He was sorry the commencement of his second year of office had been marked by such insinuations. Councillor PEMBERTON : Will you allow me to make an explanation on that point? The MAYOR: No. You have already spoken. Councillor PEMBERTON : I did not cast insinuations at any chairman. The MAYOR: You are out of order, and ought to be satisfied.
Councillor PEMBERTON attempted to address the meeting, but was greeted with cries of "Chair !" It was decided to refer the standing order to the sub- committee.
THE CONTRACTS QUESTION.

Councillor TINSION alluded to the appointment of a sub-committee to revise the standing orders governing Corporation contracts, and pointed out that pending tileir decision it had been decided to adhere to the original clause that contractors should pay the standard rute of wages for the district. He was not sure whether the sub-committee, which consisted of Coun- cillors Maginn, Wilkinson, Evans, Tinnion, and P. Peacock, had yet power to act, and he therefore pro- posed that the committee be formally appointed and empowered to take into consideration the fair wage clauses and the standing order regarding the printing of minutes, and to receive evidence from other boroughs. and if considered ne3essary from employers and employees, so that the contracts question could be thoroughly thrashed out. He desired to make an explanation with reference to his remarks at the last meeting. He was reported to have said that if the new standing orders were read strictly,no Corporation print- ing could be done in Warrington. He did not know that he did say it; certainly it was not his intention to do so. He had in mind the newspaper offices, for he understood that if the standing orders were carried out in their entirety it would be impossible for the three newspaper offices to do the work. He understood his remarks had given offence, not at the newspaper offices but to some printers, and helherefore wished to correct,

div.head: MAYORALTY.
div.p: THE MAYORALTY.
TOWN COUNCIL RE-ELECT ALDERMAN BOLTON.
Discussion on Standing Orders.
THE CONSTITUTION OF COMMITTEES.

In common with other municipal bodies throughout the country the Warrington Town Council met on Tuesday for the purpose of electing the Mayor for the ensuing year and trangacting other business. The honour of occupying the Mayoral chair has for a second time been bestowed upon Alderman William Bolton, and before the election took place speeches eulogistic of his past services were delivered. At the outset Alderman Sutton presided, and there were present in addition to Mrs. Bolton, Aldermen Francomb, Hutchinson, Smethurst, Bennett and Evans, Councillors Duncan, Roberts, Ellison, Clegg, Fulton Smith, Tinnion, Sankey, Pember- ton, Lord, Brongh, Skeßand, Benson, Forshaw, Wright, Crqik, Evans, Barton, Ashcroft, Wilson, Stott, A. Peacock, and Maginn, Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), J. Deas (water engineer), G-. F. F. White (magistrates' clerk), and J. Moore Murray (director of education). There was a good attendance of the general public. The Town Clerk read the returns for the municipal elections on November Ist, and the by-election in Town Hall Ward.

div.head: ELECTION OF MAYOR.
div.p: THE ELECTION OF MAYOR.

Alderman SOTTON said he had the honour to propose: —"That William Bolton, Esquire, be and he is hereby re-elected Mayor for the ensuing year, and until the acceptance of office by his successor." He remarked that Alderman Pierpoint would probably have proposed the resolution,but owing to indisposition he was unable to be present. After the long experience they had had of Alderman Bolton's ability as a member of the Council and especially of the manner in which he had filled the office of Mayor during the past year, it would be quite unnecessary for him, continued Alderman Sntton, to describe his various qualifications and special fitness for the position, and his just claim to occupy it for another year. Alderman Bolton had not only shown a determina- tion to make himself master of all the important matters which the Corporation had had to transact—and some of them he thought he might readily say had been of equal importance to anything the Corporation had ever dealt with—but he had throughout been most attentive and devoted to the duties devolving upon him as Mayor,—(hear, hear,)—and had proved himself fully capable of conducting the work of the Corporation with credit to himself and in the best interests of the Borough. He had no doubt whatever that with the help of his good wife—(applause)—Alderman Bolton would again acquit himself in the same creditable manner, and with the same satisfaction to everybody. He (Alderman Sutton) thought it was very desirable indeed that every Mayor should have a second year of office because, as they all knew, it took _nearly the whole of the first year to get the Mayor and the members well acquainted and to thoroughly understand each other. In the second yearthe Mayor was betteyable to conduct the business and was more competent in every way to undertake the duties of the office. He had muchpleasure in proposing the resolution. (Applause). Councillor TiNxioN hadvery much pleasure in second- ing the resolution which Alderman Sutton had so ably proposed. They had in the person of Alderman Bolton a gentleman who had for a very considerable time taken a very keen interest in the municipal work of the borough, and during the first year of his Mayoralty he had discharged the duties of the office with very great care and attention. He had set an example to future Mayors as too the amount of interest it was possible to take in all the business—in fact he (Councillor Tinnion) believed Alderman Bolton had established a record in attendances at the various committee meetings. (Hear. hear). On the committees on whichhe(the speaker)had met him, Alderman Bolton had always shown himself anxious to impart advice which, through his worship's long experience,was not only necessary but very accept- able. He felt sure that during the coming year, with the advantage of his past experience and the hearty co-operation of the Council, Alderman Bolton would discharge all his duties with infinite credit to himself and with dignity and honour to the chair, and that he would work for all that was conducive to the material and social prosperity of the Borough. Alderman Bolton was very fortunate in having such a very estimable lady for his wife. (Applause.) He (Councillor Tinnion) had known Mrs. Bolton for many years and he felt sure she would do all she possibly could to assist the Mayor in carrying out his duty and would add grace and dignity to the position she was called upon to occupy. (Applause). The motion was then put to the meeting and carried with acclammation.
THE MAYOR AND THE Y EAR'S WORK.
THE WIDENING OF WARRINGTON BRIDGE.

The mover and seconder of the resolution then pro- ceeded to the Mayor's parlour andacquainted Alderman Bolton with the decision of the Council. Having donned the Mayoral robes and chain his worship entered the Council Chamber and made the customary declaration. He then addressed the Council, and thanked the mem- bers very heartily for their vote of confidence in him. The Council had gone through a very troublesome year —he hoped in the future they would not have half the trouble—but they had much to be thankful for. One important subject which had occupied their attention was the Manchester Ship Canal clauses, and he thought the Council had come eff very satisfactorily indeed. He hoped the clauses would be a boon to Warrington and put an end to litigation of a peculiar character thA, was likely to make anything but friends. war reference to the action pending between the Compan y and the traders and Corporation, he thought that see- ing the Corporation had got everything theyhad fought for, the best thing they could do would be for all the parties to arrive at an amicable settlement and cease litigation. He had not the slightest doubt that some- thing of that nature would take place. The rates were gradually but surely going higher and higher' but the Council could not help that. They had to face the erection of two new schools in the Latchford and Orford districts, but by providing more accommodation they would be doing something for the benefit of the future generation, and he thought the ratepayers could not crumble at the little extra expenditure on that account. With reference to the improvement at Market Gati, he hoped that before very long they would see the work progressing more expeditiously and satisfac- torily. (Hear, hear.) The tramway system had come to stay in Warrington, and the sooner they widened the main streets the better. He understood the tramway to Stockton Heath would soon ,be an accomplished fact, and also that the Northwich people were endeavouring to m.et the Corporation and continue the service into their district. Another ex- penditure the Corporation would be called upon to incur would be the provision of a new cattle market. He had not the slightest idea that such a market and abbatoir if erected on a sound basis would prove a sound paying concern and the rates would not suffer. During the year the Corporation would have to again consider the widening of Warrington bridge which was becoming a serious question. They had undertaken one step, but the question was whether owing to litigation 'and various threatening they had received it would not be better to reconsider the matter on another basis. Several what he might term antagonistic views were being expressed and they would be brought before the Council at the next General Purposes Com- mittee meeting to see whether some arrangement that would be satisfactory to all parties could be arrived at. They did not want litigation, but they wanted the bridge widening. They wanted another footpath but they did not want to get into trouble, so far as litigation was concerned, with Captain Nares or anyone else. He believed the Council would do the best they could for the town generally and not try to make trouble for the sake of a few pounds of expendi- ture. His Worship proceeded to commend the scheme for the erection of a memorial to the men of the South Lancashire Regiment who fell in South Africa. The fund, he said, had gone on so satisfactorily during the year that he thought with a continuance of careful management the scheme might be completed during the next twelve months. He would be pleased to see a memorial because it was only fitting that the services of those who laid down their lives in that campaign should be permanently "placed on record. During the second year of his Mayoralty it would be his earnest endeavour to eo the best he possibly could for the town and for the members of the Council, and he hoped they would have very satisfactory and amicable meetings,which instead of lasting for four or five hours would be concluded in about twenty minutes. (Laughter and applause). RE-ELECTION OF ALDERMEN.

The Council then proceeded with the election of four aldermen to supply the places of those whose period of office terminated on that day, vi v. :—Aldermen Arthur Bennett, James Fairclough, William Pierpoint and Thomas H. Sutton.

Ballot papers were handed round, and on a scrutiny being made it was found that all the members had recorded their votes in favour of the retiring aldermen, who were consequently declared re-elected for six years. Having signed the customary declaration, Alderman Sutton thanked the Council for the honour they had conferred upon him and remarked that he had that day commenced his thirty-first year of office as a member of the Corporation. (Applause). Alderman BEN-Err also returned thanks. H. had, he said, been a member of the Council for eleven years and an alderman for a year and a half, and during that time it had been one of his greatest pleasures to do what little he could for the benefit of his native town. He loved the town very dearly : he believed in it very pro- foundly; and he was proud of it in spite of everything that had been said against it. As long as he lived, he would'do everything he could to promote its welfare. (Applause).
the statement and to say that he did not mean that no printing shop in Warrington could do the work. He was simply referring to the newspaper offices.
Alderman SMETHTIRST SOCOOded. Councillor FORSHAW moved that the names of Coun- cillors Lord and Pemberton be added to the committee. Councillor ROBERTS seconded.

Councillor T.cgmoN said he thought the committee was altogether too large, and he would willingly retire in place of anyone the Council desired to substitute. The MA.YOR : I think you are getting too many of one side on the committee. It ought to be representa- tive of all shades of opinion. Councillor LORD said he would withdraw in favour of Councillor Pemberton. Councillor Trsmos said he did not think the com- mittee was representative of the Council. He under- stood the members were all of one shade of politics. They were all Liberals, to put it plainly, and he would rather they had a mixture. He hardly thought all the goodness—although it might—belonged to the Liberal party,but there was a prepon ierance of it—(laughter)— and he would like a little leaven from the Conservatives.
Councillor PEMBERTON suggested the names of Alder- man Bennett and Councillor Ashcroft, but Alderman Bennett declined the position as he would not have sufficient'time to devote to the duties.
The MAYOR suggested that the committee as at present constituted should present its report, and if it was onesided the Council could alter it.

Councillor MA.GINN said it would be a pity since Councillor Pemberton wasa member of the late-existing Non-Trading Association- The MAYOR: I would not bring that in to-day. Councillor MA.GINN : He objects to certain standing orders and it is only fair that he should be on the com- mittee. If you think it is too large I have no objection to retiring from it. Ultimately the committee as already constituted was appointed, with the addition of Councillor Pemberton. The whole of the remaining standing orders were then passed. COUNCILLOR CRATE AND THE CONSTITUTION

div.head: OF COMMITTEES.
div.p: OF COMMITTEES.

Before the appointment of committees was proceeded with, Councillor Craik said he would like to draw attention to standing order 29 which provided that no member of the Council should be appointed to serve on more thav six committees. Three aldermen and two councillors held seats on seven ; and he would like to know whether any of them were prepared to retire. The MAYOR said the Council had power to appoint members to serve on additional committees if they thought fit. Councillor CRAM: What is the use orpassiug stand- ing orders if the Council choose to ignore them? The MAYOR: The standing order says that members can remain on extra committees if the Council think fit.
It was stated that Alderman Evans, Hutchinson, Smethurst, and Councillors Evans, Roberts, Tinnion, and Wilkinson held seats on seven committees.
Councillor Roberts said he would resign from the Rivers Committee.
Councillor EVANS offered to resign from the Rivers and Markets Committee.

Alderman Smethurst said he would resign from the Health Committee. He did not think their friends need grumble about aldermen being placed on extra committees, becausethe record of attendances showed that they had diligently attended to their duties. Alderman Evans had made 163 and Alderman Hutchinson 153 attendances and he (Alderman Smethurst) had been present at 219 meetings. Some of the councillors had attended about forty. Councillor Ca : No one is grumbling about the aldermen. Councillor PEMBERTON : The other councillors have not the sable chance of attending as the aldermen. Alderman BENNErr said he sympathised a great deal with what Councillor Pemberton had said. He did not think it quite fair that certain mem- bers should monopolise so many committees. He admitted that they rendered valuable services but the principle was not a sound one. ALDERMEN AND THE WATCH COMMITTEE. The MA.YOR moved that the following members be appointed the Watch Committee for the ensuing year : The Mayor, Aldermen Fairclough, Francomb, Hutchin- son, Pierpoint, Smethurst and Sutton, Councillors Burton, Roberts and Wilkinson._ _

Alderman SMETHURST seconded. Councillor CRAIK moved that the names of Coun- cillors Ellison, Sankey and Lord be added to the com- mittee. He did not think there ought to be seven aldermen as members. He did not believe it was for the good of the town. Councillor Ellison, as one of the leaders of the temperance party, had a claim to member- ship of such an important committee.

Councillor PEMBERTON seconded. The MA.YOR said they could not increase the member- ship to thirteen, and Councillor Craik would have to name those whom he intended the new members to replace. Councillor CRAW moved that Councillors Ellison, Sankey, and Lord be appointed instead of Aldermen Francomb, Hutchinson, and Smethurst. Councillor PEMBERTON said an important committee like the Watch Committee ought to have more members who were directly responsible to the ratepayers. The aldermen were not amenable to the public opinion of the town. There was no personal objection to the three gentlemen who had been named. Alderman FRA.NCOMB expressed his willingness to retire as he could not, owing to county engagements, attend the meetings regularly. Alderman SMETHURST proposed that Councillor Ellison be elected in place of Alderman Francomb. Councillor A. PEA.COCIC. seconded. He thought if Councillor Craik had recommended more senior coun- cillors for election on an important committee, his proposition would have been better received. Alderman SUTTON said it had always been considered since he became a member of the Corporation that the Watch Committee was the most important committee of the Council and consisted of the most experienced members, men who had served on other'committees and had a fair acq_uaintance with the routine work of the Corporation. It was rather extraordinary that anyone should propose that members should, without any experi- ence whatever, become members of one of the most important committees requiring a great deal of knowledge and information. There were some members of the Coun- cil who were continually wanting alterations. The only way to satisfy them was to put them on the committees or whatever they said wanted altering. (Laughter.) They thought themselves cleverer than anyone else, and thought they knew more, and ought therefore to take a higher position than the other members. Councillor CRA.IK said he should press his amend- ment.

The MAYOR said the names would have to be voted upon separately. Councillor LORD said he was not particularly anxious to be on the Watch Committee but he thought it was time there was an alteration. They had sadly too many aldermen and too few councillors on the committee. As his name had been nominated, he should decline to take part in the voting, and he hoped the aldermen would do the same. Alderman Surrox : No fear.

Councillor MAGINN said it was very generous on Alderman Francomb's part to retire, and he believed Councillor Ellison was a suitable man to succeed him, as representing the temperance party. He could easily see that the Watch Committee was the most important committee of the Corporation. Gentlemen as a rule were only elected aldermen after long service, and the business of the Watch Committee which was to main- tain law and order required to be transacted by members of experience. He thought it was rather ridiculous to propose much younger men, of only a day or two's standing in the Council, to replace aldermen. Councillor WRIGHT agreed with the principle that more members who were responsible to the ratepayers should be on the Watch Committee, but without any disrespect to that gentleman he was not agreeable to the election of Councillor Sankey who was a compara- tively new member of the Council. He would prefer to see the name of Councillor Evans substituted.
Eventually Councillor CRAIK withdrew the amend- ment, and the committee was elected as proposed with the substitution of Councillor Ellison for Alderman Franc o mb
OTHER COMMITTEES.

It was unanimously decided that the Finance and Estate Committee be constitutedas follows :—Aldermen Bennett and Fairclough, Councillors Craik, Forshaw, Fulton Smith, Hulse, Lord, A. Peacock and Wilkinson. Alderman StYrroN moved that the following members be appointed the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee :—Aldermen Bennett, Hutchinson, Pierpoint, and Sutton, Councillors Barton, Evans, Forshaw, Hulse, Wilkinson and P. Peacock. Alderman BENNETT seconded.

Councillor CRAIK moved that Couneillor Lord be appointed instead of Councillor P. Peacock, but on a vote being taken the amendment was defeated, and the committee was appointed as above. Alderman SUTTON moved that the Health Committee consist of the following members: Alderman Sutton, Councillors Barton, Brough, Burton, Clegg, Evans, Sankey, Tinnion, Wilkinson, and Wilson. Councillor TINNION seconded. Councillor CRAIK moved that the name of Councillor Stott be substituted for that of Councillor Wilkinson. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded. On a vote being taken, Councillor Wilkinson was elec- ted by the vote a the Mayor. _ _ .
The committee was ftrp linted as proposed. The following committees were appointed without discussion : . - _

SANITAFtY WORKS.—Aldermen Evans and Smethurst, Councillors Burton, Duncan, Evans, Maginn, Stott, Tinnion, Wilkinson and Wilson. MUSEUM.—Alderman Bennett, Councillors Barton, Brough, Ellison, Forshaw, Horrocks, P. Peacock, Pem- berton, Fulton Smith and Skelland, and the following non-members of the Council, viz. : Messrs. Robert Pier- point. M.P., T. J. Ridgway, Thomas May, J. F. Dutton, A. J. Jolley, Rev. Morley Stevenson and Mr. John Upson. CEMETERX.—AIderman Evans, Councillors. Barton, Brough, Clegg, Craik, Duncan, Horrocks, Hulse, A. Peacock and Skelland. -

_ MARKETS.—Alderman Hutchinson, Councillors Ash- croft, Brough, Duncan, Sankey, Hulse, Lord, IVlaginn, A. Peacock and Roberts. (Councillor Evans retired and Councillor Sankey was appointed in his place.) TOWN HALL, PARKS, AND BATHs.—Aldermen Bolton (Mayor), Francomb, Hutchinson, Pierpoint, Smethurst, and Sutton, Councillors Ellison, Roberts, Wilkinson and Benson. (Aide man Francomb retired from this com- mittee and Councillor Benson was appointed in his place).

Councillor TENSION moved that the Paving and Sewerage Committee consist of Aldermen Hutchinson and Smethurst, Councillors Burton, Evans, Forshaw, Hulse, PuPeacock, Pemberton, Roberts and Tinnion. Alderdran SmETHURST seconded. _

Councillor CRA.IK proposed that Councillor Wright be appointed a member in place of Councillor Evans. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded. Only the proposer and seconder voted for the amend- ment and the committee was elected as above. An amendment that Councillor Stott should be elected a member of the Gas Committee in place of Councillor Sankey was defeated, and the committee was elected as follows :—The Mayor, Aldermen Evans, Fairclough and Pierpoint, Councillors Duncan, Ellison,Evans, Roberts, Sankey and Tinnion. The MAYOR moved that the following, members form the Rivers Committee :—The Mayor, Aldermen Bennett Evans, Fairclough, Hutchinson, Sutton, Councillors Evans, Forshaw, Roberts and Tinnion. Councillor EVANS and ROBERTS expressed a wish to retire, and their example was followed by Alderman HUTCLIDISON who said he had a very good average of attendances,and had always tried to discharge the duties satisfactorily. Councillor TmiroNsaid he also was one of the guilty sinners who did too much work for the Corporation and he would retire from the committee. Alderman EVANS intimated that he would retire.

The MAYOR : Am I going tO-lia.;.;--87 comniittee without any members of experiences? We have gone through serious litigation alid we should have members who understand the business. I would rather you did not retire.

Ultimately it was decided to substitute Councillors Fulton Smith, Benson and Ashcroft for Alderman Hutchison,and Councillors Evans and Roberts. The other members of the committee were appointed as selected. When the appointment of the Fire Engine Committee came up for consideration, some amusement was caused by Councillor Tinnion moving an amendment that Councillor Cmik should.be elected a member in the place of Alderman Smethurst.

- The Council made a show of voting on the matter and it was announced that Alderman Smethurst was "just elected." The committee was constituted as follows :—Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Ashcroft, Barton, Brough, Burton, Duncan, A. Peacock, P. Pea- cock, Wilson, and Wright. Other committees were appointed as follow : WATER COMMITTEE.—The Mayor, Aldermen Evans, Francomb, Hutchinson, and Smethurst; Councillors Duncan, Forshaw, Pemberton, Roberts and Fulton Smith.

GYMNASIUM.—AIderman Evans, Councillors Ash- croft, Hulse, Tinnion, Wilson, Sire Hand, Clegg, and Wright; and the following non-members of the Coun- cil, viz :—Messrs. Hugh Ferguson, Thomas Locker, and John Upson. ELECTRICITY AND TRAMWAYS.—The Mayor, Alder- men Evans, Pierpoint, Smethurst, and Sutton ; 'Coun- cillors Craik, Ellison, Lord, Maginn, A. Peacock Pemberton, Tinnion and Wilkinson.

Councillor PEmßEßroN—to-u-gii-t-- Eei; OUgiit to be a special committee to "push" the town with the object of bringing new works to Warrington.He did not see why Warrington should not have a committee just as Black- pool, the Isle of Man, and Southport had committees to advertise the places as pleasure resorts. (Laughter.) Of course, he did not suggest that they should advertise Warrington in that direction, but the town stood pre- eminent as a manufacturing centre just as Southport and Blackpool occupied high positions as health resorts. The MAYOR pointed out that such a committee would have to be a sub-commiftee of the General Pur- poses Committee. It was understood that Councillor Pemberton would introduce the matter at the next General Purposes Com- mittee meeting. Councillor PEACOCK also intimated his intention of bringing before the General Purposes Committee the desirability of having a specially constituted Open Spaces Committee instead of the existing sub-com- mittee.

div.head: RETURNING OFFICERS.
div.p: RETURNING OFFICERS.

The following returning officers were elected :—Town Hall Ward, Alderman Smethurst; Whitecross Ward, Alderman Pierpoint ' • Bewsey Ward, Alderman Fair- dough ; Orford Ward, Alderman Hutchinson; St. John's Ward, Alderman Sutton; Fairfield Ward, Alder- man Evans; Howley Ward, Alderman Francomb • St. John's Ward, Alderman Bennett; Latchford Ward, the Mayor. NEW MEMBERS OF THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE. _

Councillors Fulton Smith and Barton were appointed members of the Education Committee in place of Messrs. S. Davies and W. Rogers. Alderman BENNETT pointed out that Mr. Fulton Smith had already been a member as representing the Chamber of Commerce but as he had been elected to the Council he could not sit any longer in that capacity. They all realized the value of his past services and felt it would be a misfortune if he ceased to be a member. Mr. Josiah Longland was appointed a representative manager of St. Peter's school in place of Mr. E. J. Guest.

REPRESENTATIVES ON COUNTY AUTHORITIES. Alderman Francomb was re-appointed the representa- tive of the Council on the Lancashire Asylums Board and Alderman Hutchinson was deputed to represent the Council on the Lancashire Inebriates' Acts Board.
Alderman BENNETT moved that Councillor A. Peacock be appointed the representative on the County Rate Joint Committee in place of Mr. James Dodds.

Councillor CRAIK moved and Councillor PEN' B ERTON seconded an amendment that Mr. Fulton Smith be ap- pointed. The MAYOR: I would like to say that the representa- tive will have nothing to do for four years. (Laughter.) On the vote being taken, Councillor Peacock was appointed. THE KING'S BIRTHDAY. - -
The Council heartily approved the suggestion of the Mayor to dispatch a telegram to thP King congratulat- ing him on the happy occasion of his birthday.

div.head: NEW SAILING AND BOATING CLUB.
div.p: NEW SAILING AND BOATING CLUB.

A meeting of gentlemen interested in sailing and boating upon the River Mersey was held at the Norton Arms Hotel on Thursday evening last, with a view to the formation of a club to facilitate those objects upon the river, and was largely attended. It is about six years since there was a sailing club upon the river at Warrington. At that time there was a club cal led the Warrington and Bank Quay Sailing Club which had its headquarters at the Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay, and previous to that there was a club which was in existence in 1886 called the Warrington Sailing Club, with its headquarters in the neighbour- hood of Warrington Bridge. However, since the Ship Canal has been formed the river has so silted up that it is impossible for boats of any draught to sail up to Warrington Bridge at low tide, and gentlemen owning boats have had to remove their anchorage to Fiddlers' Ferry. Mr. W. E. Fowler was asked to take the chair and briefly explained the objects of the meeting. A resolution that a club be formed with its head- quarters at the Fiddlers' Ferry Hotel and to be called the Fiddlers' Ferry Sailing and Boating Club was pro- posed by Mr. Lister and seconded by Mr. Woolstencroft and carried unanimously.—The following gentlemen were elected as officers and a committee of the new club, viz. :—Mr. H. Frankish, commodore; Mr. W. Knowles, vice-commodore; Mr. H. Bennet, hon. secre- tary; and Mr. W. Knowles, hon. treasurer; and the following members to constitute a committee of eight: —Mr. R. 'Burthem, Mr. H. P. Turner, Mr. T. Bennett, Mr. A. Swift, Mr. W. Whittle, Mr. W. Warburton, Mr. S. Meacock, and Mr. W. McClew. After some discus- sion an annual subscription of ss. for each member was agreed upon, in addition to a subscription of 15s. for each boat upon the river belonging to members of the club.

Mr. Fowler explained to the meeting that it was the intention of the promoters, and that he considered it would be entirely to the benefit of the club, that it should be conducted on a strictly amateur basis, and any prizes to be awarded were to consist of cups and flags only, and that no money prizes would be giyen,and further that the subscriptions would be used entirely to further the best interests of the club.

Considerable discussion took place with regard to rule 12 of the proposed rules of the new club as to the composition of the crews of any boats sailing in races, and the following rule was adopted:—"That any boat racing must have at least ono owner a member of the club, and that all crews sailing in races must also be members of the club." _ _ _

It was arranged that the colours should be the same as those of the old Warrington Sailing Club, i.e., the club flag to be a burgee having a Maltese cross on a dark-blue ground, the Commodore's flag to be a swallow- tail burgee of the same colours. The names of 38 gentlemen were enrolled as members of the club and the Chairman announced that at no distant date, it was proposed to hold a smoking concert of the members. _

Votes of thanks to Mr. Fowler for presiding and to Mr. H. Bennet for the trouble he had taken towards the formation of the club concluded the proceedings. Any gentleman wishing to join the club should com- municate with Mr. H. Bennet, 13, Hoyle-street, War- rington, the hon. sec., who will give them every nformation.

div.head: Serious Farm Fire at Winwick.
div.p: Serious Farm Fire at Winwick.

Shortly before 11 o'clock at Winwick on Tuesday night, a fire broke out on the premises of Messrs. Dan and William Massey, farmers, Winwiek. The Warrington fire brigade were informed of the out- break and were on the scene of the fire without any loss of time. The fire had assumed serious propor- tions when the brigade arrived,and despite their best efforts great damage was done, the fire raging all night. A new Dutch barn and several stacks of corn and hay were destroyed and the loss will be more than £l,OOO.

div.head: WARRINGTON DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
ANNUAL PERFORMANCES IN PARR
HALL.

Whatever trepidation may have been felt by mem- bers of the Warrington Dramatic Society in following so closely upon the heels of the opera must, we think, have been dispelled by the large and enthusiastic audiences which have assembled during the week. The opening night was certainly rather sparsely attended, but Thursday evening and last evening there were gratifyingly large gatherings. It would indeed be unfortunate if the Dramatic Society were to suffer financially as the result of the great popularity secured by the operatic performances, and we shall be very pleased to learn, as we hope to do shortly, that the proceeds from "Facing the Music" are up to the level of previous years. We can honestly and straightaway say that the quality of the acting adds to, rather than diminishes the reputation of the society. This is especially gratifying, seeing that of late the society has suffered the loss of a "leading lady" in the person of Miss Margaret Pierpoint, who is making a prolonged stay in Amsterdam. The society is blessed with a number of very promising recruits, of whom we shall doubtless hear and see more in the future.

• As already indicated the piece de resistance for this week is "Facing the Music," the well-known farcical comedy by Mr. James Henry Darnley. This is a distinct change from" The Idler," and perhaps not an advance dramatically, but "variety's the very spice of life," and the society has certainly not lost anything in favour by the reversion to farcical comedy. "Facing the Music" is one of the funniest pieces. ever staged, and the uproarious laughter which greets every fresh denouement is sterling testi- mony to the 'excellence of the acting and stage management. There is the usual confusion of individuals bearing the same name but pursuing vastly different avocations, and an additional com- plication by the fact that the two "Mr. Smith's " both reside in " Mona Mansions." The cast, which we here :append, is almost explanatory of the farce :

div.head: CHARACTERS ':
div.p: CHARACTERS ':
Rev. John Smith (The Curate of St. Andrew's), Mr. Cecil Bond.
John Smith (The other Mr. Smith), Mr. Sidney Wallhead.
Dick Desmond (The other Mr. Smith's Guest), Mr. H. M. Ashton. ___ _

Colonel Duncan Smith (The other Mr. Sniith's Uncle), Mr. Geoffrey Dodd. Sergeant Duffell (Attached to Vine-street Po lice Station), Mr. Harry Mosley. Mabel (The Curate's Wife), Miss Lucy Wenham. Nora (The other Mr. Smith's Wife), Miss Bessie Pierpoint. Miss Fotheringay (Of the Bijou Theatre), Mrs. Jennings. Mrs. Pouting (The other Mr. Smith's Housekeeper),. Mrs. James Fairclough).

There are some -excellent parts in the comedy and it is difficult to discriminate between artistes who have so much to do and do it so well. Miss Bessie. Pierpoint achieves a striking success in the varied roles of "The other Mrs. Smith," the "Duchess of Piccadilly," and " Matilda Scraggs." She fully interprets the aim of the author and nothing couldbe more laughable than her artistically assumed distress and indignation ato being supplanted in her own flat by Mrs. Smith No. 1. In her many trying situations she is excellent and deserves the hearty applause so generously given. Miss Wenham does equally well in a quieter vein,and these two ladies prove admirable- foils for one another. The heaviest part in the piece is unquestionably that of John Smith, and we must. congratulate Mr. Sidney Wallhead on his really excellent study of this trying rale. He has an enor- mous lot to say and do and is never at fault in any of the many remarkable situations whsch occur. Perhaps he is just a little too tearful at times when the com- bination of circumstances seems likely to overwhelm him, but one has to be critical to notice this. On the- other hand nothing but the highest praise can be given to his pourtrayal of " poor Smith when temporarily insane and seeing visions. Mr. Harry Mosley is once again well suited with his part and the fussy self— satisfied detective could not be better exemplified The pale young curate of St. Andrew's is admirably sketched by Mr. C. H. Bond, who has previously taken only minor parts in the society's performances- That he is capable of much better things is proved over and over again this week by the real humour of his acting and the uproarious applause accorded his efforts. Mr. H. M. Ashton' as Dick Desmond, is on the stage almost continuously, and it is questionable whether anyone could play the part of the giddy bachelor friend more easily and naturally., John Smith (No. 2.) has an uncle at the war office, and this uncln gives Mr. Geoffrey Dodd an opportunity of exercising his varied abilities. Mr. Dodd is an undoubted acquisition to the society. Mrs. James Fairclough as usual pleases everybody in the part she has undertaken, and Mrs. Jemungs also gives satis- faction in the minor character of Miss Fotheringay (of the Bijou Theatre), the unwitting cause of all the complication between two husbands, two wives and various other people. Prior to "Facing the Music" there is a "curtain raiser" entitled Under the Old Name," taken part in by Mr. Geoffrey Dodd, Mr. Harold Joseph, Mr. Harry Mosley, Mrs. Lightburn, and Miss Rose Wall- head. Except that the play affords a contrast to the farce to follow, we cannot say much for it. The style of the thing is too orthodox and old fashioned for a. Present-day audience, though it was pleasantly per- formed. Messrs. Mosley and Dodd were splendida and a promising debut was made by Mr. Joseph and Miss Wallhead. Mrs. Lightburn was quite at home in the small role falling to her lot. Finally, and this is a point that the - society ought to seriously consider, why should there be slow music at the most touching episodes? It is a bit of sentimental stage-fakery which irritates more than it pleases. People, as a rule, do not pass through the most pathetic incidents of a lifetime to the accompaniment of a subdued orchestra. Where "the book" says "slow music," we hope, in future,. the 'society will use a blue pencil. The idea is " played ' out, and ought to be left out. Thee comments, of courso, have no reference, particularly, to Mr. Boothroyd's orchestra, which. played with fine force and spirit during the intervals. In conclusion we must add a word of praise for the labours of Mr. Q. H. Wood (stage-manager), Mr. A. Browne (hon. treasurer), and Mr. J. W. Bullen (hon. secretary). They have been largely responsible for making the wheels go smoothly round, and as they are denied the plaudits of the multitude they merit recognition here. _
The performances will be continued this evening', and we advise our readers not to miss so excellent an entertainment.

Dated 14th September, 1904. SEcTiox 8 (1) OF THF. EDUCATION ACT, 1902, PROVIDES AS FOLLOWS • •. (1) Where the Local Education Authority or any other persons propose to provide a new public elementary school they shall give public notice of their intention to do so, and the Managers of any existing school, or the Local Education Authority (where they are not them- selves the persons proposing to provide the'school), or any ten ratepayers in the area for which it is proposed to provide the school, may, within three months after the notice is given, appeal to the Board of Education on the ground that the proposed school is not required or that a school provided by the Local Education Authority, or not so provided, as the case may be, is better suited to meet the wants of the district than the school proposed to be provided, and any school built in contravention of the decision of the Board of Edo cation on such appeal shall be treated as unnecessary."

Coming Events. The anniversary of the dedication of Emmanuel Church will be celebrated to-morrow by the holding of special services. A. special feature of the services will be an address which which will be given in the .evening by Bishop Eldridge. A public meeting in connection with the Northern Council of the Reformed Episcopal Church will be held in the Winwick-street Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. Bishop Eldridge will preside and the speakers will be the Revs. S. Naish and T. W. Bowman. An open meeting of the Warrington P.S.A.. Society will be held to-morrow afternoon in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street. Councillor Clegg will preside and an address will be delivered by the Rev. J. S. Hughes. The Pioneer Band will be in attendance. Local Prize Winners at St. Louis Exhibition The name of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons Ltd., figures prominently in the list of prize-xvinners in the international exhibition at St. Louis, United States of America. They were awarded the grand prize in the Chemical and Pharrnarceutical arts, and the grand prize for vegetable and food products. BASSINETTES AND MAIL CARTS in latest art ehades.—J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Trap Accident at Lymm. While driving in his trap in Whitbarrow-lane, Mr, Henry Palmer, of Cherry-lane, Lymm, who only recently returned from a trip to America "met with an accident. A furniture van in turning a sharp curve caused Mr. Palmer's horse to swerve, breaking the shafts of the trap. Mr. Palmer was thrown to the ground and badly injured. Brass Band Reform: It will be interesting to local bandsmen to know that Mr. Fred Podmore has bad another lengthy article accepted by the "Musical Opinion." There has been a great desl of controversy as the outcome of his first artacleg but many of the suggested improvements have been adopted. An extract from this article will be included in this week's edition of the " British Bandsmen." SUGAR IS D. PER LB. DEARER.—AdVt. Presentation at Walton. There was a pleasant gathering at Walton on Friday evening when Mrs. Darwall, on behalf of the members of Walton Church -choir, presented to Mr. Albert Weir a clock on the occasion of his marriage. He has been a member of the choir for the last 20 years, and in making the presentation Mrs. Darwall spoke of the esteem in which Mr. Weir was held. Mr. W. T. Kipps, an old chorister at Walton Church, and now residing in Manchester, has also presented to Mr. Weir a very handsome barometer. Claim Against Mr. S. Gough. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, Mr. Fowler' solicitor, brought an action against Mr. 'Samuel Gough, to recover £l. is. for professional services. Mr. Fowler stated that Mr. Gough engaged him in May 1899 to raise a mortgage for him. He raised the mortgage but for some unstated reason Mr. Gough did not take the money up.—Mr. Gough denied that Mr. Fowler had obtained the money for him. He engaged Mr. Fowler but as Mr. Fowler did not get the money for him he went to another solicitor.—Mr. Fowler produced the copy of a letter he had written to Mr. Geugh in which he told him he had a client who was prepared to advance the money and asking him to take it up. To that letter Mr. Gough did not reply. —His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed with costs. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLA.Ss NILNERAL WATERS.—Advt. Funeral of the late Mr. W. Bellian. The remains of thelllr.William Bellittn,were interred at the Warrington Cemetery on Sunday afternoon, in the presence of a large number of relatives and friends. The following were the chief mourners : Messrs. William Henry Bellian, John Bellian and Walter Bellian. (sons), Joseph Bellian (brother), H. Holt (brother-in-law), T. Bellian J. Bellian and J. Sudlow (nephews), G. H. Smith (executor), and W. Walker. Representatives of the Warrington Cycling Club and the Masonic Lodge with which the deceased had been connected were also present. A large num- ber of floral tributes were received. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. H. V. Pigot, vicar of St. Thomas's, Stockton Heath. GREAT SALE OP BOOTS AND SHOES now on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Factory Act Prosecution. At the Warringtan Police Court, yesterday, the Orford Mill Company were summoned for employing a girl aged 13 years without the necessary certificate from the Board of Education.—Miss Patterson, H.M. Inspector of Factories, explained that to employ a girl of 13 the defendants required a certificate as to her educational fitness, and also a certificate to show that she had attended school 350 times a year for the past five years. In that case the certificate had not been obtained.—Defendant's representative stated that his firm engaged he girl out of sympathy. Had they known they were doing anything illegal they would not have engaged her.—A fine of is. and costs was inflicted. FOR CLASS AND CHINA of every description try ti. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street. Warrington.—Advt. Concert at Ebenezer Church. There was a large attendance at the Ebenezer Church, Buttermhrket-street, on Monday, at a band of hope concert, organized by the Misses Lee and Holmes. Mr. Thornton presided. An excellent programme was submitted and all the items were highly appreciated. The programme was commenced with a well played pianoforte solo by Miss Harris, "Liberty Bell March," Recitations were given by Mr. Davies and Miss Furness and solos by Mr. Walmsldy and Mr. Walker. The Misses Lee and Bowyer contributed two duets, while a couple of mandoline solos were given by Miss Turner. A sketch by Mr. Davis and a mandoline duet by Miss Payton and Miss Turner added to the enjoyment of all present. A successful evening was brought to a close with a dialogue which; was given by several ladies and gentlemen. The accompanists were Mr. Monks •and Miss Lawless. On the motion of the Chairman seconded by the Pastor, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to all who had taken part in the proceedings. SUGAR IS D. PER LB. DEARER.—Advt. Buckley-street Band of Hope Juvenile Choir. A concert in aid of the above was held in the schoolroom on Monday, Councillor Ashcroft presiding. The choir gave nice renderings of" Sweet and Low and "Sailor's Lullaby," and had to respond to encores. Mr. A. E. Trow conducted and Miss M. Plinston, A.L.C.M., accompanied. Miss A Bridge tastefully sang "Dear Heart and "The Carnival" being very successful with the latter. For her render of"rag Flight of Ages" and "Come back to me" Miss L. Fairhurrt well earned the demand for encores, Mr. W. Booth, who possesses a sweet tenor voice sang " Mona " and "Take a pair of sparkling eyes." Mr. J. Monks i sanga bass song in fine style, and joined with Mr. Booth n the duet "Love and War,' for a spirited rendering of which they had to respond to an encore. Mr. A. Bennett displayed cleverness in his two violin solos, as also did Mr. Jackson with his 'cello. Mr. E. A. Sanders' name will be enough to satisfy as being humorist. He caused continuous laughter. Mr. A. E. Trow accompanied. FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bri dge-street,Warrinßinn Advt. Cemetery Hotel Bowling Club. The tea and distribution of prizes in connection with the Closing Handicap were held at the Cemetery ttotel on Thursday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. A. H. Crosfield (president), supported by Captain Crosfield, Mr. S. Taylor occupying the vice- chair. Upwards of fifty members sat down to an excellent repast provided by Mr. and Mrs. 'Allison 'which was followed by a most enjoyable smoking concert. The programme was contributed to by Captain Crosfield, Messrs. H. Sanders, J. Draper, T. liumphreys, and T. Healing. The toast of the President moved by Mr. S. Taylor, was enthusiastic- ally received and the hope was expressed that he Would continue to honour the Club in that Dosition for many years to come. The health of the vice-presidents was proposed by Mr. W. Haigh with 'aPpropriate reference, Mr. J. W. Kay responding. Following the distribution of prizes a testimonial in the shape of a handsome watch, subscribed by the members of the club was presented to Mr. J. T. Whittle, as a mark of esteem for the very valuable services rendered to the club during a period of 12 Years as secretary. He has now relinquished the Office to take up the treasurership of the club. THE NORTHERN UNION. NORTHERN LEAGUE. First Division. HULL V. RUNCORN. At Hull, before 7,000 spectators. Runcorn were short of several regular players. In a short time Goodfellow scored a try, the kick failing. Burchell crossed the line Harrison converting. Freear scored a try the kick failing, and Goodfellow also scored an unconverted try. On the r..start Freear scored a try, Goodfellow converting, and Hall also scored an unconverted try. Moran scored a try and a goal, and Walker a try, the kick failing. Butterworth kicked a penalty goal. Result :—Hull, 2 goals 6 tries (22 points) ; Runcorn, 2 tries 2 goals (10 points). WIDNES v. BATLEY. At Widnes, before 2,000 spectators. Both teams were well represented. Widnes pressed, but could not score. In the second half the 11,..me team had all the play, and Sam Aspey scored. after a rush by the forwards. All Taylor failed at the goal kick. Result—Widnes, 1 try (3 points) ; Batley, nil. OLDHAM v. HALIFAX. At Oldham, before 8,000 sppctators. Oldham attacked right through the game in vigorous style, but 35 minutes elapsed before Lees scored. In the second half Oldham were far the best. Cash scored twice and Williams once, and Fmter kicked a goal from a try. Albon kicked a penalty goal for Halifax. The feature of the game was the fine exhibition by M`Lean, Oldham's new centre. Result :—Oldham, 14 points ; Halifax, 2 points. WAKEFIELD TRINITY v. SWINTON. At Wakefield. The forwards played s magnificent game, and it was mainly through their fine efforts that Trinity gained the victory. Snlsles crossed for Wake- field, i3ennett landing the goal, while Metcalfe landed three goals. The backs were pretty evenly matched,but Swinton lost one or two good opportunities by failir g to accept passes. Result—Wakefield, 11 points ; Swinton, nil. SALFORD v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS. At Weaste, in fine weather, before 4,000 people. Salford attacked, and Clayton scored. Carmichael landed a penalty goal for Hull, and Lomas did the same for Salford. In the second half Salford pressed, and Thomas and Richards scored. Lomas kicked two goals and Carmichael one for the visitors. Result— Salford, 3 goals 3 tries (15 points) ; Hull Kingston Rovers, 2 goals (4 points). BRADFORD v. LEEDS. At Park-avenue,Bradford, before about 13,000 specta- tors. Thomas scored after passing, and later Littlewood kicked a penalty cool, Mosby doing the same twice for Bradford. On change of ends Bradford were 1 point behind, Greenwood putting them ahead with a try. Leeds pressed in the last 20 minutes. Result—Bradford goals 1 try (7 points) ; Leeds, 1 goal 1 try (5 points).
